Severe drought declared and hosepipe bans in force - is your area affected?

BBC News Thu, 15 Oct 2026 15:42:37 GMT

Severe drought has been declared in parts of southern England after months of dry weather drove some reservoirs to exceptionally low levels.

Most of England and all of Wales were already under drought conditions after both nations' hottest summers on record, which has taken its toll on rivers, crops and nature.

Roughly 30 million people across parts of England and Wales are covered by hosepipe bans, as part of water companies' efforts to manage supplies.

So how is your area doing and are you in a drought?

"Severe drought" - the highest category - has now been declared for parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex.

It means environmental authorities will ramp up monitoring of reservoir levels, river flows and water quality, as well as carry out extra checks on businesses withdrawing water from natural sources.

The "severe drought" classification was introduced following the 2012 drought and this is the first time it has been implemented.

The UK government says two previous events would have met the "severe drought" classification, had it been in place. They are:

Most of England and all of Wales were already in drought, following earlier announcements by the Environment Agency (EA) and Natural Resources Wales.

Parts of north-east and north-west England are in the category below drought, called "prolonged dry weather".

There are no official droughts currently in Northern Ireland.

There is no single definition of drought, but it is characterised by a period of low rainfall. As the ground dries out, crops and vegetation can begin to struggle.

If dry conditions persist, rivers, reservoirs and groundwater levels can also fall, putting pressure on water supplies.

The EA says that south-east and south-west England have experienced their driest April to September in more than a century.

Scotland does not declare droughts but monitors "water scarcity" - when there is not enough water of sufficient quality to meet demands of people and the environment.

While conditions have improved in parts of Scotland following recent rainfall, some south-eastern areas remain in the most extreme categories of "moderate" or "significant" scarcity, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.

Both drought and water scarcity can lead to hosepipe bans - officially called "temporary use bans" - if they are not already in place.

So far, 11 UK water companies have announced hosepipe bans in 2026. This means hosepipes cannot be used for watering gardens, washing vehicles and windows, and filling pools.

Ten companies are spread across central, southern and eastern parts of England, and one is in Wales.

Our three main sources of water are reservoirs, rivers and from deep underground.

A key reason why parts of southern England have entered "severe drought" is low reservoir levels.

At this time of year, the Environment Agency says it would expect England's reservoirs to be about three-quarters full, but they are just over half full on average.

Ardingly Reservoir in West Sussex and Wimbleball Reservoir in Somerset are among those at "exceptionally low" levels.

Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water says most reservoir levels in Wales are normal for the time of year.

And reservoir levels in Northern Ireland and Scotland are close to average, according to the latest available data.

Many of the UK's rivers have also been affected by the low rainfall.

Most monitored river flows in England were classed as "below normal", "notably low" or "exceptionally low" in July, according to the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH).

South-east England relies more heavily on groundwater than reservoirs. Groundwater originates as rainfall and is naturally stored beneath the surface in the pore spaces and fractures in rocks.

Groundwater levels are generally declining following the prolonged dry weather. In September, about half of monitored sites across the UK recorded levels considered "below normal" or lower, with southern England and Wales typically faring worst.

Water can flow more slowly through some rock types than others, sometimes taking years to fully respond to current conditions.

These groundwater stores "respond more slowly to changes in the climate than rivers, which is why they provide a useful buffer during periods of drought", said Prof Alan MacDonald of the British Geological Survey.

It is why groundwater droughts in the south of England generally take a longer time to develop but can be longer-lasting if they do occur.

Droughts are complex phenomena, driven by a mix of natural and human causes.

The Met Office expects the UK to experience drier summers on average in future as the world warms, though there has been no clear trend so far.

But rising temperatures can play a more direct role by drawing extra moisture from the soil via evaporation.

"A warmer atmosphere is thirstier for moisture and this can mean water in the soil, rivers and reservoirs are depleted more effectively, leading to more rapidly onsetting droughts, heatwaves and wildfires," said Richard Allan, professor of climate science at the University of Reading.

But there are other factors that determine whether dry conditions lead to water shortages, including how we use water.

In a landmark review into the water sector of England and Wales, water companies were criticised for historic underinvestment in water infrastructure.

And while spring and summer were relatively dry for much of the UK, winter was much wetter than usual, raising questions about how effectively water is being managed.

As part of plans to address water shortages, the government and water companies are planning nine new reservoirs for England by 2050, in addition to one under construction at Havant Thicket in Hampshire.

But the EA has warned that measures to tackle water leaks and control water demand - potentially including hosepipe bans - may be needed in England too.

Water companies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland - which are all public bodies or non-profit - also said they were taking steps to secure future supplies.

Walsh vomit & Ponga pain - the physical toll of World Cup opener

BBC News Thu, 15 Oct 2026 15:07:28 GMT

This video can not be played

Australia clinch thrilling World Cup opener against New Zealand

If anyone doubted the physical commitment of rugby league's greatest stars, they only needed to watch an exhausted Reece Walsh doubled up and vomiting during Thursday's epic World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand.

The Kangaroos' dramatic 24-22 victory in Sydney featured plenty of other examples of that commitment - aside from the normal rough and tumble this punishing sport regularly delivers.

New Zealand full-back Kalyn Ponga bravely battled on for 20 minutes with a suspected broken arm before almost having to be scraped off the pitch minutes before hat-trick hero Jack Bostock's winning try for Australia.

Mitchell Moses initially tried to run off a calf issue before being forced from the field just after the break, while Australia captain Isaah Yeo demonstrated his durability against a powerhouse Kiwis pack, having elected to delay surgery on his injured pectoral muscle just in order play in the tournament.

But understandably, much of the focus was on the star full-backs - Ponga and Walsh.

The Kangaroos number one was playing for the first time for eight weeks after recovering from an ankle injury.

Reece Walsh & Kalyn Ponga have both played for Queensland in State of Origin

Reece Walsh was Australia's star player in the 2025 Ashes series

And Walsh delivered a superb try-saving tackle on Ponga during the first half before scoring with a sensational 60-metre burst to lay the platform for the Kangaroos' last-gasp victory.

"Walshy was very good tonight, having not played for eight weeks," said Australia head coach Kevin Walters.

"I thought he was really good. That try-saving tackle he did is equal to anything that he can do an attack, and then he comes up with a couple of big plays in attack as well.

"He's cramping and vomiting and all sorts of things. He didn't have the energy to kick the goal. He's a chucker [he throws up]. People get nicknames and his nickname is 'Chucker'.

"He's not an endurance athlete. He's a power athlete and he had some big efforts there a couple of times, back-to-back and we've seen him do that before."

Yeo added: "For Reece to come back in a contest like that with some of those plays is a massive effort after not playing for eight weeks. It won't get spoken about enough, but it is really hard to do at this level.

"He has just got the ability to just make people miss. I think he made two people miss on the one move, but he's just one of those players that can just break a game open, and we probably needed that."

Australia edge New Zealand in epic World Cup opener

Kalyn Ponga (left) switched his international allegiance to New Zealand before the tournament

Having finally fulfilled a long-held desire to represent New Zealand, Ponga's night was going sweetly - he scored two tries that included one trademark run from deep and elusive step that left Walsh clutching at air - but it ended on a bitter note.

For one thing, Australia swiped victory from the grasp of Stacey Jones' team. For another, Ponga's future participation in the World Cup is now in serious doubt.

Speaking after the game, Jones admitted that the Newcastle Knights man would now have medical checks after playing on for a quarter of the contest with an injury sustained in a tackle with Cameron Munster.

"It's a possible fracture of the arm, but he's going to go for scans and we're not going to make a call on him right now where he's at," said Jones.

"He had a pretty good game.

"I think he played on for 20 minutes, he toughed it out. It's a tough one. They scored a try and that's when we were told what it possibly was and that he would have to come off.

"He couldn't catch the ball or anything like that. He was in a lot of discomfort."

Should Ponga be ruled out it would be a huge blow to New Zealand's hopes of winning a second World Cup, 18 years on from their first.

Was Neanderthal life violent? This wound suggests lethal fighting was more common

BBC News Thu, 15 Oct 2026 15:00:05 GMT

A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.

They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon.

From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole.

The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought.

Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens.

The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found.

A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology.

"The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News.

Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s.

The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy.

"It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone."

But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident.

But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation.

"The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said.

This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear.

We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival. But they join a small but growing body of evidence which point to the possibility that human-on-human violence was more common and goes back further than the current scientific consensus would suggest.

"I unfortunately see the growing body of evidence as an indication that interpersonal violence goes deep into human prehistory," Stringer told BBC News.

A key piece of that evidence is a study published in 2022 of very early Neanderthal skulls from northern Spain at an archaeological site called "the Pit of Bones". It suggests that deadly violence was taking place about 430,000 years ago.

Researchers found 57 healed head injuries among 20 individuals. Nine individuals had potentially fatal skull fractures. Six had similar puncture wounds at the back-left of the head. Because the wounds repeatedly occurred in almost the same place, the researchers concluded that deliberate blows were more likely than accidental damage. One skull had two wounds that had probably been inflicted with the same object.

The Pit of Bones findings do not show that everyone in this population was habitually violent, but they provide strong evidence that repeated killing occurred among these people hundreds of thousands of years ago.

For decades, many archaeologists linked the beginnings of organised warfare to farming, when people began living in permanent settlements and competing over land, livestock and food stores.

But evidence from earlier hunter-gatherers and still older human relatives has since shown that individual killings pre-date farming by a very long way.

The live scientific debate is over how common such violence was, and when sporadic attacks became organised conflict and wars between groups.

The research has been published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm

BBC News Thu, 15 Oct 2026 14:55:21 GMT

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.

Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.

Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal.

"We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said.

ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries".

The two companies announced in July that Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service.

The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix.

But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and regulator Ofcom, forcing an investigation into the tie-up.

In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the probe to address public interest considerations including:

The letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of those viewing news on linear TV.

Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added.

But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the linear TV news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV.

The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued.

This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added.

Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns.

A Sky spokesperson said: "We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices."

An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process.

"This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries."

Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration.

This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes.

She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes."

Infantino apologises to Fifa Council - but told he is still not fit to lead

BBC News Thu, 15 Oct 2026 14:46:09 GMT

This video can not be played

Fifa president Gianni Infantino admits he apologised at council meeting

President Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council for his World Cup sell-off plan - but has been told he is not fit to lead unless he releases all the documents and answers key questions.

The Fifa Council met in Zurich on Thursday for the first time since Infantino's secret Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal emerged.

Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of football's world governing body would have been given to a private investment firm.

In a three-and-a-half-hour meeting, Infantino also faced questions about US striker Folarin Balogun's suspended red-card ban, the Fifa Peace Prize and funding for national associations.

Hours later, Fifa released a video statement from Infantino. He had declined to speak to or take questions from the media, including the BBC.

In the Fifa video, he said: "First of all I apologised for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the Fifa Forward Enterprise project which led to many consequences.

"But what is important to remember is that it was a proposal and in no way a done deal, that actually intended to enable Fifa to invest more in our member associations, as opposed to replacing support from existing resources."

Infantino said he would answer questions in writing "in due course" following what he said had been a "constructive discussion" with "different opinions and points of view".

Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt - a Fifa vice-president - said afterwards that many questions remained unanswered despite the "most robust, most frank, most open Council meeting" she had experienced.

"One of the disappointing things is that we didn't get answers to anything that we had specifically requested - for example getting the papers from FFE," Hewitt said.

"I asked the question 'why not?' - and we were asked to submit those questions in writing.

"I think the man has to answer those questions and if he doesn't answer those questions now, he's not fit to be Fifa president - and that was what was shared in the meeting."

Hewitt added: "I've repeatedly asked for the papers to be shared. I haven't received them and still in spite of the request today, I haven't received them.

"It is the rationale for why FFE happened in the way that it did, the Balogun case, the Peace Prize.

"The responses to those questions, which I still don't have answers to, will determine from my personal point of view whether or not Gianni is the right candidate.

"That will be the point at which or not we can say that any individual that was involved in FFE can or cannot be trusted because until we see what actually happened it's very difficult to say behaviour needs or not to change."

Hewitt acknowledged there had been "some contrition" in Infantino's apology.

"Then there were no holds barred in terms of what we felt about what had happened," she added.

"What he really apologised for was not bringing it to the Council. If you regret it that deeply, share it with us."

Uefa - European football's governing body - has been one of Infantino's fiercest critics and has repeatedly called on him to stand down.

It has prepared criminal legal proceedings against Infantino and lodged a claim in three US courts for all documents related to FFE to be released.

Hewitt hopes Infantino now freely releases the documents so the Council can understand what happened.

"Those papers coming to Council are a crucial next part of us feeling comfortable as to what, if any, criminal proceedings need to take place," Hewitt said.

Asked if there was any change in stance from Uefa about Infantino, she added: "From my position, nothing has shifted. I've no new information that makes me feel any differently, other than we do have a president who is apologetic."

Gianni Infantino celebrated 10 years as Fifa president in February 2026

This video can not be played

'Nothing has changed' - FA chair on Infantino

Could Wenger really take on Infantino and run for Fifa presidency?

Infantino says he is open to talks over Fifa reform

Infantino will stand for re-election as Fifa president for a third time in March, and as yet no credible candidate has emerged to challenge the Swiss-Italian.

Former Tottenham and Switzerland defender Ramon Vega has said he intends to run, but it appears unlikely he will get the five letters of support from member associations let alone be a serious contender.

Senior figures within European football have told BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run.

But it is unclear whether Wenger would be prepared to give up his position as Fifa's global head of football development for a fight against his boss that he may not win.

Hewitt accepted Uefa - and Infantino's other opponents around the world - must find someone to put their name on the ballot before the deadline of 18 November.

She also indicated it would be important for the president to have a rival after being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.

"I think it's important to Gianni to have somebody who stands with a different manifesto, and good for Fifa to have that choice," Hewitt added.

"We're in a democracy here. We must remember there are 211 associations and it's really important that all 211 associations have the opportunity to vote according to how they feel.

"This is somebody first and foremost who puts football first right at the heart of everything that they do. Secondly, it has to be somebody who unites the world. Thirdly, somebody who needs to have the courage to bring about reforms."

Hewitt said Balogun avoiding a suspension after being sent off at the World Cup was one of the "biggest issues".

Balogun's ban was suspended after US President Donald Trump asked for the decision to be reviewed.

BBC Sport understands a proposal was put to the Council to amend the Fifa disciplinary code, which would prevent a repeat.

Under that, regulations would be amended to state the disciplinary committee could not suspend an automatic one-match ban for a red card.

Fifa's legal committee will review and update Fifa Council in December.

"What happened in July did not serve football... whether it's the Balogun case, the FFE case... the reputation of football was put under serious threat," said Hewitt.

"Once behaviour starts to influence what happens on the pitch, then I think it's a dark day for football and a number of people said that in the room."

The Fifa Peace Prize - awarded to President Trump - was also raised, but Hewitt said Infantino's behaviour with "other maybe celebrities and dignitaries" was also discussed.

"When he puts other dignitaries in front of his 211 associations, then he's lost what football is about," Hewitt said.

"And that was said by a number of people, not just the Europeans."

How the Peace Prize came to be awarded will be the subject of an investigation by the Fifa social committee which will report back in December.

"They will consider, first of all, how the Peace Prize came about, whether it should have come about, whether it should have been awarded in the way that it was, who made that decision and whether or not it should be taken out or whether it should be reformed," Hewitt said.

"That committee will report back to Council in December and then Council will make the decision based on its recommendation.

"Today there was a watershed moment where it's very clear in order to move forward, which we all want to do, we have to understand the past."

Everton's Thierno Barry on the video he was scared to post

BBC News Thu, 15 Oct 2026 11:27:07 GMT

Head in hands, tears flowing.

It's not a sight you often, if ever, see from a top-flight footballer.

Keeping calm under pressure comes with the job description, but there's a sense it's what's expected from fans and team-mates.

So when Everton striker Thierno Barry posted a video last month of him breaking down during a private training session, it sparked conversation around showing emotion in an industry where revealing any sort of vulnerability can be a risk.

BBC Newsbeat met the French footballer at the club's training ground to find out why he chose to show the raw moment - and how he's using it to drive forward.

"I was really scared about posting that.

"And I said: 'No, I just need to show myself'," says Barry of the video released on his YouTube channel last month.

"Last season I showed a version of me [that wasn't] me and [people] need to learn about me."

In the video, the 23-year-old is seen getting frustrated and upset about his performance.

He then leaves the private training session, where he begins to cry, as his team works to reassure him.

The next day, Barry is seen reflecting on how it felt positive to let go.

"Sometimes it feels good to just lose it," he says to the camera.

Barry reveals he sat on the video for three weeks before choosing to release it.

"It's the first time I cried in front of my friends, they always see me as a strong [person]," he says.

"I'm happy that I can show that moment. They know I care about the club and I care about playing good on the pitch."

A Premier League move from Villarreal for £27m at the age of 22 was always going to be a jump for the Lyon-born player - and fans expect a lot from new signings.

Everton ended up re-posting the clip from his vlog on their own feed, with the caption "emotional resilience".

Comments streamed in underneath urging the player to keep his head up.

He acknowledges the support he has received from fans and his club.

"The people around me helped a lot because, like I said, I'm really hard with myself and the people with me try to help me to be more positive."

And for Barry, any disapproval wouldn't reach the levels of his own inner-critic.

"I'm always harder with myself, and I just need to be sometimes more calm," he says.

"Like, you're a crying guy, and I just want to show that I'm strong to show that, because I'm not scared to show that.

"That's why I posted this video."

He also spoke about the early days of adjusting to a new club and home, something he describes as "really difficult".

"It's hard because it's the hardest league in the world. New league, a new language."

Last season he made 41 appearances and scored just eight goals.

This season he's already scored six.

"People can say I miss a lot of chances, but I also create a lot of chances," he says in his defence.

But he also knows the cost of not capitalising on chances.

"Every fan counts on you to score goals, so imagine you didn't score, you know, for three months like me [last season] it's difficult."

And he won't fully relax.

After Barry scored against Hull last weekend, he posted on his Instagram that he was "still learning".

"This season is more easy to switch because I know I have time on the pitch," he says.

"And I think when I miss that chance, seven minutes later, I have another opportunity to score. That's a real pressure.

"When I come to the ball, in my head, it's like time stops."

Barry is also finding time to celebrate on the pitch, even rolling back the years by bringing back the dab and hip-swinging celebrations.

As for his second year with the club, the 6ft 5in player says he wants to keep focus.

Does he see a call up to the French team any time soon?

"I didn't think a lot about that because for me it's like really far, you know?

"I just do my job, if something happens, something happens."

Professor shares 'most important thing to do' when someone is grieving

BBC News Thu, 15 Oct 2026 05:11:16 GMT

Knowing what to say or how to support someone after a bereavement can be difficult. Fear of saying the wrong thing or intruding at a sensitive time can leave people worried about getting it wrong and avoiding reaching out altogether.

But Dr Lesel Dawson, from the University of Bristol, said this is the worst thing people can do.

Speaking ahead of an annual Good Grief Festival that Dawson is co-director of, she said: "The most important thing when helping someone dealing with grief isn't what you say, but that you don't turn away.

"A simple acknowledgement like 'I'm so sorry and I'm here' can mean a great deal, and it's vital to let the grieving person lead - to follow their pace, their language and their need to talk about the person who died."

The associate professor in Literature and Culture also said people avoiding dealing with their own grief can create lifelong challenges.

Dawson's own understanding of grief was shaped by the stillbirth of her younger sister when she was eight years old and learning that for many years her mother blamed herself for the child's death.

"The way we avoid grief can be really harmful to us," Dawson said. "Being able to turn toward the pain of the experience is the only way we process what's happened."

She said the lack of conversation about grief meant it took "a while" to fully grasp what had happened.

Research commissioned by Marie Curie found that while 70% of people feel comfortable talking about death, far fewer have actually had those conversations with family, friends or healthcare professionals.

While her mother struggled to cope with the bereavement, Dawson found an interest in psychology and emotions.

But after Dawson's first son was born at 29 weeks and suffered complications linked to the premature birth, the loss of her sister and the memory of her mother's "great pain" came to the forefront of her mind.

When Dawson revisited the difficult topic of conversation with her mother after her own pregnancy experience, she realised that her mother "felt [the stillbirth] was her fault".

"I said to her, 'was it my fault that my son was born early?' and she said, 'no of course not'.

"I said, 'okay, why can you not show the same compassion to yourself and your own loss?'" Dawson told BBC Radio Bristol.

She added that feelings of blame and guilt were "very common" during bereavement and could lead to "destructive" coping mechanisms.

"The biggest myth about grief is that it happens in neat, orderly stages and that you eventually get over it," said Dawson.

"In reality, grief is messy, unpredictable and deeply individual. People move back and forth between feelings, and the idea of a tidy, linear process simply doesn't reflect how grief actually works."

Following her own experiences with grief, Dawson took up the role of co-director of Good Grief, a festival in Weston-super-Mare that aims to start and normalise conversations about death, dying and bereavement.

The festival, which begins later, offers a number of workshops, music events, talks and light installations until Sunday.

"Grief involves lots of emotions, it involves sadness, but also anger, numbness, jealousy, rage… they're not sequential.

"Everybody's individual. We have our own ways of grieving and coping and we have our own timelines," Dawson said.

If you or someone you know has been affected by the details raised in this story, advice on where to find help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.

Hundreds of IDF investigations into killings still have no public outcome, BBC Verify finds

BBC News Thu, 15 Oct 2026 05:00:23 GMT

BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of killing or injuring people in Gaza, Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Israel that it said it was investigating, but have no public outcome.

Using purpose-built AI tools, BBC Verify combed through more than 60,000 news reports and examined hundreds of incidents in which the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) faced allegations of harm since the start of the Gaza war. Following extensive manual checking of each incident, we found 300 cases that the military said it was looking into, only 28 of which had outcomes published on the IDF website. For a further 18 incidents it was unclear if the investigation has been concluded.

BBC Verify approached the IDF about each case multiple times but only received information on two incidents, which the IDF said are still under review. "The IDF takes every allegation or report raising concerns about conduct that may be inconsistent with the law or IDF directives with the utmost seriousness," it said in a statement.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which works in warzones to uphold the Geneva Conventions, publishes guidelines that state investigations into potential violations of international humanitarian law, whether criminal or otherwise, should be as transparent as possible.

Of the 254 incidents identified by BBC Verify, 158 occurred in Gaza, 48 in the West Bank and 32 in Lebanon. A further 16 took place in Israel or in IDF detention. All happened between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026, and at least one person was reportedly killed in more than 200 of them.

Some of the incidents without public outcomes date back to late 2023. One of the deadliest cases involved a strike on a school building in Gaza in August 2024 when at least 93 people were reportedly killed, including six women and 11 children.

For three years, the Israeli military has often responded to accusations of harm by stating an incident is being investigated in some form, for example that it is being "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined". Often, that is the last that is heard about a case.

A number of incidents have been escalated for criminal investigation by the IDF. Two that came under intense public scrutiny involved the killings of five-year-old Hind Rajab, and of 15 Palestinian Red Crescent emergency workers who were shot more than 100 times and allegedly targeted at close range.

The results of IDF military investigations are not routinely made public, including those leading to criminal investigations of its soldiers.

A number that have been published relate to hostages in Gaza who were allegedly killed as a result of Israeli operations. In some cases, the military has only announced it is investigating an incident after being approached by BBC Verify or other media organisations.

In August, the IDF published a rare report detailing internal probes into five incidents in Gaza, including the killings of Hind Rajab and the 15 Palestinian emergency workers, which it revealed had been escalated to criminal investigations.

In the three other cases, which involved the killings of seven aid workers from the World Central Kitchen (WCK) in an air strike and the killing of four Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) aid workers in two separate Gaza attacks, the IDF said it did not find a basis for or reasonable suspicion to begin a criminal investigation.

The report also stated Israel's General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM), which handles IDF investigations into "exceptional operational incidents", had completed the review of approximately 150 cases since the start of the war.

These cases have now been transferred to the IDF's Military Prosecution for examination, according to the report. The IDF did not outline what the 150 incidents were, and did not clarify whether they were separate to the cases identified by BBC Verify when asked.

Despite multiple requests, the IDF has not provided a transparent breakdown of the status of the 300 investigations identified by BBC Verify.

In a statement, the IDF said it "publishes information regarding the outcomes of investigations and examinations when possible, subject to legal and operational considerations, as well as restrictions relating to privacy and information security".

It added that certain incidents are examined through command-level operational reviews, which are "intended to establish the sequence of events, identify failures and draw lessons for the purpose of improving operational conduct and taking any necessary command measures".

The IDF also said that during the war it has taken disciplinary action in dozens of cases against soldiers who failed to meet the standards expected of them and acted contrary to IDF directives, including being removed from combat positions and from reserve service.

Freedom of Information data obtained by Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group, showed that between October 2023 and August 2024 at least 1,456 Gaza-related incidents were referred to the FFAM. Twelve of these reviews were completed and referred to the Military Advocate General (MAG) Corps, two of which resulted in criminal investigations.

Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din which has been monitoring military investigations since 2006, told BBC Verify that he believes the IDF will often try to "prolong" investigations. "They try to stretch out these processes to the point where people forget and people don't care about them," he said.

Janina Dill, a professor of international law at the University of Oxford, said that according to the Geneva Conventions a party to armed conflict has a responsibility to "investigate and potentially prosecute its own".

"That's the absolute clear bottom line," she added. "There are also guidelines for investigation, endorsed by the ICRC, so they have some authority. And they emphasise promptness, thoroughness, impartiality."

Eran Shamir-Borer, director of the Center for Security and Democracy at the Israeli Democracy Institute (IDI) and a former top lawyer for the IDF, said there are "genuine challenges" investigating allegations in conflicts Israel is involved in, given the complex combat environments.

"[In] a territory which is hostile, not always under your control, collecting evidence could be very challenging. Lots of forces on the ground, many of them executing fire," he said.

Shamir-Borer added: "The idea of investigating soldiers in the context of a war is never a popular thing to do," which he said is also seen in other law abiding countries.

He added that Israel would only benefit from being more transparent about its investigations, and he would encourage the IDF to be "more forthcoming with information that they are sharing with the public on the progress they are making in investigating various allegations".

Since the Hamas-led attacks in Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage, the IDF has carried out extensive military operations in Gaza which it said aimed to bring back the hostages and dismantle Hamas.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the war, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.

BBC Verify has reported on the killing of emergency workers and people trying to access aid inside Gaza, the levelling of thousands of buildings in the strip and incidents of alleged misconduct carried out by Israeli soldiers over the last three years.

Just two months into the war, two women were killed by Israeli troops in the only Catholic church in the territory in December 2023, during an incident that the IDF later said was under review.

A mother, Nahida Anton, and her daughter, Samar Anton, were killed by sniper fire inside the grounds of the Holy Family church in Gaza, according to the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem.

BBC Verify contacted the IDF about the report at the time. The military said that an initial review suggested troops had been operating against a Hamas threat they had identified "in the area of the church". The IDF added that it was "conducting a thorough review of the incident".

In September 2025, BBC Verify asked for an update on the review and was told that the incident was "still being reviewed by the FFAM".

Now, almost three years since Nahida and Samar were killed, the IDF has again said the incident is under review.

Following the latest request for information, the IDF said: "Complex incidents may require considerable time to collect, cross-check, and verify the relevant factual information."

It added: "The IDF does not shorten or forgo examination or investigative procedures in order to meet external timelines."

One of the deadliest incidents that remains under investigation by the Israeli military is an air strike carried out on a school building in eastern Gaza city in August 2024.

The Hamas-run civil defence agency said at least 93 people, including six women and 11 children, were killed in the strike on the Tabaeen school complex and nearby mosque.

The buildings had been housing displaced Palestinians when multiple Israeli strikes hit the area at the time of dawn prayers. Videos verified by the BBC of the aftermath showed a cloud of dust as emergency workers worked their way through small fires, rubble and body parts strewn on the floor. Photos taken in daylight showed blood-soaked floors, debris and people's clothes scattered around.

Experts told BBC Verify munition fragments visible at the scene matched that of a GBU-39 - a precision-guided bomb supplied by the US to the Israeli military.

The IDF at the time said a Hamas command and control centre had been embedded in the school building, and that IDF soldiers killed 31 fighters in the incident. It added that according to an "initial review" the casualty numbers did not align with the information held by the IDF, the precise munitions used and the accuracy of the strike. The IDF told BBC Verify this incident remains under review.

BBC Verify also looked into incidents the IDF said it was investigating in the West Bank. Israel has occupied the territory since the 1967 war and built dozens of settlements there, which is illegal under international law.

More than 1,000 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces since 11 October 2023, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. BBC Verify examined more than 50 IDF investigations into incidents in the territory, at least 26 of which involved women and children being killed or injured.

One of those incidents took place just outside of Jenin in September 2024, when Israeli forces reportedly killed 16-year-old Lujain Musleh during an Israeli operation.

Lujain's father said she was shot in the head as she looked out of the window at her house in Kafr Dan, after soldiers had surrounded a neighbouring house.

The Israeli military said at the time that armed fighters had fired on the soldiers, who had "fired back at a suspect who observed" them, and that the details of the incident were under review.

BBC Verify also found nearly 40 IDF investigations into incidents of harm in Lebanon.

The Shia Muslim armed group Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel in support of Hamas following the 7 October attacks. Israel has since launched two major invasions into Lebanon, where more than 4,000 people have been killed according to the country's health authorities.

One IDF investigation identified by BBC Verify took place on 10 November 2024. An Israeli strike killed 23 people, including seven children, near the city of Byblos, according to the Lebanese health ministry.

Verified footage of the aftermath showed smoke rising between rubble and warped metal strewn across the ground where buildings had been destroyed. The IDF said at the time it had targeted a site where Hezbollah had been operating from and storing weapons, and that the incident was under review.

Michael Schmitt is a professor of international law at the University of Reading who has previously worked closely with the IDF. He said the Israeli military's legal division is the "gold standard in terms of understanding the law", and added that "every allegation that there was a violation does not necessarily trigger a full-blown investigation".

Schmitt said there can be a number of reasons why the IDF may be unable to publicly reveal the details of an investigation or a decision not to pursue one. "For example, you do not want to reveal operational details or particular rules of engagement because the enemy forces will adapt," he said, adding: "And even if you did pursue an investigation, many elements of [it] would remain confidential."

Dill, who is also a co-director of the Oxford Institute for Ethics, Law and Armed Conflict (ELAC), said: "Three years into this operation, some of these investigations should have been concluded."

She said that when it comes to investigating incidents of harm, "Israel has relied heavily on the argument that it is a rule-of-law country to delegitimatise attempts by the international community to investigate".

"If we have cases of documented abuse that either don't get investigated or the investigations get stuck, and we have reasonable grounds to believe that they get kicked into the long grass, then that would undermine the narrative that Israel is fully capable of taking care of providing accountability," she added.

BBC Verify gathered 61,000 reports from BBC News and Reuters which mentioned Gaza, the West Bank or Lebanon, published between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026.

We built an AI search engine to look through those reports for incidents where people may have been injured or killed by Israeli forces, and where the IDF said the report was being investigated, or for example "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined".

This identified almost 5,000 reports. Each one was manually checked by BBC Verify reporters, who excluded any which did not meet the criteria above.

This left 1,343 reports of incidents that the IDF said it was looking into. Some of these reports described the same incidents.

We built another AI tool to remove these duplicate reports. It grouped reports into unique incidents based on the publication date, incident date, location, and numbers reported injured or killed.

We then manually checked that each report had been assigned to the correct group, leaving us with 300 unique incidents.

For each of these incidents we then manually checked our records including the incident date, location, and how many people were killed or injured against the original BBC News or Reuters report.

We shared the details of each case with the IDF including the incident date, location, the news report describing the incident, and the IDF's original comment indicating it was looking into the matter. We asked the IDF for comment and the latest status of each case. The IDF did not say whether any of these investigations had concluded in response to the BBC's requests.

For each incident we also looked for statements on the IDF's website suggesting that the investigation had been concluded, using two different AI assisted web search engines. We found evidence that 28 cases were closed based on statements detailing the findings or indicating that no further steps would be taken.

For a further 18 incidents, it was unclear whether the investigation had been concluded. This included cases where the IDF published initial information about the incident without a clear indication it was closed, and cases where the IDF had characterised some or all of the people killed or injured as combatants, in statements on its own website.

This left us with at least 254 incidents of harm the Israeli military had said it was looking into, for which we did not find a public outcome on the IDF's website.

This was not an exhaustive search, and it is likely that there are more investigations into incidents of harm that were not captured in our search.

Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler.

I'm 12 and I want to try protein powder - should I?

BBC News Thu, 15 Oct 2026 00:00:35 GMT

Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum.

"I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!", he says, claiming it would make him "fitter and bigger" and that his male friends use it.

In recent years, there's been an explosion of products marketed as "high protein", including milk, yoghurt, breads, cereals, bars and powders.

Social media is flooded with adverts for various supplements, including protein powder.

As a health journalist, I'm sceptical and think at Ben's age he must be getting enough protein through his diet.

So, do experts think it's safe for pre-teens and teenagers or is a big, juicy steak just as good?

My sport-obsessed son, who already eats a healthy balanced diet, asks me about protein powder on a regular basis.

His friend Louis, 12, has been using protein powder once or twice a week for nearly a year, after a workout and on top of whole foods. His parents are aware of this.

"I think it's helped, it gives me more energy and it's helped me grow, probably," he says.

But Ben's other friend Otis, who is 13, is not keen on the idea and feels there is pressure on young people to take protein supplements.

"They might just start using them without thinking about the consequences or what effects it may have on them."

Proteins break down into amino acids that help the body grow and repair.

But your body can't make all the amino acids it needs on its own, so you need to get more - known as essential amino acids - through your diet.

For an adult with a healthy weight, the recommended daily amount of protein you should be eating is 0.75 grams per kg of body weight, according to the NHS.

A good rule of thumb is that the amount of protein you have for each meal should fit into the palm of your hand.

If you exercise a lot, and when you get older, you need more protein so you could have up to 2 grams per kg of body weight.

But do teens really need it if they're eating well?

For teenage boys and girls "you can get all the protein that you need from food alone", says registered dietitian Nichola Ludlam-Raine.

It is important that teenage girls, especially, get enough iron and calcium, so Ludlam-Raine says not to become overly focused on protein at the expense of other nutrients.

Protein shakes, powders or bars can be useful for some, including high-level athletes and those who have certain allergies, but they should not replace a healthy diet.

There can also be some unwanted side effects from using protein powders such as bloating, gas, cramps, and diarrhoea.

Those with pre-existing health conditions should not use it unless they have been told they can by their doctor.

Ludlam-Raine points out that the protein powder market is not as tightly regulated as medicines.

"Of course, you can get reputable companies who do third-party testing and make sure that what you see on the label is what is in the inside, but that's not always the case," she says.

"And ultimately you can't just have a shake and your biceps grow."

Some protein powders contain high amounts of added sugar, artificial ingredients, and hidden stimulants.

Dr Ramnik Mathur is a consultant paediatrician from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Trust.

He explains that we need micronutrients like zinc, calcium and magnesium, which are found in whole foods.

So, if meals are replaced with protein shakes, those nutrients are lost.

Experts suggest spreading out protein across the day and aiming for 20-25g per meal. If you're keen to up your intake, try some of these recipes.

During puberty when children have growth spurts, they do need more protein because their body is growing rapidly, building new muscle and bone mass.

But Mathur says there are risks to eating too much protein.

"If you look at social media, they'll say you need to eat a lot of protein, but your body can handle only so much."

He explains that if you eat too much, it has to be excreted by the kidneys and liver which can become overloaded.

Mathur explains: "We had a child here at the hospital where I work - he was taking so much protein that his kidneys just stopped working and he actually passed away."

The key takeaway from Mathur: "If a 12-year-old child is eating a healthy balanced diet then they shouldn't need any more protein."

Ludlam-Raine's advice is to get teens to improve their diet first before taking any protein powder, especially regularly.

If they still want to use it, speak to a registered dietitian or nutritionist first.

Now off I go to tell my son the answer is still no - and the experts say the same.

Antarctica’s ‘doomsday’ glacier will keep melting even if oceans cool

New Scientist October 15, 2026

The world’s widest glacier – Thwaites glacier in Antarctica – is already collapsing at an alarming rate due to ocean warming, with worrying implications for global sea-level rise. Now, a new study shows that it will continue to lose ice for at least the next 150 years, even under the impossible scenario of extremely cool oceans.

This means that future ice loss from the glacier is unavoidable, even under the most optimistic climate mitigation scenarios.

Dubbed the “doomsday glacier”, this vast mass of ice is roughly the size of Great Britain or the state of Florida. Together with the neighbouring Pine Island Glacier, it’s the area of Antarctica losing the most ice, mainly due to melting by the warmer ocean waters.

Advertisement

The race to understand how and when Thwaites glacier will collapse

“The Pine Island and Thwaites glaciers are the biggest contributors to sea level rise in Antarctica at the moment, and they’re losing ice at an increasing rate,” says Rosie Williams of the British Antarctic Survey.

If Thwaites glacier collapses completely, it is expected to trigger a more widespread loss of the ice sheet covering West Antarctica, causing a calamitous sea level rise of 5 metres. So determining how it behaves in future is crucial.

To explore this, Williams and her colleagues “did something quite wild”, she says. In three different computer models of the ice sheet, they turned off all ocean-driven melting – an impossible condition in reality, even under the most extreme ocean cooling scenarios – and watched what would happen over the next 150 years. The aim was to see the future trajectory of Thwaites glacier and Pine Island glacier, even without warming oceans.

Free newsletter

Surprisingly, the glaciers followed opposite paths. Pine Island glacier re-advanced and became more stable. “But with Thwaites glacier, we found something really different,” says Williams. Over the entire 150 years of the simulations, the glacier continued to lose ice, even though the rate of loss slowed over time. “Our general expectation was …that if you turned off that ocean melting, the ice would be able to thicken and re-advance. It’s somewhat of a surprise that Thwaites glacier can’t do that.”

The researchers think that Thwaites is still being affected by extreme El Niño conditions in the 1940s which destabilised Antarctica’s glaciers and kick-started their retreat. “We’re still seeing some effect of that playing out today with Thwaites. [Glaciers] are really slow-moving. They have a long memory,” she says.

On top of this, human-induced climate change has probably accelerated the melt, says Ted Scambos at the University of Colorado Boulder, who wasn’t involved in the analysis. “Ocean heat delivered to the base of the ice …. over the past four decades or so, as a result of anthropogenic warming, has pushed the Thwaites system into an inherently unstable configuration,” he says.

Warmer ocean is driving the Antarctic sea ice ‘regime shift’

But despite future ice loss being locked-in, this doesn’t mean that strategies to reduce climate change and ocean warming are futile. “Almost the opposite,” says Williams. “Under the zero-melt scenario, [Thwaites glacier] still loses ice, but the more warming you have in the ocean, the faster that ice is lost, so it’s still really essential to bring down our emissions and control that rate of ice loss.”

“Every fraction of a degree really matters for trying to preserve these glaciers into the future, which matters for all of us, in terms of sea level rise globally,” says Williams.

The temperature of the ocean adjacent to Thwaites glacier is projected to rise at triple the historic rate throughout the 21st century, leading to increased ice melting. The big worry is that this may trigger a doomsday scenario of run-away collapse of Thwaites glacier that, in turn, would trigger the collapse of the whole of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet in a process called marine ice sheet instability.

The floating ice shelf of world’s widest glacier – Thwaites glacier in Antarctica – is detaching, with worrying implications for global sea-level rise

Here, the study by Williams and her colleagues offers slight hope. “We haven’t crossed the point of no return,” says Mattieu Morlighem of Dartmouth College, New Hampshire, who was not involved with the study. “In the best case scenario…if melt from the ocean stops, Thwaites doesn’t… lead to a collapse of the West Atlantic ice sheet.”

The big question for the future is what happens with realistic ocean temperatures, says Williams, who is now working on this.

Meanwhile, another study published this week revealed other worrying news about Thwaites glacier. A more precise model of how the glacier interacts with the ocean indicates that it might retreat more rapidly than previously thought, potentially contributing to double the sea-level rise previously projected.

Making quantum computers error-proof is one of the biggest challenges currently facing the technology. Researchers at Google Quantum AI have now demonstrated one way to do so more efficiently. Their work suggests the smaller quantum computers that will be available in the next few years could be more impactful than expected.

Quantum computers can run mathematical operations, analogous to addition or multiplication, that conventional computers cannot. This makes them suitable for solving some problems that had previously been considered unsolvable, such as those that underpin cryptography.

Most important among the quantum operations the computers run are “non-Clifford gates”, which are the key ingredients for algorithms that transcend conventional computation.

Advertisement

We may finally have a way to rate a quantum computer’s usefulness

But there is a problem. Quantum computers are very error-prone, and their building blocks, called qubits, must be encoded into special groups, or “logical qubits”, before they can execute operations reliably. Executing non-Clifford gates in an error-corrected way requires large numbers of qubits, which means having to build very large quantum computers – a formidable engineering challenge.

Now, Emma Rosenfeld at Google Quantum AI and her colleagues have used the firm’s Willow quantum computer to show that the error-correction process can be made more efficient. Their new technique ultimately reduced Willow’s errors 40 times.

At the centre of their advance is the idea of a “magic state”, which is a special quantum state that qubits must assume before the quantum computer can run error-corrected non-Clifford operations. Creating these states had, so far, been a real bottleneck for quantum computing, says Rosenfeld. “It eats up a lot of qubits and a lot of time,” she says.

Free newsletter

In 2024, her colleagues at Google Quantum AI proposed a more efficient method for creating magic states called “magic state cultivation”. Here, instead of many imperfect qubits being repeatedly combined and manipulated into a magic state that is then put towards running an error-corrected operation, the magic state is “grown” within a smaller patch of qubits.

The Google researchers showed that magic state cultivation could, in theory, enable quantum computers to run consequential programs with just one-tenth the number of qubits we had expected they would need. The new experiment by Rosenfeld and her colleagues proves that magic state cultivation works in practice.

This is not the first time that new methods for making magic states have lowered a quantum computer’s error rates. Advances in creating magic states and error-correcting non-Clifford gates have also been achieved in experiments with quantum computers that have qubits based on ions. Willow’s qubits, which are based on tiny superconducting circuits, achieved error rates similar to those past experiments, but Rosenfeld says that they work more quickly, potentially reducing the quantum computer’s overall runtime.

A quantum computer made from extremely cold atoms can correct its own errors during long computations, an important prerequisite for becoming truly useful

“This is an impressive demonstration of a promising recent idea pioneered by Google,” says Isaac Kim at the University of California, Davis. “It’s an approach that can make fault-tolerant quantum computing substantially cheaper.” The new work demonstrates one of the building blocks necessary for universal quantum computing and could be a “gamechanger” in terms of building intermediately sized quantum computers with hundreds of logical qubits, says Dominik Hangleiter at ETH Zurich in Switzerland.

Zhenyu Cai at Imperial College London says that while this experiment is a significant step forward, Willow’s errors will need to be reduced further before it can tackle truly useful problems. Additionally, Kim says that in the experiment, Willow generated good magic states only for a fraction of its computational runs: only 8 per cent of Willow’s computations produced high-quality magic states that could then be put into further use.

Rosenfeld says that this percentage ought to increase as she and her colleagues refine the technique and improve Willow’s hardware. It is, in this case, also affected by a very careful benchmarking technique that the team used, which may not be used in future applications, she says. “This is the first demonstration that the concepts work. We’re not done.”

The world’s thickest glaciers may “calve” icebergs up to three times faster than previously predicted. However, such rapid retreat may not be sustained over long periods.

Instead, the large bodies of ice – which include Antarctica’s Thwaites glacier – may collapse in bursts, with intervening periods of stability.

The behaviour of tall ice cliffs is one of the biggest sources of uncertainty in predicting future sea level rise. Several of the world’s largest glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica extend out to sea, with their bases resting on the sea floor. Their coastal edges can form ice cliffs looming as high as 100 metres above the ocean’s surface.

Advertisement

The race to understand how and when Thwaites glacier will collapse

For years, researchers have feared that such marine-based glaciers might be vulnerable to runaway cliff collapse. The idea here is that each time an ice cliff collapses, it exposes a new, taller – and so potentially even less stable – ice cliff further towards the glacier’s interior. The loss of ice due to runaway collapse of these ever-taller cliffs could potentially double the amount of sea level rise expected over the next 100 years, according to an Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change report. But we don’t yet have enough empirical data to know how likely it is that runaway cliff collapse will occur, so previous studies have relied on ideal mathematical models to envision the process instead.

Caroline Needell at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology-Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute Joint Program and her colleagues used satellite data to provide the first direct, large-scale observations of how the tallest ice cliffs actually behave, offering a firmer basis for estimating the danger of runaway collapse – and the rapid sea level rise that could result.

According to the study, the risk of runaway collapse depends on two main factors: how steeply the sea floor beneath the glacial ice deepens, and how quickly the ice flows seawards. Imagine an up-ended jar of thick honey spilling onto a plate: it won’t remain in a tall, stable shape, but will thin outwards at the edges. In a similar way, if the viscous flow of ice is fast enough, it will thin out the edge of a glacier, reducing cliff height. Even if the glacier is thicker further towards its interior, sufficiently rapid ice flow appears able to compensate, lowering those ice cliffs and preventing a runaway effect.

This idea has been suggested by idealised mathematical models, but had never been systematically measured in real glaciers. “None of the glaciers we observed underwent unstable retreat, even though they did retreat much faster than our current models predict,” says Needell.

That retreat could speed up even further in the future. Needell notes that most glaciers in the study are “buttressed” by sea-floor features. For instance, a series of underwater ridges currently help stabilise Thwaites from beneath.

“Over the next decades, it’s going to jump from one pinning ridge to another,” almost like “tripping” downhill, says Douglas Benn at the University of St Andrews in the UK. Eventually, Thwaites will reach a point where those ridges disappear. “The bed then begins to get real deep,” says Benn. At that point, which the glacier may reach within the current century, “the whole structural integrity of the ice becomes unviable”.

The floating ice shelf of world’s widest glacier – Thwaites glacier in Antarctica – is detaching, with worrying implications for global sea-level rise

That is when runaway collapse becomes a real possibility. However, those conditions may also speed up the flow of ice, thus thinning out any looming cliffs. The key question, says Needell, is whether thinning can outcompete rapid ice loss, restabilising the glacier. Her study suggests that it might – but the question remains open.

Robert Larter at the British Antarctic Survey points out that we haven’t yet seen this kind of runaway cliff collapse. One study suggests that it may have happened in the vicinity of Thwaites around 12,000 years ago. “The problem is, nobody was around to take observations at the time,” he says. “It’s a possibility we have to keep our eye on.”

The remains of a Neanderthal recently discovered in a cave in Iraq demonstrate the excruciating brutality of life in the Palaeolithic. The Neanderthal had a severely smashed but healed jaw and a spear hole straight through their shoulder, which is evidence of a likely fatal injury.

However, given that survival after such a massive, earlier dental injury would only have been possible with long-term care, the remarkable find may also provide early evidence of compassion, says Emma Pomeroy at the University of Cambridge.

“We sometime romanticise hunter-gatherer or pre-agriculture lifestyles as peaceful and close to the natural world, or at the other extreme, we think of life in the Palaeolithic as [Thomas] Hobbes described it,” says Pomeroy. In 1651, the political philosopher Hobbes wrote about life in ungoverned societies as “solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short”. “But it’s not that simple, and both are extreme stereotypes,” she says.

Advertisement

What the remains of the last Neanderthals tell us about their demise

The 75,000-year-old partial skeleton, known as Shanidar A, was recovered in 2019 and 2022 from the Shanidar cave in northern Iraq and consists of a largely complete right hand, two left ribs, a right rib fragment, a left scapula and six teeth. At least five Neanderthal individuals have been found at Shanidar since it was first excavated in the 1950s, and the way they were placed in the ground is often seen as evidence that these ancient humans buried some of their dead.

While the sex of Shanidar A couldn’t be determined, the wear on the teeth suggested that the remains were those of an individual who lived to be about 45 years old – a long life by Neanderthal standards.

They must have been hit very hard in the face at some point in their life, which made one of their bottom front teeth split in half and also probably fractured their jaw, says Pomeroy.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The broken edge of the tooth became covered in hardened plaque, showing they continued living afterwards without that part of the tooth.

But, says Pomeroy, the person must have been in terrible pain. Although there is evidence from other archaeological sites that Neanderthals used mild, natural painkillers, “I don’t think they would have touched this pain”, she says.

Such a dental injury would have also made it difficult to eat, drink or talk, and would almost certainly have required a period of intensive care from the individual’s group, she says.

“The half tooth that remained in their mouth must have stuck out through the bone and the gums, meaning the hardened plaque, known as calculus, formed all over the top and bottom of the tooth,” says Pomeroy.

She says the force of the blow also made the teeth next to the broken one rotate slightly.

Shanidar A’s scapula, or shoulder blade, had also survived – and the team were stunned to see that it carried a perfectly round hole that was probably made by a wooden spear rather than a stone-tipped weapon.

Genetic clues tell the story of Neanderthals’ decline

The location of bone fragments also recovered from Shanidar A’s remains indicate that the spear entered the individual’s body on the left-hand side while they were facing forward.

The team says such an injury would have “penetrated all the way through the chest, including the lungs and potentially major blood vessels, likely leading to a rapid death”.

What is unknown is whether the injury was sustained while hunting or through violence.

Palmira Saladié, at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution in Spain, wasn’t part of the team but recently helped discover the remains of wooden Neanderthal spears at site called Abric Romaní near Barcelona.

She says Neanderthals, like us, were complex beings, capable of very different behaviours depending on the circumstances.

“What I find most striking about Shanidar is how it brings together two seemingly opposite sides of human behaviour,” says Saladié. “We have evidence of lethal violence, but also evidence of care for injured individuals and complex funerary practices.”
