4 of the most memorable biotech moments in modern scientific history

New Scientist October 15, 2026

Born two years before me, New Scientist has documented unprecedented change since 1956 – the moon landings, nuclear energy, the digital age. It was my privilege to greet such whirlwind change during my time on the newsdesk from 1986 to 2018, a period that had no shortage of big discoveries, especially on the medical and biotechnology beat. I noisily (and literally) banged out my earliest stories on a typewriter, in an age of journalism that depended on telephones, notebooks, shorthand, faxes and a lot of red ink. Now, journalists can rapidly check facts and find expert sources on the internet – a real perk, amid the industry’s new challenge from AI.

Trustworthy science journalism is more essential than ever

Whatever happens, I’m sure New Scientist will always be there reporting truthfully from the forefront of science and technology – just like I did during these four of my most-memorable stories from my time writing up the world’s biggest science news.

Gobsmacked! Udder madness! That’s how I and colleagues reacted after scanning Nature’s press release in early 1997 about the creation of Dolly, the first animal cloned from mature bodily tissue. This was biological heresy. It challenged the textbook rule that once cells have developed into a particular bodily tissue – in Dolly’s case, udder tissue – it is a one-way street and they can’t be rewound backwards to their origins in the embryo.

Advertisement

But that is what the team under Ian Wilmut at the Roslin Institute in Scotland had done. They succeeded by implanting the udder cell in a sheep egg emptied of its original nucleus. Given an electric pulse, biochemical factors in the egg completely rewound the udder cell back to an embryo, which then became Dolly after implantation in a foster mother’s womb. We recognised immediately this was very big news, and prepared a multi-page news splash for the coming issue of New Scientist.

Could the super-rich be cloning themselves? And why would they?

The breakthrough prompted a media frenzy. Not surprisingly, the focus was on whether people could be cloned in the same way from their own tissue. Suddenly, we had dire predictions of dictators cloning their way to worldwide domination. More positively, some scientists speculated that the cloning method could potentially yield fresh, limitless tissue from patients themselves for transplant or grafts, avoiding risks of tissue rejection. But anti-abortion groups raised objections to any kind of human cloning, on the basis that it would require tinkering around with human eggs.

Moral panic over Dolly continued for a while – a UFO religion in Canada called the Raelians even claimed they had plans in place to clone a dead girl – but the fuss eventually fizzled out as the limitations of the technique emerged. Dolly herself was the only successful birth from 277 rewound udder cells, and a 2004 claim of the first cloned human embryos by Wu Suk Hwang turned out to be fraudulent.

After all the hype and hope, the Dolly technique simply failed to deliver the goods and, other than niche applications such as cloning pets and rare animals, it gradually faded from the limelight.

The unveiling of the first draft of the human genome was a monumental landmark following a 10-year marathon sequencing effort. “The most wondrous map ever produced by mankind”, as US president Bill Clinton described it, was simultaneously announced by him at the White House and UK prime minister Tony Blair at 10 Downing Street, but I didn’t get to visit either place. Instead, I and dozens of other journalists watched the synchronised video conference from the London headquarters of the Wellcome Trust – an exciting moment indeed, although I do wish we could have been at Number 10 instead.

The draft genome was originally scheduled for completion in 2005 but arrived five years early in part thanks to gene entrepreneur Craig Venter whose private company, Celera Genomics, developed a faster way to sequence DNA. His entry into the fray sparked a race with the multinational, publicly funded Human Genome Project that had been running since 1990, prompting the latter to accelerate its efforts for fear that the genome sequence would otherwise become privately owned. In the end, it was more-or-less declared a draw, with both versions of the draft published simultaneously, and the credit shared across both efforts. Although we quizzed him about it afterwards, it took nearly two years for Venter to admit that the draft genome he sequenced was largely his own.

Most detailed human genome sequence yet reveals our hidden variation

It was all very exciting, but everyone knew it would take many years to unravel how our 3 billion base pairs of DNA actually function, and how this might help us tackle disease and chart our evolution. Some of the first surprises included the puzzlingly low number of genes we appeared to have (although we now know that this was an underestimate), and discoveries of seemingly simpler organisms like fish and ferns that have far bigger genomes than us. Although it took time to reap big benefits from the genome, in the 26 years since it was published it has gone on to provide huge insights into human diseases and how to treat them, from cancer to covid-19, as well helping to reveal our evolutionary history and what makes us human.

More than 20 years on, I can remember the name of the recipient of the first ever face transplant without having to look it up. Isabelle Dinoire suffered damage to her face when her dog tried to wake her after she had taken sleeping pills. A surgical team in France, led by Jean-Michel Dubernard, said that a transplant was the only way her lips and chin could be restored and rewired into her nervous system, a procedure that would also restore the muscular function she needed to speak and eat.

It was a privilege to report on this astonishing breakthrough. Think about it! You’re taking a face from someone who has died and putting it on someone who has never looked like that before. The recipient, their family and that of the donor all have to get their heads around that. And then there is the medical complexity of detaching a face from one person and then grafting it – skin, flesh, nerves, muscles – to someone else.

The transplant was considered a success, and a few months later, Dinoire shared that she was beginning to recover much of the function of her face.

The success of Dinoire’s operation prompted other teams to try, and a review in 2025 by the American College of Surgeons reported that by then, 54 had been performed globally, mostly with some degree of success. Dinoire herself died of cancer in 2016 aged 49, but I’ll never forget her name or her bravery.

Like the other journalists in the room, I didn’t get a bite of the first lab-grown burger to be consumed in public at a press conference in London, but it was fun to watch. The burger had cost £250,000 and five years of research to get to that point, and was sampled by Hanni Rützler, an Austrian nutrition scientist. She said its flavour was “intense”, but that the texture lacked the fattiness of real beef. At the time, fellow journalists harrumphed about not getting a bite, and were mostly dismissive that it was all theatre, no substance.

There was, however, huge interest in producing meat in giant fermenters – a way to cut the heavy environmental and ethical costs of producing meat. But 13 years on, I’m still waiting for my chance to take a bite of a lab-grown burger. While the field is still pushing forwards – there are a few places in the world where you can track down lab-grown chicken strips, for example – any progress has seemed glacial, and there are now many cheaper and easier-to-produce fake meat options made from plants like soya. I guess I’ll just have to keep waiting.

That is, if you can persuade anyone to watch it with you – not a single person of my acquaintance took up the spare ticket I had on offer, or even made it through the stomach-churning trailer.

The unfortunate star of our story is Jay, played by the up-and-coming Austin Abrams, whose recent roles could all be described as “a guy having the worst day of his, or anyone’s, life”. Jay is no natural diver, but his father, Mitt (an especially grizzled Josh Brolin), has subjected him to unwanted trips beneath the waves his entire life. Mitt is at once a belligerent silverback hammering nails of survival knowledge into his son’s brain and a spiritualist attuned to the rhythms of the California coastline where he lives, especially the local whales.

Advertisement

As Jay reaches adulthood and Mitt’s worsening health prevents him from diving, their relationship sours further and the two become estranged. Their rift never gets a chance to heal because, not long after Jay moves to Iowa to continue his studies, Mitt takes his own life by jumping into the sea. On the anniversary of Mitt’s death, Jay returns home and resolves to find his father’s lost remains.

None of this angst is rendered on screen with particular grace, but this didn’t initially bother me. The film needed a reason to put Jay in a whale and to give him the strength to try to get out, and a boilerplate father-son trauma plot certainly lets us get to the good stuff as quickly as possible. Accordingly, it doesn’t take long for Jay’s dive to go south – caught up in a whale’s pursuit of a squid, he is buffeted into its gaping maw. It is a testament to Whalefall’s strengths that this scene still feels agonising even when you know it’s coming.

Somehow, Jay’s situation manages to get worse once he is inside the whale. To avoid spoiling the exact nature of these travails, let’s just say he isn’t the only creature the whale has swallowed up, and things get increasingly bloody. All of this is terrifically gruesome, as is the claustrophobia-inducing movement of the whale’s digestive tract, squeezing and chewing Jay’s fragile form. If anyone has further examples of this “peristaltic horror” subgenre, do send them my way.

Once Jay is able to calm himself down, he hatches a plan to escape using only his diving gear, the jetsam in the whale and his memories of his father’s teachings. It’s an odd mix of MacGyver and Slumdog Millionaire, only slimier and built on shaky emotional ground. Jay’s internal narrative is necessarily spoken aloud as dialogue in the film, making it feel artless and detracting from much of his terror.

And in telling a conventional father-son story in the least conventional of circumstances, Whalefall often gives into a masculinist impulse at the expense of Jay’s mother and sisters, who scarcely register as anything more than stock characters. Indeed, it’s unclear why Mitt – who it is later indicated is no bigot or traditionalist – spends so much time trying to coax Jay into diving when his lively daughters may be better suited to it.

In the film’s final act, the sentimentalism shifts into a truly unbearable register, undermining the admirably grisly tone of what came before. To me, Whalefall would have worked better as a full-blown horror, rather than a quasi-mystical meditation on the flaws of our parents – but perhaps it’s just that a part of me is still stuck inside that whale.

Need a listening ear? UK Samaritans: 116123; US 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: 988; hotlines in other countries.

Russia and China are using AI to stage relentless cyberattacks against the UK

New Scientist October 15, 2026

Russia and China are staging “relentless” cyberattacks against the UK using AI, according to one of the nation’s top spy chiefs. But AI is also being used to help defend against such attacks.

Paul Chichester, director of operations at the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) – the government department tasked with securing the nation’s IT infrastructure – says the UK’s four main cyber adversaries – Russia, China, North Korea and Iran – are all using AI to boost their ability to attack the country.

“They don’t need sleep, coffee, food or anything like that,” says Chichester. “AI is certainly being used by all our adversaries.”

Advertisement

NCSC was formed 10 years ago this month by amalgamating a disparate group of departments that all had overlapping aims to protect against cyberattacks. Chichester says that, over that decade, cyberattacks have become a standard part of the intelligence activity of nation states.

“It feels more relentless now than it did 10 years ago,” says Chichester. “This is now an absolutely critical part of covert statecraft, and we obviously live in a world that is more uncertain and geopolitically there is more tension. So that will manifest in the cyber domain and that will manifest in our workload. All of a sudden [with AI], the productivity of their operations is certainly increasing.”

Rogue hacking AIs have changed the cybersecurity landscape

In recent months, a string of stories about AI models inadvertantly escaping test environments and hacking computers in the real world have emerged from large AI companies. And the use of AI models by security companies paid to break into clients’ machines to test defences has become commonplace. These models can not only design new types of attack, but they can carry them out at astonishing pace and operate without rest.

Chichester says that AI is being used in all stages of the “cyber kill chain”, from reconnaissance to developing a vulnerability to actually carrying out attacks on a target. He also warns that when humans staged attacks, there was a de facto limit to how much intelligence or data they could steal, but in a world where AI can carry out attacks that limiting factor is gone.

“What you’re seeing is always something new. Because if they don’t get it, they’re gonna try something else,” says Chichester. “No two days are the same; you’re always seeing different kinds of attack. You’re always trying to defend against things.”

Their aims vary, from espionage to economic advantage to disruption and, in the case of North Korea, simple financial crime and fraud.

OpenAI’s hacking agent went rogue. Should we be worried?

Chichester would not be drawn on the extent that the UK takes part in similar attacks, but says that “there are capabilities that are avowed and the UK uses”. The secretive National Cyber Force is a joint operation between the UK Ministry of Defence and GCHQ (the UK’s cybersecurity agency), which has offensive cyber capabilities.

However, Chichester says that NCSC is open about using commercial frontier models in its work, and in developing its own AI tools.

“Building an LLM [large language model] in a way that you might look at some of the frontier models obviously takes a ridiculous amount of computing and machinery, but building smaller models that do particular specific things is a very different proposition,” says Chichester. “For instance, in the way that we do malware research or malware engineering investigations, there are elements of artificial intelligence in the tooling and the systems we build, and that’s been in there for a long time – but it’s very bespoke, it’s very specific to that task.”

NZ apple sector helps Indian growers to expand orchards under FTA commitment

New Zealand Herald October 15, 2026

Danielle Adsett is the chief executive of New Zealand Apples and Pears. Photo / RNZ, Blessen Tom

By Monique Steele of RNZ

New Zealand’s apple industry is sharing the secrets of its pipfruit success with growers in India, but insists that its efforts will not hurt exporters’ competitiveness.

Sector leaders and diplomats have returned from a week in India, where they met state officials and apple growers in the state of Himachal Pradesh, known as the apple bowl of India, in the western Himalayas.

New Zealand is setting up a centre of excellence there as part of a co-operation commitment under the free-trade agreement (FTA) with India that comes into effect on Tuesday next week.

In addition to bolstering online data and resources, the centre will feature an orchard with different apple varieties, a research centre and will foster collaboration with New Zealand experts to expand India’s domestic production.

The project builds on earlier efforts of sending scientists from Plant and Food Research (now under the Bioeconomy Science Institute) to the region to help growers improve production.

New centres will be established in India for kiwifruit development too.

Danielle Adsett, chief executive of industry group New Zealand Apples and Pears, was accompanied by special agricultural trade envoy Nathan Guy on the trip in late September and early October.

She said the project was a result of FTA provisions.

“India should absolutely benefit. For New Zealand, we have been provided with tariff concessions and a quota.

“So that’s what we managed to get on the table, and the co-operation plan is what we offered up to get that result.”

Adsett said India deeply trusted New Zealand and its expertise, and there were good opportunities to help Indian growers increase productivity on their orchards.

Indian apples sat in a different market segment to more premium New Zealand apples, and would also be counter-seasonal.

“India relies on imported apples, and they’ve got 1.4 billion people to feed.

“And India fundamentally cannot produce enough apples for the demand that they have.

“There are hundreds of thousands of growers in India farming on very, very difficult terrain with very difficult access and fundamentally growing a different variety mix to what we can offer the Indian consumer.

“So I do not see a world in which New Zealand apples would compete directly with Indian apples.”

But the work would not be without its challenges, including access to nursery stock and cold chain issues.

“Very, very old orchards. Very, very big trees that are not producing much at all.

“So there’s a real opportunity to help that shift, but the opportunity obviously will have a lot of challenges alongside.”

India was New Zealand’s fourth-largest export market for apples and pears in the year to June, worth about $100 million, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

A recent Ministry for Primary Industries report showed apple exports to India reached more than 38,564 tonnes in the year to December, according to its Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries report.

But Adsett said exports would be close to 50,000 tonnes this year, mostly of royal gala, which faced the current 50% import tariff on top of the sale price.

“So a very, very difficult market to make any margin on.

“In fact, most of our product struggles to be competitive in that market, due to the nature of the other markets that they import from.”

The FTA will see new quotas for apples from year one during India’s off-season, between April and the end of August.

The first 32,500 tonnes will be subject to 25% tariffs, and the current 50% tariff will apply for volumes above that.

Adsett said exporters would likely exceed that volume next season.

India’s import quota concessions would reduce over the next six years, expanding to 45,000 tonnes at the 25% tariff.

Tariffs on pears into India will drop to 16.5% over the next decade, with no quota limit.

For kiwifruit, New Zealand exporters would face duty-free access for 6250 tonnes each year, widening to up to 15,000 tonnes by year six.

Out-of-tariff quotas will halve to 16.5%.

The FTA comes into effect on Tuesday.

The Australia-India Economic Co-operation and Trade Agreement, which came into effect in December 2022, excluded provisions for apples.

National’s campaign chair Simeon Brown has poured cold water on remarks by leader Christopher Luxon that suggested National was open to doing a deal with Opportunity after the election.

At a public meeting in Greymouth on Thursday, Luxon was reported by The Press as saying he would work with “whoever” he had to ensure a second term. Luxon’s office has since said he was talking about working with Act and NZ First and that his ruling out of Opportunity still stood.

Luxon’s remarks appeared to refer to the controversy around deliberately splitting votes to trigger an overhang rather than ruling Opportunity in.

With most polls showing National would need the support of Opportunity to govern, this was interpreted as meaning Luxon was softening his months-old position of ruling out Opportunity from any post-election coalition.

Not so, said Brown this morning. Speaking to the Mike Hosking Breakfast on Newstalk ZB.

“No, I don’t think so,” Brown said when asked if Opportunity was now in play.

“We’ve been very clear as the National Party, we’re not doing a deal with the Opportunity Party … we’ve been very clear we’ll work with Act and NZ First, we’ve been very clear we’re not going to work with the Opportunity Party, that’s been our clear position that the Prime Minister has been saying.”

Brown said National was campaigning for a National Party vote and a vote for “anyone else” puts that at risk.

Brown claimed Luxon had been clear about the position, using the words “clear” or “very clear” five times in the space of about 90 seconds as he sought to clarify Luxon’s remarks.

Hosking disputed that Luxon had been clear, noting his remarks on the West Coast were not very clear.

Luxon told the Greymouth meeting: “There’s no value giving it [the party vote] to Act, there’s no value giving it to New Zealand First, you’re not helping me,” he said.

“I’ll make it work with whoever I have to in order to make sure we win and make it, take the show forward.

“But it is a lot easier when you’ve got a big, active party sitting around 20, 30 seats in that Cabinet to get that job done.”

Luxon vowed to support mining and work with “whoever” he has to, to ensure a second term, while campaigning on the West Coast.

Luxon, who has repeatedly ruled out working with the Opportunity Party, told the gathering of National supporters in Greymouth on Thursday night he would work with “whoever I have to” to ensure a second term.

However, his office says the Prime Minister’s comment was not a turnaround.

“The PM was referring to MPs from NZF and Act,” Luxon’s chief press secretary, Finn Stichbury, said on Friday morning.

MP Paul Goldsmith this morning backed his National leader in ruling out working with TOP.

“No, no”, Goldsmith said when asked by Nadine Higgins on Ryan Bridge TODAY if Seymour was “showing you guys some sense” in keeping the door open to the Opportunity Party rather than risk being in opposition.

“TOP are to the left of the Greens. The Prime Minister has been very clear … a vote for TOP is a vote for the left,” Goldsmith said.

Starship cancer delays: Father says using sick kids politically is cruel

New Zealand Herald October 15, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

The father of a little girl who had surgery at Starship for a brain tumour before undergoing six rounds of chemotherapy has hit out at the politicising of child cancer in the run-up to an election.

Timaru dad Shaun Todd says downplaying cancer treatment delays for sick children is a cruel blow to desperate families for whom days, or even hours, can mean the difference for their survival.

Contact the New Zealand Herald newsroom

“Just do better,” Todd told the Herald. “Fix it. Stop using cancer kids as a political football.”

The Herald revealed yesterday that cancer treatment for patients at Starship children’s hospital’s oncology department had been delayed by up to a week due to nursing shortages and high demand.

Health New Zealand Te Whatu Ora confirmed that 20 cycles of chemotherapy were delayed over the last four months by up to seven days and two bone marrow transplants were delayed by “a short amount of time”.

Sources said staff were “horrified” after learning of the postponements and feared they could adversely affect patient outcomes.

Health Minister Simeon Brown hit back by denying treatment had been “suspended” and claiming there was no hiring freeze at Health NZ.

Todd’s daughter celebrated her third birthday at Starship last year after undergoing “debulking” surgery to remove a brain tumour.

The family spent a month at the hospital before they were transferred to Christchurch, where his daughter endured six rounds of high-dose chemotherapy.

“We got all the terrible things told to us. ‘Don’t expect her to survive. We don’t know what this is. Don’t expect chemo to work’.”

The family later travelled to the US for proton treatment and Todd’s daughter is now doing well, undergoing regular scans, “going to kindy and doing the things a normal 4-year-old kid should do”.

He said the nurses and doctors were fantastic and “I should be sitting here singing the praises of the health system because they do wonderful things”.

However, Todd was furious to read Brown’s comments yesterday, which he claimed flew in the face of reality.

“To see the minister’s post and to claim that’s not actually what’s happening angered me – upset the hell out of me,” he said.

“Frankly it’s just a load of s***. To see cancer kids being used as political footballs ... I’m equally p***** off with Labour.”

Todd said his family saw first-hand the pressure that health staff were under and nursing vacancies not being filled “because there isn’t the money”.

Having been in the shoes of parents at Starship’s oncology ward, Todd said learning of treatment delays “makes the whole situation even more scary than it already is”.

“Families are already going through the most unimaginable situation. I know what those families are going through.

“You’re talking about days, you’re talking about hours sometimes, on what makes the difference in these kids’ chances to actually fight. And taking days away can be the difference between a kid surviving and a kid not.

“The fact that that is a political football is disgusting. I think the minister should be ashamed.”

Claims by Brown that no treatments had been suspended were disingenuous, Todd said.

“Of course they haven’t been suspended because no doctor or nurse is going to walk away from that, but there have been delays. Face into that, own up, do better.”

The Herald has sought comment from Brown.

Yesterday, the nurses union claimed nearly half of shifts at Starship’s oncology ward were below safe staffing levels this year.

Nurses Organisation president Kerri Nuku said health bosses should have hired more nurses rather than delaying vital cancer treatments for sick kids.

“It shouldn’t have come to this.

“Health Minister Simeon Brown can argue oncology services are being postponed and not suspended, but such semantics are unlikely to be important to whānau with children with cancer.”

Brown has now asked Health NZ chief executive Dale Bramley for an explanation after being alerted to the delays by the Herald.

He confirmed yesterday that “a handful” of chemotherapy sessions had been delayed by up to seven days and two bone marrow transplants had been “moved slightly” from their original dates.

Brown said Starship was managing demand and winter pressures as usual, and clinical teams were involved in the decisions.

Meanwhile, another Starship source told the Herald that understaffing was causing severe pressure in the oncology ward, which they claimed had resulted in several clinical errors this year relating to medicines.

The source described what they believed was an “effective sinking lid policy”.

“We’re not allowed to replace people. We’re down to low numbers. And also, they’re only allowed to hire junior nurses so if an experienced nurse leaves, you’re not allowed to get like for like.

“So over time there’s a depletion of clinical knowledge and experience. Those staff are under much more pressure, which can lead to errors.”

A statement from Brown’s office said Starship nursing vacancies were because of natural attrition. The staffing situation had improved since August and all vacancies were expected to be filled by December-January.

The statement claimed there was no hiring freeze at Health NZ.

Health New Zealand’s Auckland group director of operations, Dr Mike Shepherd, said patient safety and high-quality care was always the highest priority.

“Starship has not suspended any cancer treatments and no children have missed out on cancer care.

“Treatment schedules are routinely adjusted to match capacity and this has been done more frequently during recent staffing challenges. This is prioritised in a way which ensures the highest risk patients have little to no delay in treatment.”

Shepherd said finding the right trained and experienced staff took time for a specialist area.

Workload challenges in the oncology ward had been exacerbated by winter, with staff sickness and high demand, but staffing levels had improved in recent months.

A Starship nurse said the severe shortage was not simply related to the winter flu spike. It had been critical “all of this year”.

She feared the postponements could adversely affect patient outcomes.

“You’re increasing the risk of complications and death from cancers.

“It’s so wrong. It’s ridiculous that it’s even happening. You can delay other things without impacting a child’s outcomes.”

Child Cancer Foundation chief executive Monica Briggs said uncertainty around treatment delays could be “deeply unsettling” for families.

“Our hearts are with every child with cancer and their whānau who may be feeling anxious in light of this news.”

Briggs said the foundation recognised the extraordinary work of the healthcare professionals who cared for these children and families in increasingly challenging circumstances.

“While clinical decisions and hospital operations sit with health providers, our commitment to families remains unwavering. We will continue to provide practical and emotional support – drawing our families closer at this time.

“Our purpose has always been to ensure no family faces childhood cancer alone. Now, more than ever, we want families to know that we are here, we care deeply and we will continue walking alongside them every step of the way.”

Lane Nichols is Auckland Desk Editor and a senior journalist for the New Zealand Herald with more than 20 years’ experience in the industry.

Huntly woman’s breast cancer returns for the third time, now terminal

New Zealand Herald October 15, 2026

Rose Thompson says her dog Tama Nui is the reason she gets up every day and fights the progress of her breast cancer.

A Waikato woman almost gave up when her cancer returned. She beat it again, but now it’s back and she’s preparing to fight it a third time.

Rose Thompson, 42, of Huntly, has stage 4 breast cancer.

She has been told it’s terminal and has spread to more than 23 parts of her body, including her bones, lungs and scalp.

While her cancer cannot be cured, treatments can slow tumour growth and help her live longer.

Thompson was 34 when she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in 2018 while living in Australia.

She told the Waikato Herald a former partner felt a lump on her chest while they were lying in bed and he encouraged her to get it checked.

“I just thought nothing of it, being as young as I was at that time,” she said.

A biopsy confirmed stage 1 breast cancer and she was “fast-tracked” for chemotherapy while living in Australia’s Gold Coast.

She also had a double mastectomy.

“They hit me with everything but the kitchen sink,” Thompson said.

After that, she underwent elective surgery to get breast implants and she was in remission.

She returned home to New Zealand to visit her family when the Covid-19 pandemic hit and the borders closed.

It was here in 2020 that she realised her cancer was growing back in her lymph nodes under her left arm beside the implant.

Doctors confirmed she had stage 1 breast cancer again.

Thompson said she couldn’t handle it.

“I didn’t want to fight the cancer again; I was willing to give up,” she said.

Her former partner bought her a dog, an American Bully named Tama Nui (Māori for big boy), to help keep her going.

“I had to stay during the lockdown and when I went back to Australia, they removed [the implant] and I received radiation.”

She went into remission for the second time.

Thompson moved back to New Zealand in 2024 after hearing her dad’s health was declining.

But while his health improved, Thompson’s worsened.

However, she lived life as usual, working as a carer at Huntly’s Kimihia Home & Hospital for two years before taking on an activities co-ordinator role there.

“I just thought everything was okay,” she said.

In June this year, things took a turn.

She was admitted to Waikato Hospital with “profound” anaemia and doctors requested her Australian medical records after noticing lesions on her head, neck and arms.

Further testing confirmed breast cancer again but this time it was stage 4, metastatic and had spread to more areas, including her spine and liver.

Thompson thought the worst.

“I convinced myself that I was going to lose all my hair again, and I was going to be hooked up to a machine [again] once a week,” she said.

“But [I’ve] come to learn that it’s gone past them trying to get rid of the tumours. They just need to keep it at bay.”

After her third diagnosis, she left her job.

“That was quite sad ... that’s how I identify myself a lot of the time, through my work.”

But she remains optimistic.

“It’s disheartening ... I have my bad days and my good days. I’ve just got to suck it up and be hopeful.

“Income is obviously a major factor now that I’ve had to try and adjust ... but that’s part of my resilience. There’s nothing more I can do.”

A former colleague set up a Givealittle page to help Thompson cover treatment, travel, medication and everyday living costs.

Her 24-year-old son still lives in Australia but her four-legged companion is always by her side.

“He’s the reason I get up every day and fight. He’s part of my medicine.”

Thompson encouraged other women to get checked if they felt unusual, especially younger women because she once felt she was too young for breast cancer.

“I would love to ... get back into work and still be here for a very long time.

“There’s a lot of us out there fighting [and] we can still have our lives.”

Malisha Kumar is a multimedia journalist based in Hamilton. She joined the Waikato Herald in 2023 after working for Radio 1XX in Whakatāne.

Emergency services were called about 12.40am after reports that a car had entered the water off Chapel St, near the shopping centre.

“One person in the vehicle is out and is in hospital, while police are continuing to work to determine whether a second person was in the car,” police said.

Chapel St was closed early this morning. It reopened during the morning rush, but was closed again before 9am.

Hato Hone St John was called at 12.36am. One person was taken to Tauranga Hospital in a moderate condition.

Power Rankings: The top sporting schools in New Zealand in 2026

New Zealand Herald October 15, 2026

Which school can legitimately claim to be New Zealand’s biggest sporting powerhouse? The Herald’s power rankings have the (debatable) answers.

With all but two major secondary school sports tournaments decided in 2026, the Herald has done the numbers to find New Zealand’s top sports schools.

December will see the national secondary school cricket tournaments held at Lincoln University and Gisborne will host the national finals of the latest sport to be included in the Herald rankings, touch rugby.

Last year, the rankings included volleyball for the first time and this year, touch makes the list with 13,000 players.

Other sports with high and rising numbers include badminton and athletics – but the rankings focus on major team sports.

The Herald’s power ranking formula allocates five points for current national champions, three points for runners-up, two points for third – and if applicable, one point for notable placings.

It also rewards recent success by granting three points for the previous year’s winner, two points for the year before and one point beyond that – as far back as 2021 (2020 for cricket and touch).

Some schools are dominant in one sport – but they’re unlikely to rank higher than a school that has success across multiple codes. That’s certainly the case with 2026’s top boys’ school – and it’s a repeat performance.

Westlake Boys’ High School (16 points) teams are quite simply very good at virtually everything. This year, they claimed the national basketball title in Palmerston North, beating Auckland Grammar School in a tight final (90-82). No other team got close to them. They beat Napier Boys’ High School by 40 points in the semi-finals after they dismissed the South Island champions (St Andrew’s College) in the quarter-finals by a similar margin. And it was a team effort, with none of the squad featuring in the top 10 tournament scorers; the points were shared around.

Westlake went within a whisker of adding the Rankin Cup to their cabinet this year too, before going down 3-2 in a penalty shootout to eventual national hockey champions King’s College. A Matthew Knight double saw his side equalise twice in the final to force the shootout. Knight then scored to equalise in the shootout but King’s keeper Ben Woodhams blocked enough shots to deny Westlake a come-from-behind victory.

While the basketball title was the school’s only national win this year, it comes on the back of a Maadi Cup victory in 2025 and national titles in touch, hockey and football in recent years.

Their First XV took another trip to the Top 4 national rugby finals after winning their local competition (a heart-stopping 45-43 win over Rosmini College) and then scoring first against Kelston Boys’ High School (40-40) to win the Blues regional final. They struck a determined Tauranga Boys’ College (losing 31-17) before claiming third place with an action-packed 52-42 win over St Pat’s Silverstream.

Westlake Boys’ High School is among the most sought-after public schools in the country and recently turned away more than 500 hopefuls in its recent ballot for out-of-zone students. The ballot is a randomly generated “names from a hat” process rather than cherry-picking “talent”. It doesn’t have boarders and it doesn’t offer scholarships.

It does offer an environment, expertise and a culture that makes it the envy of many other schools.

“We do have good facilities and that’s something we focus on,” headmaster Paul Fordham told the Herald in 2025.

Its reputation as New Zealand’s best sporting school is only growing stronger.

In second place, it’s another North Island powerhouse in Hamilton Boys’ High School (14 points) – ironically in a year when they missed the podium at the Maadi Cup and were absent from the Top 4 First XV tournament. They claimed the national touch title (8-6) against King’s College and had top-four finishes in both hockey and football.

King’s College (13 points) were just behind Hamilton Boys’ High School with a strong showing in 2026. Their coxed eight powered down Lake Ruataniwha to win the Maadi Cup for the first time since 1960. They also won the national hockey title for the first time since 2012 and went close to claiming the touch crown too.

Tauranga Boys’ College (12) had another stellar year and, like Westlake, seem to have strong talent in most sports. Their First XV fell one short of a maiden national title, going down 34-24 in the final to St Andrew’s College (Christchurch). A third place at the volleyball nationals and sustained success in recent years makes them a more than honourable mention.

In the girls’ rankings, much like the boys, there is a repeat winner at the top.

St Margaret’s College (17 points) teams amassed more points than they did in 2025, when they won a staggering three national titles. Strangely, this year they didn’t win one. But such is their varied and continued success across rowing, hockey, volleyball and cricket, the Christchurch school again came out on top.

Despite the lack of trophies, there were still many successes. Rowing to retain the Levin Jubilee Cup, the St Margaret’s eight couldn’t keep up with the hot pace set by Waikato Diocesan School for Girls and saw crosstown rivals Rangi Ruru Girls’ School beat them for second.

Their volleyballers fell one short of back-to-back titles, going down 3-1 to Rangitoto College in the final. The First XI cricket side won through to the national finals and managed an impressive second behind Palmerston North Girls’ High School.

St Margaret’s College is a school of over 900 girls – but that’s across Years 1-13. The secondary school-aged student numbers are closer to 600. To achieve across so many sports with such a limited roll is quite remarkable.

Second place is tied between three schools who have had sustained success in particular sports.

Mount Albert Grammar School (14) were gunning for a three-peat at the football nationals, but fell in the final to Baradene College 2-0. They also had their eyes on retaining the national netball title but couldn’t overcome a determined St Kentigern College in the final, losing 30-25. Just making national finals in any sport is a great achievement – to do it the year after claiming a national title is even more impressive, given the potential for squad turnover from one year to the next.

Hamilton Girls’ High School (14) have now won four of the past five national touch titles. Last December, they were too strong for Dunedin’s Columba College, winning 6-2. The only other team to have tasted success at the tournament over that five-year period is Manukura School. The two schools are familiar foes; it was Manukura who once again halted Hamilton Girls’ High School’s run at the Top 4 First XV rugby tournament in Palmerston North in a high-scoring 48-38 win. Hamilton Girls’ basketballers also finished a credible fourth.

Manukura School (14). The Manawatū-based, Māori-focused co-ed school’s team are absolute juggernauts on the rugby field with five titles in a row – although the 2022 title was shared with Christchurch Girls’ High School. It’s not just that they win – it’s the way they win, with an exciting and entertaining brand of rugby. And as good as they are with ball in hand, they’re equally as deadly on defence. When a team can cycle through an entire school career – as in Year 9 to Year 13 – and maintain that dominance in a fiercely competitive competition, it shows that the environment created by the girls rugby programme lead and former Black Fern, Kristina Sue, is truly exceptional. The school is not big in roll size – it has fewer than 200 students – but its teams are colossuses in schoolgirl rugby.

Netball Girls – St Kentigern College

Volleyball Boys – Takapuna Grammar School, Girls – Rangitoto High School

Rugby Boys – St Andrew’s College (Christchurch), Girls – Manukura School (Manawatū)

Rugby League Boys – Kelston Boys’ High School, Girls – Auckland Girls’ Grammar School

Cricket Boys – Wellington College, Girls – Palmerston North Girls’ High School

Football Boys – St Kentigern College (Wellington), Girls – Baradene College of the Sacred Heart

Hockey Boys – King’s College, Girls – St Cuthbert’s College

It has been a lean 12 months for South Island schools hunting national success, with just two titles going to the Mainland – and both to the same school.

St Andrew’s College, a co-educational private school in Christchurch, won their first-ever national First XV rugby title when they outlasted Tauranga Boys’ College in the wind at Palmerston North. What made the win even sweeter was the fact that they had been left out of a new premier schoolboy rugby competition in the South Island, which caters exclusively for boys’ schools. Now they’re national champions and holders of the famous Moascar Cup.

Soon after the boys had put their school name up in lights, it was the turn of their girls’ basketball team, who also travelled to Palmerston North and returned home with the silverware. After destroying their opponents in pool play and the quarter-finals, they struck their closest match of the week against heavyweights Westlake Girls’ High School in the semi-finals. They won 90-66 and then swept aside Mount Maunganui College in the final (100-75).

Mike Thorpe is a senior multimedia journalist for the Herald, based in Christchurch. He has been a broadcast journalist across television and radio for 20 years and joined the Herald in August 2024.

Just days after several centres sweltered in near-30C, snow is forecast and temperatures are plunging towards freezing.

NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi imposed restrictions on State Highway 73 between Otira and Springfield last night because of snow, with towing vehicles prohibited and chains essential. Up to 10cm was forecast around Porters Pass.

MetService meteorologist Sophie Huntington told the Herald “light and brief” snowfall was also possible across higher parts of the North Island, including the Central Plateau and Hawke’s Bay high country.

Huntington said the cold snap, driven by a front from the Southern Ocean, would be especially noticeable in Napier and Hastings.

“They were definitely in the high 20s earlier this week, and they’re only getting to 12C today. That’s about 6C cooler than average.”

Christchurch and Ashburton are also facing a sharp drop, with temperatures expected to peak at 10C and 11C respectively.

The Garden City reached 26.5C on Tuesday, marking a plunge of more than 16C in just three days.

Further north, snow is also forecast for Lewis Pass, where about 1cm could accumulate above 600m this morning.

Huntington urged caution on alpine roads, with snowfall potentially affecting motorists travelling through the passes.

Frosts are also expected across parts of both islands tomorrow morning, with overnight temperatures forecast to fall to around 2C in some areas.

Huntington said Taupō, Taumarunui, Waiouru and Te Kūiti were among the North Island locations likely to feel the chill.

In the South Island, Ashburton, Timaru, Alexandra, Queenstown and Wānaka could also wake to frosty conditions.

MetService meteorologist John Law, speaking in a video published by Earth Sciences New Zealand, warned the chilly start could catch people by surprise.

“It’s going to come as a bit of a shock,” he said.

“If you’re up early on Saturday morning, perhaps out for a bit of an early morning run or some early morning sports, you’re going to need those extra layers.

“If you’ve got anything delicate in the garden, perhaps think about that.”

Showers are expected to ease across much of the country today, though eastern parts of the North Island could remain cloudy and wet, Huntington said.

Strong southerlies will keep Wellington feeling cold, while Coromandel could experience heavy showers and isolated thunderstorms.

However, Huntington said temperatures would begin recovering over the weekend.

“By the end of the weekend into Monday, temperatures are looking better again,” she said.

Law said: “That high pressure keeps things relatively fine and settled for most of the country.”

They asked for 80 homes – she gave them 157! Council-housing miracle named Britain’s best new building

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 20:30:40 GMT

Rising from bluebell woodlands and framed by rolling hills, this cluster of pink and brown brick towers in Croydon is a bittersweet winner of the prestigious RIBA Stirling prize

If Andy Burnham is looking for inspiration for his great “council housebuilding comeback”, he would do well to visit Croydon. There, nestled into a steeply sloping site, sheltered by a canopy of mature trees, stands a cluster of crystalline pink and brown brick towers, where generous flats look on to a landscape of allotments, playgrounds and to the rolling hills of south London beyond. Designed by Mary Duggan Architects, with Ruff Architects, it is a model of council-led housebuilding – so much so that it has also been named this year’s best building in the UK, confounding the bookies’ outsider odds.

Only once before has the RIBA Stirling prize ever been awarded to a council housing project, when Goldsmith Street in Norwich scooped the gong in 2019, for its rows of low-energy brick terraces, designed by Mikhail Riches Architects and Cathy Hawley. This year’s winner, Lion Green Road in Coulsdon, is an entirely different animal, and it puts a welcome spotlight back on housing design at a time when the government plans to pump £39bn into the sector. It is also a bittersweet vindication of Croydon council’s erstwhile housebuilding company, Brick by Brick, a bold and sadly brief experiment by the previous Labour administration, which was halted in 2020 when the council went bankrupt, seeing numerous projects cancelled.

“At a time when we urgently need to deliver more homes,” says RIBA president, Chris Williamson, “Lion Green Road shows that density can be achieved without compromising the quality of the places we create. Through a consistent specification, with subtle variation in height and orientation, it offers housing at scale without uniformity.”

Burnham’s first allocation of £10bn, announced in August, is planned to kickstart 70,000 affordable homes across the country. Yet few people in Britain welcome the prospect of new housing in their backyards, even if it’s prize-winning. The planning application for Lion Green Road, submitted in 2017, received 18 letters of support and 257 objections, mostly about the loss of parking. Now built, almost a decade later, the project demonstrates how more homes than you might imagine can be constructed on the most unpromising of sites in a sympathetic way, without sacrificing greenery, views and public access – and keeping plenty of parking, too.

“We really pushed against the suburban model of terraces dominated by cars, with little front and back gardens,” says Duggan. The original brief asked for 80 homes, arranged as she describes, but Duggan proved she could fit 157 flats, distributed between five pavilion-like towers, retaining the mature trees and bluebell woodland on the site. The result feels like it has grown out of its woodland setting, with a public route that winds its way through the site, up to a historic railway embankment at the rear, and not a perimeter fence in sight.

“Brick by Brick was an amazing client,” says Duggan, who also had a small mews project in Crystal Palace on the drawing board for the council’s housebuilder, before the plug was pulled. “It was a refreshing change from how private developers think about affordable housing. Here, they weren’t talking about the land as a commodity, but as a genuinely public asset.”

The council cared about the interior spaces, too. Thanks to the “pinwheel” plan of the blocks, with flats radiating outwards from a central lift core, each home is dual aspect, maximising natural light, cross-ventilation and views. The flats all enjoy an inset loggia balcony, with a bulge at the base of the balustrades to accommodate plant pots, while cuts in the form (to preserve historic views) create some with larger roof terraces. In the interests of efficiency, the five towers all have the same star-shaped plan, but each is subtly rotated to reduce direct overlooking between neighbouring homes, enabling the buildings to stand close together without sacrificing privacy. Half of the flats are private rental, in two towers, while half are affordable, in three blocks retained by the council, rented at local housing allowance rates. Unlike the Norwich project, this is not true social housing.

The RIBA judges describe the project as a “new kind of garden neighbourhood”. The space between the blocks feels consciously planned, rather than a leftover afterthought, designed with landscape architecture practice Planit-IE to include a sensory garden, allotment plots and play areas. Walking around the development’s zig-zagging slopes and stepped pathways gives the feeling of exploring a bucolic hill town. Little bug hotels in the same faceted star-shaped form as the towers are a delightful touch; even the insects get a dignified dwelling.

Duggan says the project “expands the idea of the threshold”, and the arrival feels more welcoming than most. The entrance of each block is framed by a paved terrace, with seating and planting, while all have generous lobbies, no matter the tenure. It’s a far cry from the “poor door” apartheid of so much developer-built housing, where private owners get the hotel concierge treatment, while affordable tenants enter around the back by the bins. It all oozes quality on a budget, down to the choice of three dusty colours of brick, some projecting to create a textured, tweedy finish. The quality belies the tight construction budget of £2,500/sq metre – making it the cheapest project on the shortlist by far. Other Stirling Prize contenders this year included two exquisitely built projects for well-heeled Cambridge colleges, a large private house in Essex, an arts centre in Hertford, and an £825m office block in Paddington.

If there is a cloud hanging over Croydon’s triumph, it is the fate of Brick by Brick. It was established in 2015, as a wholly council-owned company, because the conventional development model was failing to deliver enough affordable homes. The idea was that Croydon would use its own land, often small leftover sites, and borrow against its own resources, to build a mix of private and affordable housing, while turning a profit for the public purse. But the sites often proved to be trickier than expected, adding additional costs, while the financial forecasts were overly optimistic, with Brexit and Covid introducing huge delays. Housing experts attribute its collapse to poor financial structuring, governance and risk management, rather than a failure in development expertise or quality of delivery.

Nonetheless, Brick by Brick built 751 homes, over half of which are affordable, of a design quality higher than most standard developer fare. With renewed housing cash from central government, might there be a chance for some of the halted schemes to be resurrected, and more of the imagination and innovation of Lion Green Road spread across the borough and beyond?

Klara and the Sun review – Taika Waititi’s manic pixie dream robot sci-fi is a sentimental mess

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 20:15:40 GMT

The director of Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Jojo Rabbit turns Kazuo Ishiguro’s AI fable into a twee, tiresome tale of love and grief

Taika Waititi detonates an explosion of postmodern quirkiness and ironic dorkiness in this unbearably mannered, unspeakably acted film. It’s a slice of sentimental whimsy-futurism and non-satire, adapted by Waititi from the Kazuo Ishiguro novel, which winds up saying nothing substantial or meaningful (or funny) about artificial intelligence, love or grief. Klara and the Sun is soft-centred sci-fi-lite, simultaneously demanding we laugh at its (unfunny) humour and wipe away a tear at its pass-agg poignancy. With earlier films like Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Thor: Ragnarok, Waititi showed he can do comedy. But this, sadly, is closer to his notorious fey-Hitler fantasy – misjudged and self-admiring.

In the world to come in an uncanny valley of the almost-real, families can buy “artificial friend” or AF robots for their kids. In terms of tech plausibility overall, incidentally, their status isn’t entirely clear: AF salesperson (Natasha Lyonne) says that the recent third world war has wiped out the internet. (This post-WW3 world looks in pretty good shape apart from that.) And these AF humanoids incidentally have a kind of purple blood called PEC-9 running through them which one character incidentally tells us is “highly flammable”. (Uh-oh. Quite the design fault.)

One such AF is teen girl Klara, played by Jenna Ortega as a ditsy, cutesy, supremely lovable innocent: a manic pixie dream robot – only nice – who is solar-powered and who therefore, in her adorable childlike robot way, worships the sun as a god. But Klara is an earlier, more rudimentary AF model, less sophisticated and robust apparently than the newer upgrades which run on Bluetooth as opposed to solar. (Is that really better?)

At all events, her flaws are presented as analogous to the vulnerabilities of the human teen who wants Klara; this is Josie (Mia Tharia), a 14-year-old genius-prodigy due to be expensively “lifted” into a super-IQ class via a new surgical procedure, but who is also very lonely and suffering from an unspecified illness. Her uptight mom is played by Amy Adams and the grumpy housekeeper Melania – whose appearance is the nearest the film comes to comedy – is played by Rachel House. Klara goes to live with her new family in their distant home in a weirdly dreamlike Midwest farming landscape from which the city can only be glimpsed distantly, like Oz. Klara becomes certain that the sun lives in the nearby barn above, from which she can see it rising every morning; what a sweetly naive belief. And so it goes on, to a twist ending that is as unsatisfying and contrived as everything that has gone before.

The thought of robots or replicant youngsters having real intelligence or real feelings is a difficult subject; Hirokazu Kore-eda came unstuck with the idea of robot child replacements in his recent film Sheep in the Box. Kogonada’s parable After Yang, about AI child robots, was a more interesting and persuasive movie. But this is a sentimental and laborious mess.

Klara and the Sun screened at the London film festival; released on 22 October in Australia, and 23 October in the UK and US.

Houthi missiles strike Saudi-led forces HQ at presidential palace in Aden

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 20:00:36 GMT

Witnesses report at least six explosions near palace used by Yemen's internationally recognized government

At least six explosions struck on Thursday near the palace used by Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the port city of Aden, witnesses said.

An official told the Associated Press that at least two people were killed, and Iran-backed Houthi rebels based in northern Yemen quickly claimed responsibility. Government military sources in Yemen told Agence-France Press (AFP) that at least four people were killed and 10 wounded.

An AFP journalist saw smoke rising and residents of the city reported hearing explosions during the attack, the first on the complex since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July.

A government minister said on condition of anonymity that the Yemeni prime minister, Shaya al-Zindani, had been present at the time, but “was not harmed in any way”.

It was a rare attack on the palace area, as fighting has escalated between the rebels and a Saudi-led coalition on the latest front in the Iran war. The explosions caused panic among residents, who fled the area.

At least two people were killed and six wounded, said the official, who spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the press. The government said the Houthis attacked with missiles and drones, the Aden-based Saba news agency reported.

A security official told the AP that at least two explosions were on top of the hill near Al-Maashiq palace, and two others were near the security gate.

AFP also reported that a Yemeni government minister said on condition of anonymity on Thursday that a Houthi missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden had hit a command center for the Saudi-led coalition. The official added that the command center was hit by three missiles, and the headquarters of the coalition forces at the presidential complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.

There was no immediate confirmation of the report that the prime minister was in the presidential palace at the time of Houthi attack. Many of Yemen’s government leaders are living in exile, and those in Aden were safe, a government official told the AP.

The Houthis said they attacked a military operations headquarters with the “Saudi enemy”, part of their strategy of attacking Saudi targets that has included a series of attacks on airports and oil infrastructure inside the kingdom.

The escalation has complicated efforts to end the wider Iran war and further rattled global markets as Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s top oil exporters, faces repeated attacks. Regional aviation is affected, too, as the rebels have warned airlines about their use of Saudi airspace for attacks. Thousands of flights across the kingdom have been disrupted.

Earlier on Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted a cruise missile over the province of Medina. Flightradar24, a tracking platform, said dozens of flights were canceled or delayed at Jeddah’s airport.

The coalition statement did not assign blame for the attack. The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig Gen Yahya Saree, denied the rebels carried it out. The group previously pledged not to attack airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia.

Saudi Arabia also said it destroyed a drone over the country’s eastern province, a major oil-producing region, and intercepted a drone in Khamis Mushait, near a major military airbase.

Earlier this week, Saudi Arabia said the headquarters of the oil giant Saudi Aramco were hit by Houthi attacks, and reported damage to the building.

Inside Yemen, the fighting has revived a devastating civil war after four years of relative calm. One focus of alarm is the Houthi-besieged city of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, where residents were running short of basic necessities.

France drops opposition to UK being included in ‘Made in Europe’ legislation

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 19:28:34 GMT

British government must however align with the European Union’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs

France has dropped its opposition to the UK being included in the EU’s “Made in Europe” legislation as long as the British government aligns with the bloc’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs.

France on Thursday came round to backing Germany, which has always supported the UK’s calls to be designated European for the purposes of the Industrial Accelerator Act. The legislation, which is in its draft stage, is designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition.

According to a joint Franco-German paper seen by the Guardian, the two countries are now proposing that for the car industry specifically the UK could be included in Made in Europe.

“For the automotive sector, ‘Made in Europe’ should comprise the EU27 and an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 01/01/2020, subject to an agreement on full reciprocity – i. e. adopting the European preference scheme relevant to the automotive sector,” it says in a clear reference to the UK, which was still in the single market as an EU member in January 2020.

It would also include Norway, which is in the single market but not a member of the EU.

The paper added that the opt-in would come with conditions, including alignment on trade defence measures, which have included tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the EU in 2024 and any future trade barriers, such as the quota deal being finalised with China on its exports of hybrid cars.

The paper says that “as well as relevant anti-circumvention measures”, these “opt-in” countries would have to accept “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.

Liam Byrne, the chair of the UK’s business, innovation, science and trade committee, said he believed aligning with the EU on trade defence measures was a small price to pay to save British manufacturing.

“Sometimes politics is the least worst choice – aligning with Europe on trade defence against an over-subsidised China is the way we deliver for all of us,” he said.

“Tariffs on these would be a small price to pay for the protection of a European manufacturing industry which safeguards jobs across supply chains in the UK and makes us less prone to coercion from China in the future.”

On Wednesday the head of Mercedes implored EU leaders to let the UK join the package.

Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial Made in Europe legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz said.

The UK has been under pressure for weeks to align with the EU on tariffs on Chinese vehicles, but this week the business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.

However the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK was locked out of supply chains in the EU.

Earlier on Thursday trade minister Anas Sarwar hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs.

He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.

Bernd Lange, the chair of the European parliament’s influential international trade committee, told the Guardian the UK should “of course” be included in the Made in Europe legislation, calling France’s opposition “not rational”.

A Downing Street spokesperson said it had yet to see the detail but saw the development as positive. “This is a Franco-German proposal and there is still a European process to run, but if confirmed, we welcome the objective to have UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act and this would be good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the UK.”

Europa League: Lyon take down Crystal Palace, Cissè’s Milan hat-trick sinks Salzburg

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 19:18:53 GMT

Sage loses 3-2 to former side; Leverkusen go top

Alphadjo Cissè lights up 4-0 away victory

Pierre Sage endured a frustrating return to Lyon in the Europa League as his Crystal Palace side lost 3-2 to his former employers at the Groupama Stadium.

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 19:14:50 GMT

Three minutes into stoppage time Noah Sadiki hurdled a set of advertising hoardings, sprinted across a running track and hurled himself towards the ecstatic Sunderland fans.

Just as those supporters’ long-awaited party in Portugal had looked in peril of falling a little flat, the Democratic Republic of the Congo midfielder capitalised on excellent work from Enzo Le Fée and Granit Xhaka to half-volley an eye-catching first goal for Régis Le Bris’s side.

It ensured a largely unconvincing Sunderland came from behind to secure a second straight Europa League win and their relief was evident as every outfield player followed Sadiki in vaulting those hoardings to join the celebrations.

“It was a difficult game,” said Le Bris, Sunderland’s manager, with considerable understatement. “Torreense are a good team.”

With their home ground too small to accommodate European football, Leiria’s stadium stood in. It proved quite some substitute. An arena overlooked by a 12th-century castle constructed to defend this attractive medieval town against reconquest by the Moors created an imposing backdrop to Sunderland’s first competitive trip to the continent for 53 years.

Back in 1973 they were second division FA Cup holders. Torreense know the feeling. Having provoked widespread shock by beating Sporting to win the Portuguese Cup last spring, Luís Tralhão’s second-tier side relish their underdog status.

After winning at Lillestrøm last month, Torreense aimed to keep the surprises coming and duly left a heavily rotated Sunderland trailing at the break. Le Bris had left, among others, Xhaka, Le Fée and Nordi Mukiele on the bench ahead of Sunday’s vital Premier League trip to Bournemouth. This reshuffle permitted Luke O’Nien, a survivor from League One days, to captain Sunderland at a ground transformed into a sea of red and white. Although only 4,000 official tickets were allocated to the visitors more were readily available locally and estimates suggested the formal allocation had doubled.

As the sun dropped and the temperature fell from a high of 28C those fans watched a disjointed first half on Sunderland’s part. It seemed telling that the normally fairly impassive Le Bris looked distinctly, and unusually, irritated and frustrated at times.

Granted his humour was hardly helped by the referee’s penchant for detecting phantom Sunderland fouls but ominously Malick Fofana, a £30m summer signing from Lyon, struggled wide on the left. Ditto Nilson Angulo on the right wing.

Torreense, 15th in Portugal’s second tier might not have been threatening Robin Roefs’s goal but they succeeded in blocking and clearing pretty much everything that came their way. Indeed Tralhão’s defence looked almost as well fortified as that ancient castle towering over them.

Admittedly, midway through the first half Timur Tutierov, Sunderland’s centre-forward, thought he had headed the opener but that effort was disallowed due to shirt pulling on Omar Alderete’s part.

Then, with the interval fast approaching, Le Bris adopted hand-on-hips mode as Torreense reminded everyone precisely why they have built such a giantkilling reputation by scoring with their first shot.

It came from centre-back Volnei Feltes. With Sunderland losing concentration and standing off, he was permitted to advance unopposed before cutting in on his right foot and sending a sublime 20-yard curler into the top corner.

This infusion of quality left Torreense a little groggy and the midfielder Jules Ahoka –a highly impressive 20-year-old £8.5m summer buy from Royal Antwerp – was able to equalise by heading his first goal for Sunderland courtesy of Mukiele’s deft dink.

When the lively Tutierov went down in the box, the referee immediately pointed to the spot. However, a linesman’s flag indicated an offside so it seemed there would be no penalty. The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged that he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds do not have a primary loyalty towards the UK.

Just what damage can the emissions from a new fossil fuel facility cause? A new tool has estimates

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 19:00:38 GMT

From crop failures to coral bleaching, a new tool developed by climate scientists aims to predict in detail the impacts of each megatonne of carbon emissions

Want to get more charts in your inbox every fortnight? Sign up for The Crunch here

The emissions from a single coalmine expansion might not seem like a lot when compared with the scale of global emissions, which are measured in gigatonnes (that’s one thousand million tonnes).

However, scientists have been saying for years that every tonne of carbon dioxide adds to global warming, and every fraction of a degree increase matters.

Now, a group of climate scientists have released a new tool that shows the possible consequences of those emissions in detail. The Carbon Impacts Tracer uses peer-reviewed studies to estimate the impact of every megatonne of emissions on people and the environment.

Here, you can see how the emissions from a coalmine expansion in Australia’s Hunter Valley could affect food security and human exposure to heat stress globally.

You can read about the science underlying these projections on the Carbon Impacts Tracer website here.

There are further predicted impacts from releasing 809m tonnes of emissions not listed in the graphic above, including an estimated 107 deaths in Europe, 41,800 additional people put into extreme poverty, 19.4km square of additional glacier area lost, and 38.8m additional heavy labour hours lost annually.

Wes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink row

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 18:09:14 GMT

Wes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort.

The British defence secretary, giving a speech before a meeting with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, argued that supporting Ukraine was in the long-term interests of Washington, and a business opportunity.

Taking questions after his address, Streeting acknowledged “the challenges of recent days”, a reference to the row over the sudden decision of the US government on Monday to limit the use of Starlink by Ukraine’s military.

He said it was “a reminder of two things – one is that American support in Ukraine has been significant and it has made, I think, a real impact in the Ukrainian war effort. And we and the Ukrainians would feel the absence of that.”

The second was that there was “an enormous opportunity for the US in terms of the support for Ukraine”, a reference to the future “defence-industrial relationship” between the countries.

Streeting was speaking at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US thinktank, before a potentially difficult meeting with Hegseth amid tensions over Ukraine, Iran and the Middle East.

The two men were also expected to discuss the safety of US military bases in the UK, after an Iranian threat prompted the US to withdraw B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, and whether the two countries would come together to help Saudi Arabia, which has come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis.

But it is Ukraine that is the most urgent issue. A day ago, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he felt personally betrayed by Donald Trump after the US government appeared to have throttled a version of the Starlink satellite internet service used by Ukraine’s military.

Ukrainian officials have reported that the US has also threatened to cut the sharing of intelligence used by Ukraine to detect incoming missiles if it does not abandon its attacks on refineries, aimed at hurting the Russian economy.

The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, meeting Zelenskyy in London on Wednesday, said the UK would stand by Ukraine.

Streeting said: “There’s rarely been a more important time for Britain and America to come together.”

Developing the theme, he made a direct appeal to the US audience. “The people of Ukraine are fighting for a principle that runs through the finest traditions of American political thought,” he said, which was “that a free people have a right to determine their own destiny”.

Trump has vacillated over supporting Ukraine against Russia since returning to the White House, while support among US Republicans for Kyiv has been mixed. But Streeting argued that helping Ukraine was also a matter of national self-interest for the US as well as the UK.

“Ukraine may be thousands of miles from American shores, but if aggression is rewarded, if borders can be redrawn by force, if the sovereignty of nations becomes negotiable, the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent,” he said.

The change to Starlink happened without warning at about 1am, when Ukrainian soldiers reported that terminals on drones were no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph, rendering communications inoperable.

It led to a dramatic halt to mid-strike drone attacks on targets in Russian occupied territories on the frontline, and concerns about Ukraine’s ability to intercept new Russian jet-powered attack craft that are bombing its cities.

Trump has been trying to put pressure on Ukraine to halt its bombing of Russian oil refineries in a desperate attempt to reduce world oil prices before the US midterm elections. He agreed to buy diesel from Russia earlier this month.

Brand fixed his gaze on one of the TV screens in court on Thursday morning as a video of the woman’s interview from 27 September 2023 was played. She told police she met Brand at a fringe cabaret event that he was performing in during the Labour party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. She was not attracted to the then unknown performer, whom she assumed was gay and showered her with compliments.

But she found him polite and intelligent, and the pair spoke about their work before going back to her hotel room to continue their conversation.

The woman said she “froze” in the run-down single room when she returned from the toilet to find that Brand was partly naked and “prancing around” like an ostrich. She said she asked him why he had undressed, and he told her: “Don’t worry, I’m mostly naked at home.”

The woman told how she became “frightened” when Brand made her take half-naked photographs of him. “I took pictures of him on my camera – he made me take them,” she said. “I remember feeling: ‘What on earth have I got myself into?’”

She told police he then raped her in an attack that lasted up to 10 minutes and left her feeling scared, in pain, and like she couldn’t breathe.

“He did rape, he did push me on the bed,” she told police. “He did pull my clothes off, he took my trousers off.

“I remember him on me, very heavy. I know I said no. I kind of drifted out of my head. I couldn’t get out of the situation – ‘do I shout, do I scream?’ He was very heavy, I couldn’t breathe, it didn’t take long.”

She described his body as snake-like and “disgusting” and said his tongue was “horrible” like a lizard. “I’m saying ‘no, no’ but I was really scared,” she told police. “I know he groped me. “He was just pulling my trousers down and pulling my underwear off, and he was inside me. It was not nice, it was painful and it hurt.”

Giving evidence from behind a screen in the afternoon, the woman added: “I was like a zombie on the bed. All I could think was he’s inside me and the quicker the better.”

In tense exchanges during cross-examination with the defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, the woman denied that Brand had persuaded her to have sex. “He was frightening, he seemed menacing at that point,” she replied. “He’s scary. I didn’t know what to do.”

She rejected Winter’s suggestion that she had fallen under the spell of Brand, whom the barrister described as charismatic with a magnetic personality.
