Chris Woakes: ‘It’s unacceptable seeing the way some England players have acted’

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 18:00:37 GMT

The Test stalwart on his surreal last stand at the Oval, his ‘shabby’ treatment by Rob Key and the vexed problem of cricket’s drinking culture

On a rainy October afternoon, after his 20th season as a professional cricketer, Chris Woakes sits down at Edgbaston’s indoor nets and thinks of the advice that helped him when he was 17 and about to start a career in this consuming sport. “The words came from my parents, particularly my dad, and it was to always be myself,” he says in his thoughtful way.

Woakes has just won his third County Championship with Warwickshire and he played 62 Tests for England, taking 192 wickets and scoring 2,034 runs. He also won two World Cups and experienced a range of England coaches, from Andy Flower to Brendon McCullum, and played for captains as different as Sir Alastair Cook, Eoin Morgan, Joe Root and Ben Stokes.

Woakes has been a positive and steadying presence in a tumultuous time for English cricket. “There were a couple of occasions where I stepped outside my character and tried to be something else and it backfired. I quickly learned that what I had, and the way I did it, was the way forward. I’m relatively reserved, but I had quite a bit of dog in me which I didn’t show verbally. You need that burning fire.”

Woakes is routinely described as the nicest man in cricket, but it’s a reductive view that obscures the skill and tenacity that defines him. “Ask some batters over the years and I’m sure they said: ‘He isn’t that nice.’ Once you cross the line, you need to find a way to compete and win.”

The Wizard, his fine new autobiography, has been written with the Guardian’s Ali Martin, who captures Woakes’s voice expertly while providing trenchant insights into the contrasting eras that span his long career. The book opens with his ending in Test cricket, on the bizarre morning last August when Woakes came in at No 11, with his damaged left arm in a sling, to try to help England score the 17 runs that would secure a 3-1 series victory over India.

There was a fitting symmetry as Woakes walked down the stairs at the Oval, where he had made his Test debut 12 years earlier, while typically putting the interests of the team first. Woakes had dislocated his shoulder while fielding and could hold the bat only with one hand. The pain became excruciating when he tried to run and he knew India’s bowlers would show no mercy at the climax of a riveting series.

“It was amazing to go out like that but, in another way, quite sad,” he says. “To walk out in front of a full house, and get a standing ovation, was maybe meant to be my farewell. But it was a horrible moment as well. I had the agony of the shoulder, but there’s no worse feeling, especially as a bowler, when you leave the team handicapped: 10 v 11. Not many teams win from that position. That hurts.”

How did he feel as he stepped on to the field? “I don’t think I’ve ever been as nervous because I was going into the unknown. I was going to bat with one arm, which was never going to look pretty or be great. One of the things you have to get over is the thought that, when someone’s bowling at 90mph with a hard cricket ball, it can hurt even when you’re batting the right way round. It was a challenge to build up the courage to face that.”

Was he scared? “Absolutely, because in international arena it’s dog eat dog. So there was certainly some fear in the cauldron. It would be stumps or head, so I was going to have to wear a few. Your brain naturally tells you: ‘I don’t want to do this.’ But you have to get over that. We got [the run chase] down to seven because Gus Atkinson did fantastically well. So close, yet so far.”

Atkinson was bowled before Woakes could take his mark. “In a selfish way I didn’t want my wicket to be the deciding one, but part of me still wishes I could have faced a ball.”

Woakes describes the harsh way he was soon jettisoned by England. He could accept he had not been selected for the Ashes tour last year, and that his England contract was terminated, but he was hurt by Rob Key, the England team director, breaking the news in public. “Chris Woakes isn’t in our plans,” Key said, “at all.” “That final bit felt a bit cold,” Woakes writes. “A bit shabby, really.”

He is too kind to put the boot in again. “I’ve always got on well with Rob and maybe those words slipped out, not necessarily how he meant it. But he could have easily had that conversation first with me, rather than the press.”

Has he discussed the matter with Key? “We’ve barely spoken since. He’s a busy man and moved on to different things. I’m sure at some point we’ll discuss it. But in any walk of professional sport there isn’t much loyalty because the game moves on. Rob probably had bigger fish to fry at that time. There was an Ashes series and that was his priority, which I understand.”

The Ashes were an unmitigated disaster with the familiar drubbing by Australia exacerbated by nocturnal mishaps featuring Harry Brook and Ben Duckett. Those incidents added to the pressure on McCullum and Stokes. McCullum was relieved of his role, while retaining control of the white‑ball team. Stokes remained as captain, but after leading England to victory in the first Test of the summer against New Zealand he and Atkinson were caught up in a post‑match fracas with members of the Saracens rugby academy, breaking a curfew meant to curb such skirmishes.

Stokes then looked exhausted as he announced his unexpected retirement from international cricket a few weeks later. “Being Test captain does beat you up,” Woakes says. “We saw it with Joe [Root] last time round. Cookie was the same. We saw it with Ben.

“He was desperate for that Ashes series to be a winning one, and he probably deserved it. But the game owes you nothing and he didn’t get it quite right on that tour. I think that was the nail in the coffin. Although he said he wanted to move forward, maybe deep down he knew he couldn’t re-energise himself.”

What did he say to Stokes? “On the day itself I saw him briefly at Trent Bridge and it was: ‘What a career, mate. Hope you enjoy the moment.’ All that sort of stuff because it happened quite quickly. I was on Sky commentary that day. It was a very slow day and it got to three o’clock and all of a sudden we heard the news he was going to retire and it became a bit manic. It would be nice to be able to sit down with him and discuss it.”

Woakes has always had a balanced relationship with alcohol. He enjoys a few beers after a big match but he is smart about his consumption and before the victorious 2019 World Cup he gave up drinking as part of his preparation for the sweetest moment of his career. But does English cricket have a drink problem?

Sign up to The Spin

Subscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s action

after newsletter promotion

“I’d like to say no, but drinking culture is mentioned a lot. There are lads at Warwickshire that enjoy a drink after a win or a hard four days of cricket. Other guys here are almost teetotal and this is the most professional county team I’ve ever seen. But I’ve played in teams where the majority enjoy a drink so it becomes the norm.

“People say within professional sport it should be zero alcohol. But cricket is very different to football and rugby. Test cricket is played over five days, on tours which last for months. It consumes you and people need to have a release. But that doesn’t mean they should get in trouble, like we’ve seen within the England team recently.”

Yet curfews don’t solve anything. “No. You need to give players some freedom and treat them like adults. But it’s unacceptable seeing the way some England players have acted.”

Woakes points out that, as cricketers, “we’re brought up on alcohol to a certain extent. In club cricket there’s a lot of alcohol and it becomes the norm from a young age. The professional game needs to be different, but the sport is so mentally draining it’s almost impossible to tell people they can’t have a drink. It’s a human release.”

He is optimistic, however, that England have the right Test coach in Stephen Fleming. Woakes also pays tribute to McCullum’s ability to free up players, while admitting that, as a senior player, he should have spoken out when he saw clearly that McCullum’s ultra-aggressive style, played without much thought of consequence, would fail against the best Test teams.

“There were times where we had the opposition pretty much by the balls and could have played a little more conservatively in that moment to get us to a point where the other team didn’t have a sniff,” Woakes says. “But there were too many occasions where we let them back in. We could have been more vocal in those moments and say we need to shift gears within the game. We always went up the gears, but never really came back down.”

His book offers some fascinating snapshots of how it felt being coached by men as opposite as Flower and McCullum. At the start of his Test career, Flower would shout at Woakes with withering ferocity. “He was ridiculously hard,” Woakes says. “I was almost scared to train, but that was also what I needed at the time. I just didn’t realise it. So it worked out perfectly. Flower was exactly what I needed at the start and McCullum was exactly what I needed at the back end of my career.”

After such a successful county season he is open to playing one more year for Warwickshire for his love of red-ball cricket remains undimmed. But he has already shown a deft touch in his television work. It is easy to see Woakes becoming the face of cricket on Sky and he rocks in amusement when I say I would like to see him introduce the first day of the first Ashes Test at Trent Bridge next summer – as he confirms the sudden return of Stokes to Root’s team. “Wow,” Woakes laughs. “God, could you imagine that?”

Could Stokes make one last comeback against Australia? “When it comes to Ben, I genuinely think anything is possible. A large part of me says it won’t happen. I think he’s done. But if there’s one person that could talk Ben Stokes round to playing again, it would be Joe Root. They’re very good friends and have known each other for a hell of a long time. If Joe was to say to Ben: ‘I want you back for one last series,’ it could happen. It would certainly be box office. It always is with Ben Stokes.”

The water torture goes on at Thames. Sector-wide reform isn’t moving much faster

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 18:00:31 GMT

If ‘public control’ bit is delaying overhaul, that needs to be nailed down sharpish or continued uncertainty could be costly

It is strange now to recall that Thames Water had a prominent slot on what was known as “Sue’s shit list” – the internal Labour dossier, compiled by Keir Starmer’s first chief of staff, Sue Gray, of potential crises that could erupt at short notice and force the incoming administration to make some big decisions quickly.

That was July 2024. Here we are – more than two years later – and the Thames script has barely advanced. We’re still waiting to see if the financial crisis at the over-indebted, under-performing water company will be resolved by a creditor-led recapitalisation, special administration or something else.

Now Thames is seeking another £2.4bn slug of funding from creditors to stay afloat for another year and survive yet more back and forth between ministers, regulators and those same lenders. The new mystery element in the talks is what the prime minister, Andy Burnham, actually means by “greater public control”.

Still, Thames was an outlier – albeit a biggie – one might say. At least the government in 2024 cracked on with the job of deciding how to overhaul the wider water sector in England and Wales. Indeed it did: Sir Jon Cunliffe, a former deputy governor of the Bank of England, was commissioned to review what was needed and his detailed report landed in summer last year. The centrepiece was the abolition of Ofwat, the regulator.

Steve Reed, the environment secretary at the time, embraced Cunliffe’s proposals and declared the “the biggest overhaul of water regulation in a generation” via a new water bill. Game on?

Not exactly. The bill, which should have arrived this autumn, was delayed by the change of PM. Burnham has promised a “strengthened” version, which presumably will include the “public control” elements. In the meantime, Ofwat is still in place, and nobody knows which bits of the Environment Agency will be absorbed into the new super-regulator, or what the new body’s formal status will be. Will it, for example, be as formally independent as Ofwat, or will it be under a tighter ministerial leash?

Credit rating agencies have noticed the uncertainty. In dry language, Moody’s on Thursday issued a report noting that regulatory changes “appears to have stalled”, that “political scrutiny is heightened and may cause further delay” and the “potential increase in business risk will require stronger financial ratios to maintain credit quality”.

Moody’s, note, did not downgrade its assessment of the “stability and predictability” of UK water regulation, as it did in late-2024. But it did tiptoe up to the line: one of its slides at Thursday’s conference warned: “Our score could fall further.” Why does Moody’s opinion matter? Simply because rating agencies influence the price at which companies can borrow, which can itself affect the financing costs passed on to customers in bills.

The government should take the hint and decide what it actually wants from water reform. Emma Hardy, the water minister, at least indicated to the same conference that a formal transition plan to the regulator is coming soon. But that’s not the same as an actual water bill, which would reveal if the rest of the Cunliffe changes have survived.

Sign up to Business Today

It is, of course, entirely fair for an incoming PM to review what he wants from a bill. But the “public control” bit, if that’s delaying everything, needs to be nailed down sharpish. Is it simply the Cunliffe-compliant idea of greater powers of influence for mayors and local authorities? Or bigger changes to match the summer rhetoric? It’s impossible to tell – but it’s all taking far too long.

And make a decision one way or another on Thames. Half a parliament to address a supposedly urgent 2024 problem is extreme water torture.

UK HRT shortages: which products are affected and what to do about it

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 17:58:40 GMT

Experts say seeking alternatives that deliver the same dose of oestrogen by the same method is key

Women in the UK are again facing shortages of some HRT products, with warnings they could persist for weeks. We take a look at the situation.

Hormone replacement therapy is widely used to help women manage symptoms of menopause. It can take many forms, from gels and sprays to patches, pills, creams and intrauterine systems.

As the NHS notes, HRT typically involves two hormones – oestrogen and progestogen – and replaces levels lost as women go through menopause. These can be given separately or in a single type of HRT. Women who have had a hysterectomy only require oestrogen-containing HRT.

According to the NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA), almost 2 million women in England aged 40 and above were prescribed HRT for menopause symptoms in 2025-26. Experts, however, say that access varies and shortages have been a problem.

According to a medicine supply notification issued by the Department of Health and Social Care this week, FemSeven Conti patches are out of stock and are expected to remain so until late November. The patches contain estradiol – a type of oestrogen– and a synthetic progestogen called levonorgestrel.

There are also shortages of various Estradot patches – a type of HRT that contains estradiol – and the situation is not expected to end until January.

This is not the first time there have been HRT shortages, and the supply issues affecting Estradot have been long-lasting. The shortages of some products began in December 2024, according to NHSBSA.

“When you have found an HRT treatment that helps you sleep, manage hot flushes and feel more like yourself, being told it is unavailable can be unsettling,” said Sobia Qasim, a pharmacist at the online pharmacy Curely.

Sehar Shahid, a member of the National Pharmacy Association’s board, also raised concerns. “We are deeply frustrated and concerned by shortages to a number of HRT products, with shortages of Estradot being the second longest running individual medicine shortage in the UK,” she said.

“Certain HRT products are specialised and cannot always be easily substituted for an alternative.”

According to the FemSeven Conti notification, alternative patches include Evorel Conti, Estradot Conti 30/95 and Estradot Conti 40/130. These contain estradiol and a different type of synthetic progestogen called norethisterone, and are used twice rather than once a week.

Paula Briggs, a consultant in sexual and reproductive health and a former chair of the British Menopause Society, said keeping the same dose of estradiol was the important aspect. “They have different progestogens, but I do not think that that would have any adverse impact on symptom control,” she said, noting progestogens are required to protect the lining of the womb rather than manage symptoms.

Serious shortage protocols for the Estradot products also list alternatives, such as estradiol-containing patches by Estraderm MX and Evorel. “If we’re using the same dose of oestrogen delivered in a similar patch through the skin, really there is no need to worry,” said Briggs.

Shahid said people who had experienced disruption to their usual HRT regime should speak to their clinician, while Qasim cautioned against leaving a patch on for longer than prescribed, cutting patches up or borrowing HRT treatments from others.

Briggs said shortages were likely to occur in the future “because year on year we’re seeing a more than 10% increase in use”, she said.

Shahid urged the government to take action. “The new secretary of state should convene a taskforce to fully grasp this issue, bringing together all aspects of the supply chain,” she said.

It’s not the old two-party politics – but Labour and the Tories now know they can shun their populist challengers

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 17:40:36 GMT

Though Burnham and Badenoch may still need the votes of Green and Reform supporters, both leaders have drawn clear lines in the sand

Ask a straight question, get a straight answer. It’s how politics is supposed to work but almost never does, which is why on the rare occasions it happens the result can be faintly chaotic. What did Andy Burnham mean when he said – in response to a question from the Tory MP Harriett Baldwin – that Labour couldn’t partner with the Green party while it remains wedded to the “Zionism is racism” motion its members have just endorsed? Were Green MPs now barred from a future coalition government? If so, what about councils where they are currently sharing power with Labour?

Though Burnham was only confirming what ministers have been arguing privately for days, at first nobody seemed to know: tellingly, it took almost 24 hours for the Labour party chair, Bridget Phillipson, to confirm that unless local Green groups disowned that idea sharpish, “Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end”. So much for cuddly cross-party Andy, who always seemed so relaxed about rainbow coalitions. Now elected Greens in places such as Sheffield or Lewes must choose between power and members’ wrath, a useful rehearsal for what a hung parliament might feel like.

Westminster is increasingly realising that while nobody knows quite what’s in Burnham’s head except Burnham, unlike most prime ministers he is surprisingly liable just to tell you. He did it earlier this week on a podcast, pointing out that Russia tried to interfere in the Brexit vote (which is true, albeit the sort of truth that for complicated reasons prime ministers don’t generally dwell on). Now the safety catch is off again.

What did he mean with his comments about Labour and the Greens? Most likely just what he said: that the Greens crossed a line and it cannot be overlooked, especially by a party still recovering from its own battle with antisemitism. Green members did not just vote to adopt a policy that would condemn every Jew who believes in the right to a Jewish homeland, including those who simultaneously support the creation of a Palestinian state. The motion they backed advocates turning all of historic Palestine into a Palestinian state, a one-state solution wiping Israel off the map. Much as Kemi Badenoch did recently by insisting that her English-born children have every right to be considered English, no matter what the ethno-nationalists of Reform and Restore say, Burnham was simply showing that he has limits: this far, and no further.

Something has shaken loose over the party conference season. What we are seeing isn’t the return of two-party politics – things are still too volatile for that – but the return of leaders confident enough to set boundaries on what had become an almost abusive relationship with the public. They are no longer quite so terrified of naming extremism when they see it. More surprisingly, neither is behaving like a party needing to beg for coalition partners, whatever the electoral maths says.

After a period shadow boxing a prime minister who never seemed to know what he thought, Badenoch now faces one who does. That has brought drama back to the middle of politics and not just the radical edges, with genuine differences emerging between Labour and the Tories ahead of the budget over tax and spend, national security v social security, public v private ownership and the respective claims of younger and older people.

Her new strategy is not a million miles from the one outlined this week by the thinktank Bright Blue, in a paper on how the traditional European right can combat far-right populism: adopt draconian immigration policies but make the economy the actual focus of your campaign, and hold the line that citizenship can be earned rather than being determined by ethnicity (the chilling line peddled by some of those in Reform and Restore who argue openly that you have to be white to be properly English).

Though the polls still suggest the Tories can’t win without some kind of deal with Reform, the broad message of a conference speech in which Badenoch painted her rivals as aggressive weirdos who “threaten journalists, call veterans traitors and debate whether my mixed-race children are English” was that it would be a cold day in hell before that happened. That decision looks smarter with every passing journalistic exposé involving the kind of Reform councillor who thinks King Charles should be decapitated for supposedly being a secret Muslim.

Burnham didn’t go quite so studs-up on the Greens, but then he doesn’t need to. The party is already openly agonising about that anti-Zionism motion, opposed by four out of five of its elected MPs. The prospect of being politically ostracised for it may now strengthen the hand of Greens who think this freakishly hot summer might have been better spent campaigning on the climate crisis, not swerving questions about Israel’s right to exist. Yet there are risks for Burnham here, all the same.

Research by the pollster More in Common suggests that “progressive activists”, the group most commonly torn between voting Green or Labour, are significantly more likely than the average British voter to think worse of someone identifying as a Zionist. When Burnham called the Green motion antisemitic and wrong, he was confronting people whose support he may need in some Labour seats.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Sanctioning West Bank settlements, as this government has now done, isn’t enough for some of them: they want Burnham explicitly to call the Gaza war a genocide and stop proscribing Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation. (Polanski was notably quick to leap to the defence of the Irish novelist Sally Rooney, after it emerged her books are being withdrawn from sale in Britain because of her promise to donate royalties to Palestine Action: knowing where the money could be going leaves her publishers open to potential prosecution under anti-terrorism law, just for handing over her earnings.)

It’s technically possible that like some desiccated calculating machine, Burnham has crunched the numbers on all this and concluded that distancing himself from a row that has reportedly made one in three British voters less likely to vote Green (according to Opinium) is mathematically preferable.

But it’s more likely he was just doing the thing that got him here in the first place, and following his gut. If he can’t say what he thinks even now, in what passes for a honeymoon period, he never will. If basic norms are not enforced, they very quickly cease being norms. And if the Labour party can only win by sidling uncomfortably close to the kind of people it was until recently expelling for antisemitism – well, it’s not much of a Labour party. The chaos, in that sense, is probably just beginning.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

The Guardian view on Stormont: voters in Northern Ireland deserve more than an endless cycle of dysfunction

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 17:30:37 GMT

After the executive’s failure to set a budget, and renewed culture-war confrontations, faith in the government’s ability to act in the common good is evaporating

Late last month, protesters deposited a sizable amount of foul-smelling green water on the steps of Stormont to draw attention to the appalling state of Lough Neagh, the largest freshwater lake in the British Isles. Years of agricultural pollution have created an environmental disaster in an area of huge ecological significance that once inspired the poetry of Seamus Heaney. Its plight should be a top priority for Northern Ireland’s devolved government. But the executive currently has other matters on its mind.

The sentencing of the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) Jeffrey Donaldson, after he was convicted of child sexual abuse, dominated Thursday’s headlines. Meanwhile, a cross-party political crisis continues to play out. Halfway through the financial year, Stormont has yet to set a budget. The current deadlock in negotiations with the Northern Ireland secretary, Sir Chris Bryant, could lead to one being imposed from Westminster. Cuts are already being made by default amid an atmosphere of stasis and policy drift.

An unwelcome revival of sectarian tension on the streets is further undermining the fragile political institutions established by the Good Friday agreement. On Monday, Northern Ireland assembly members debated a motion of no confidence in the first minister, Michelle O’Neill. The move followed the Sinn Féin vice-president’s participation in protests against a proposed Orange Order march on the Garvaghy Road in Portadown, controversially sanctioned by the Parades Commission for the first time in 28 years.

A prolonged standoff between unionists and mainly Catholic residents ended peacefully, after Sir Chris banned the parade on police advice. The absence of violence was a silver lining, but the episode showcased the dangers of what one politician described as “negative nostalgia”. As those seeking to revive a route notoriously associated with loyalist violence surely anticipated, the bitter row has reopened old wounds and unleashed latent animosities.

The motion of no confidence in Ms O’Neill was a performative exercise, with no chance of obtaining the necessary cross-community support. But the combination of no budget and a renewed culture-war confrontation means that Northern Ireland now risks being governed by a zombie administration until elections next May.

Given the dismal recent track record of Stormont collapses and suspensions, that should prompt some hard thinking in London and Dublin as well as Belfast. The scandalous condition of Lough Neagh symbolises the deficiencies of a polity that now seems trapped in an endless cycle of dysfunction. The steady deterioration of public services such as healthcare, education and policing can partly be attributed to underfunding. But matters have been made much worse by the existence of a political vacuum and sectarian grandstanding where effective government should be.

Power-sharing designed to reassure nationalist and unionist communities remains indispensable. But a loveless-marriage model that allows the largest party on either side of the divide to routinely bring assembly business to a halt is in urgent need of reform. Otherwise, faith in Stormont’s ability to act in the name of the common good is in danger of evaporating. Huge strides have been made in civil society since the Good Friday agreement was struck nearly three decades ago. But Northern Ireland’s voters currently do not have the politics they deserve.

The Guardian view on food security: we have just-in-time, we need just-in-case

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 17:25:36 GMT

Experts are warning that the UK is unprepared for crises. A refrigerator cyber-attack scare in France is the latest reminder of the risks

What’s worrying French supermarket bosses should be prompting British ministers to action. On Sunday, hackers forced up the temperatures of refrigerators in hundreds of food stores across France to as high as 50C, resulting in waste and fires. Beyond the immediate destruction and inconvenience, it raised the prospect of other malicious actors finding new ways to play havoc with the food chain.

Only weeks before, 150 experts together warned the British government that it does not have a plan to feed people in a crisis ­– and that the west is entering an era in which not only disruption but the weaponisation of food is a real possibility. “The public has been led to assume that food will simply be there,” they wrote. “It may not be.”

The Covid pandemic was a salutary reminder of how vulnerable modern systems are – a shock for consumers used to strawberries in October. Brexit, climate stress and the wars in Ukraine and Iran have underlined the risks and raised prices. One issue is overall supply in the UK, which imports about 40% of its food. But affordability, logistics, distribution and nutrition are also essential components of food security.

While food inflation has slowed, the cumulative impact has been severe. The Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit says that by September 2027, UK food prices are likely to be 50% higher than at the start of the cost of living crisis in mid-2021. That scale of increase previously took almost two decades. Food is a far smaller proportion of household budgets than it was 50 years ago. But the fifth of the population with the lowest incomes would need to spend 85% of their disposable income on food to meet governmental advice on healthy diets. Fruit and vegetables often give way to more filling but less nutritious options.

The government has encouraged households to stockpile several days’ worth of tinned goods and bottled water in case of an emergency. But outsourcing food security to individuals is a woefully inadequate response. Building civil food resilience will require more effort, including working with civil society.

Real improvement requires a structural shift away from the “leave it to Tesco” approach decried by Prof Tim Lang, a leading food-policy expert. As he points out, “framing markets is the job of politics”. Reliance on just-in-time last-minute deliveries and a few hubs makes economic sense for retailers, but is not conducive to national food security. Crises often winnow out smaller firms. But diversity is key to resilience. Geographical distribution – including relocalisation of food production – is also central. Almost 95% of retail food comes via 131 food-distribution centres. Disruption to just one supermarket chain’s infrastructure could have a mammoth impact.

Experts have rightly called for food supply shortages and disruption to be included as risks in their own right in the national security risk assessment. There is also a strong case for a dedicated national food council to focus on food security. The UK abandoned its strategic food stockpile in the 1990s. It should think again, as other countries around the world are doing.

Almost one in 10 households are already food-insecure. Others have become used to an age of abundance. None can count on food security without sustained action from the government, beginning with the recognition that this problem can’t be left to the market.

Trans women no longer to be placed on female-only wards under new NHS England guidance

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 17:15:01 GMT

Rules mean single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms will now be used by people based on their biological sex

Trans women will no longer be placed on female-only wards under new NHS England guidance on single-sex spaces.

The new rules, published on Thursday, mean single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms will be used by people based on their biological sex, not their gender identity.

The guidance states that trans people should be “accommodated in line with their biological sex” while ensuring their clinical needs are met and their “privacy, dignity and safety are maintained”, along with other patients sharing their accommodation.

It adds that in cases where clinical needs and same-sex accommodation requirements cannot both be met, clinical needs are the priority.

Updated guidance for NHS England staff has also been published, stating that all organisations should carry out an audit of their provision to ensure it protects the “privacy, dignity and safety of all staff”.

It states that in NHS trusts with mainly single-sex facilities, “suitable and accessible alternatives, such as single‑occupancy or mixed-sex facilities with individual lockable rooms, can be provided”.

Previous NHS England guidance said patients and staff could be accommodated on wards or use facilities based on their gender identity.

In a joint statement, TransActual and Trans+ Solidarity Alliance said the guidance would “not survive contact with reality in resource-strapped hospitals and will create unworkable operational challenges”.

“This NHS guidance emphasises clinical judgment as the priority over blanket exclusion, but leaves individual healthcare professionals unclear on how to safely look after trans patients,” they said.

“Forcing trans people into spaces for our sex assigned at birth will never be the most clinically appropriate decision, and would push trans people away from accessing care.”

They added that “the government failing to get a grip of this legal mess was sadly putting politics over patient care”.

The guidance has been updated after last year’s supreme court ruling that stated the terms “woman” and “sex” in the Equality Act referred only to a biological woman and to biological sex, and did not include transgender women with gender recognition certificates.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) code has already been revised to confirm a service must be used on the basis of biological sex for it to be classed as single sex under the Equality Act.

Maya Forstater, the chief executive and co-founder of the charity Sex Matters, said the policies “represent a momentous shift back to reality”, but she was “concerned that NHS England has not said how rules based on biological sex will be implemented”.

She also criticised the fact the guidance had been published 18 months after the supreme court judgment, saying it had initially been promised “within weeks”.

She cited the case of the female nurses at Darlington memorial hospital who won an employment tribunal case in January after being forced to share single-sex changing rooms with a trans colleague.

The tribunal found that the nurses faced “a hostile, intimidating, humiliating and degrading environment” at work and were told to “broaden their mindsets” when raising their concerns.

Bethany Hutchison, the lawyer who led the claim, said she welcomed the new “clear and necessary guidance from NHS England”.

“The test now is whether NHS trusts will actually follow it. The Darlington nurses should never have had to take their own employer to court to secure privacy, dignity and lawful single-sex facilities,” she said.

“Enforcement cannot continue to depend on the courage and personal sacrifice of individual nurses.”

Trump cancels plan to livestream execution after global condemnation

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 17:03:56 GMT

Soldier who killed 13 people in 2009 will still be executed, but president said ‘people would rather not watch him die’

Donald Trump has shelved a widely condemned plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

In a social media post on Thursday, Trump argued that broadcasting such an execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan” but said that “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device”.

“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump added. “That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose.”

Hasan, who was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot by law enforcement officers during the shooting at Fort Hood, now uses a wheelchair.

The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, said last week that the execution of Hasan would be a public event. Hasan’s sentence will be the first military execution in more than 60 years, and would have been the first in US history to be publicly broadcast.

In a statement to the Guardian on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Pentagon said Trump and Hegseth “spoke about the decision to not livestream Hasan’s execution” before Trump’s statement. Hegesth “supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned”, they added.

In an interview with Real America’s Voice last Thursday, Hegseth said he supported the public execution “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things”.

But since then, the Trump administration has faced sweeping criticism, and comparisons to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan. Many US lawmakers, from across the political spectrum, have come out and condemned the announcement, and urged Hegseth to reconsider.

Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, wrote in a post on social media: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”

In another post, Lisa Murkowski, a Republican senator from Alaska, said that there was “no need to livestream any execution, including this one”, adding that she “would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America”.

The representative Rob Bresnahan, a Republican from Pennsylvania, said in a post on social media that “an execution shouldn’t be a live-streamed spectacle”, adding that “the focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment”.

“Their pain deserves respect, not a public show,” he said.

On Friday of last week, the United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”, and the president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops also condemned the Pentagon’s plan, saying in a statement that “in no way can Hassan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.

“The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people,” the statement added.

That same day, JD Vance appeared to cast doubt on whether the Pentagon would actually livestream the execution, telling reporters that “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen” when asked about the plans. The vice-president also said that if it were livestreamed, “I’m not going to be watching it.”

But over the weekend, Markwayne Mullin, who heads the Department of Homeland Security, stood behind the administration’s decision to livestream the execution.

Speaking with CBS News, Mullin said that “no one has to watch it” and said: “I follow President Trump. He’s the commander in chief of the country, and he does a phenomenal job. He leads this country with a very, very, very direct, forward, straight hand, and he’s restoring American values.”

Trump himself had made contrasting remarks in recent days on whether the live stream would happen. On Friday, he told reporters that he “absolutely” approved the plan to livestream the execution, but on Saturday he said that he had not yet made a final decision on whether to go through with it.

“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it” he said. “’Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I’ll make a decision.”

An autism diagnosis, but where’s the treatment?

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 16:51:51 GMT

Rebecca Hope Duncan says she has not received any help after being assessed as autistic, in response to Prof Peter Fonagy’s review of mental health, ADHD and autism services. Plus letters from Jeremy Seymour, John Bryant, Peter Deadman, Steve Bamford and another reader

Your coverage of the Fonagy review concentrates on children and on the risk of diagnosing too readily (NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds, 9 October). I’d like to speak for those of us who were not diagnosed at all.

I first asked for help at 17. For 34 years I was treated for anxiety, depression and trauma. All were real; none were the whole story. I was diagnosed as autistic at 51. The same report identified ADHD, which until 2013 could not officially be diagnosed alongside autism.

I am still waiting for that ADHD assessment. ADHD is the one for which there is medication, but I cannot get to it. For autism there is nothing: you are given the diagnosis and sent home to deal with it.

The review asks for support based on need, not labels. I’d welcome that. But I have the label and the need, and neither has brought support. The diagnosis explained my life; it did not come with any help to live it. Rebecca Hope Duncan Southampton

Your editorial (11 October) correctly identifies the need for improved prevention and treatment of neurodevelopmental disorders, rather than rehearsing debates about diagnosis. Here are three additional suggestions.

First, neurodevelopment largely occurs during sleep: neuroplasticity is what sleep is for. Many infants and children are sleep-deprived, so a national public health programme on improving child sleep hygiene will prevent and ameliorate the severity of future neurodevelopment disorders.

Second, depression. Many young people with autism spectrum disorder and ADHD also fulfil criteria for depression, which is treatable at GP surgeries with combinations of exercise and pluralistic psychological therapy.

Third, work: to not work is bad for the mental health of young people with neurodivergence. If you can exercise, you can work, so the government could follow Dutch and Danish models and return to the supported employment and tax credits previously devised by Gordon Brown, undone by the political vandalism of Tory/Liberal Democrat austerity. Jeremy Seymour Retired consultant psychiatrist, Sheffield

Your editorial mentions that “the rises in psychological distress, and the need for support with neurodevelopmental differences, are real and tied to social changes”.

If the problems are tied to social changes, why is it primarily a healthcare issue? Wouldn’t we be better off calling out the “social changes” and addressing them?

It’s possible to do that while acknowledging the reality of the suffering of those involved, dignifying it in fact. By focusing entirely on the symptoms, we risk ignoring the root, and in doing so will allow more children to suffer. John Bryant GP, Bristol

Given the alarming rise in childhood mental health problems, why do we allow our children to be fed on ultra-processed foods (UPFs)? Childhood anxiety is on the rise globally, but the UK is in the worst-performing group of wealthy nations in virtually every measure of child and adolescent mental health. Coincidentally, British children also have the equal worst diets in the world – along with the US – in terms of consumption of UPFs, which make up around two-thirds of their diet. A 2026 systematic review found a clear association between child and adolescent consumption of UPFs and mental health problems such as anxiety, depression, irritability, sleep disturbances and suicidal ideation. And a Canadian study of over 2,000 children found that as children ate more UPFs, they faced increasing risk of emotional and behavioural problems, and that replacing just 10% of UPF calories with minimally processed real food, lowered children’s behaviour problem scores. Until the government is ready to stand up to the powerful food industry and ignores the inevitable cries of “nanny state”, this won’t change. Peter Deadman Hove, East Sussex

The differing explanations for the huge rise in diagnoses for autism and ADHD arise, I believe, from a general problem in the diagnosis of mental health conditions. In physical medicine, diagnosis includes not just the description and classification of symptoms, but identifying the underlying pathology that gives rise to the symptoms, and where possible the cause of this pathology.

A symptom such as a headache, for example, can arise for a variety of reasons, and a diagnosis will determine what its origin is. The characteristics of the headache, such as severity, exact location and duration, will give clues as to the underlying cause, but this can only be determined accurately by medical tests. There are some conditions where a group of symptoms regularly occur together but where the underlying pathology is unknown; these are classed as syndromes, and the names for them are descriptive rather than true diagnoses.

In the area of mental health, there are few if any diagnoses in the strict sense, and the terms used are descriptive rather than truly diagnostic. Even for the most severe conditions, such as schizophrenia, the underlying pathology is unknown, and this is even more true of conditions such as depression and anxiety, where the distinction between normal reactions and conditions severe enough to be regarded as illnesses is unclear.

Nobody seriously questions that the phenomena of autism and ADHD exist; the question is whether the concept of diagnosis is appropriate. If not, the distinction between what is “normal” and what is a “disorder” is arbitrary, based on the severity of the problems experienced and how well someone is able to function. The criteria for autism have been broadened to include people on the “spectrum” with much milder difficulties than in the past, while ADHD is a condition that has only recently been recognised at all. It is therefore not surprising that many more have been diagnosed than in the past. However, it also raises the question of whether, in the milder cases, they should be regarded as “disorders” as opposed to differences in personality. Steve Bamford Littlehampton, West Sussex

It’s not just young people who have been let down by the lack of diagnosis and care available to those with ADHD and Autism. My 70-year-old wife has suffered from one of these conditions throughout her life, along with many others of her generation. Had she been diagnosed at an early age, she would have had a much easier, more successful and fulfilling life. However, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence and NHS guidelines in the UK did not recognise ADHD as a valid condition in adults until 2008, when she was aged 52 and her condition began to become more evident postmenopause.

Being born in the north of England in the 1950s meant there was little or no chance of her receiving a childhood diagnosis that would have made her life much more understandable. Today, living in Scotland where the NHS does not offer the “right to choose” for ADHD assessments, she would face a median wait time of 111 weeks, with some waits as long as 266 weeks and currently 8,886 adults in the queue. Not surprisingly she continues to remain undiagnosed along with many others. Name and address supplied

Eritrean aggression must not be overlooked

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 16:51:26 GMT

Biruk Mekonnen, the Ethiopian ambassador to the UK, responds to an editorial on the war in Tigray

Your attention to Ethiopia is welcome, but your editorial (8 October) presents an incomplete account of the crisis, framing Ethiopia’s national interests as sources of regional instability while insufficiently examining the actions of other actors.

The opening reference to the Nobel peace prize is particularly telling. By suggesting that the committee will hope its next choice “ages better than 2019’s”, the editorial invites readers to question Abiy Ahmed’s award because of the war that followed a year later. Yet the prime minister received the prize for his efforts to achieve peace with Eritrea. The subsequent war in Tigray does not erase that achievement or, by itself, establish that the award was undeserved.

Describing the rapprochement with Eritrea as having “facilitated a war with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front” implies causation without adequately explaining the evidence. Likewise, claiming Mr Abiy’s coalition is “held together by his patronage” reduces political support to personal favours without establishing that this is what sustains it.

More seriously, the editorial overlooks the broader context of Eritrean aggression. The current crisis must also be understood in the context of an Eritrean foreign policy that, from Ethiopia’s perspective, has treated a weak Ethiopia as serving Eritrea’s interests.

The call for a truce also fails to address responsibility for renewed hostilities. Dialogue is welcome, but it must not reward armed aggression with political leverage or pressure Ethiopia into concessions. Ethiopia’s pursuit of Red Sea access and its right to develop the Nile’s resources should not be portrayed as threats simply because they challenge neighbouring states’ preferences.

Whether or not Eritrea’s strategic value to Washington explains its approach, that should not eclipse the consequences of its actions for Ethiopia’s sovereignty and security. Biruk Mekonnen Ethiopian ambassador to the UK

The UK must have digital sovereignty

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 16:51:15 GMT

The government must stop allowing foreign companies to have access to our sensitive data, writes Ian White. Plus a letter from Bill Cawley

The UK cannot become dependent on foreign AI technology that can be switched off at short notice, says George Williamson, head of the Alan Turing Institute (Report, 10 October). The growing opposition to Palantir, an American company, having government contracts that give it access to sensitive data are all part of the same issue. The UK does not have digital sovereignty.

This is not a theoretical problem. The US government imposed targeted sanctions on the international criminal court, stopping all digital services to certain individuals. This could happen to a country.

Even if you use European email and cloud services, our computer operating systems require constant software updates. This is not just to add new features. There is a constant race between the good guys patching the software bugs and the bad guys trying to gain entry to your computer using those same software bugs.

Recently, Holland and France took active steps to break the near monopoly of big Amercian tech by laying the foundations of a nationwide IT ecosystem that they would control. The UK needs to do the same. Ian White Cheltenham, Gloucestershire

The concern about the NHS’s dependence on Palantir (Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts, 9 October) is justified, but the £330m contract is a symptom of a wider habit. Whenever the government wants joined-up data, it buys one large platform from one supplier – and such projects have a long record of overrunning, costing far more than planned and locking the buyer in.

There is a working example of the alternative: the world wide web. It does not require everyone’s data to sit in one place or run on one company’s software. It simply defines how data is requested and transferred.

The NHS needs the same: an open specification for exchanging records, plus a registry of where each patient’s data is held. Any authorised clinician could then assemble the full picture of my treatment, while each hospital or practice chose its own software supplier. Specialist firms could still compete to analyse the data for planning and research – but none would own the plumbing.

The NHS already has the beginnings of this in its interoperability standards. Why do the money and political attention go to a single proprietary platform rather than to making open standards mandatory? Bill Cawley Ludlow, Shropshire

Eritrea accuses Shabana Mahmood of ‘political gimmick’ over visa ban threat

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 16:40:18 GMT

Home secretary says she will block all Eritreans from UK unless a returns deal is agreed for rejected asylum seekers and criminals

Shabana Mahmood has been accused of launching a “perfunctory political gimmick” by the Eritrean government in a row over the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals.

After the home secretary threatened to block all Eritreans from entering the UK unless a returns deal was agreed, the country’s embassy claimed the UK had failed to engage in “meaningful and appropriate” dialogue.

The spat began on Thursday morning when the Home Office claimed the east African country had abruptly withdrawn cooperation on the return of unwanted citizens earlier this year.

From Thursday, diplomats from the east African country also face restrictions on their movement outside London and VIPs will be stripped of access to fast-track visas as preferential processing is scrapped.

It prompted a statement from Eritrea’s north London embassy “categorically” rejecting Mahmood’s claims.

“Despite Eritrea’s repeated requests for constructive discussion with relevant UK authorities on the dignified return of its citizens, the UK has shown no interest to engage in meaningful and appropriate dialogue,” it said.

Describing the home secretary’s decision as regrettable, the statement added: “The act is nothing more than a perfunctory political gimmick. The fact is, the UK has not issued a single visa to an Eritrean official since 2023.”

UK government officials denied this. They insisted a confirmed exemption from immigration control for an Eritrean official took place as recently as August 2026.

Sources said Eritrea previously cooperated with the UK on returns between 2024 and March 2026, while the UK has repeatedly sought to engage with Eritrean authorities, including repeatedly offering to send a Home Office delegation to Asmara to discuss returns.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “The Eritrean government’s press notice misrepresents the UK’s position and contains numerous factual inaccuracies.”

Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat in the year ending June 2026. Returns arrangements are vital for removing people who have been refused asylum and foreign criminals.

Mahmood said on Thursday morning: “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused.

“My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK. I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to cooperate.”

The move followed similar threats of visa sanctions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2025.

Angola and Namibia subsequently agreed to cooperate with demands on migrant returns, while the DRC faced visa restrictions before reaching an agreement with the UK in February.

In March, ministers also placed an emergency brake on visas for nationals from four countries after the home secretary accused them of exploiting Britain’s generosity to claim asylum.

Study visas for nationals from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan were also halted, as were work visas for Afghans.

Just over 100 refused asylum seekers from Eritrea have been deported – a figure comprising less than 4% of the 2,626 people whose claims were rejected in the past four years. Nearly 6,000 Eritreans have reached the UK across the Channel in the year to June, the highest number of any nationality.

After the success of the previous sanction threats, Mahmood warned other countries that they faced similar visa restrictions if they continued to refuse to take back their criminals, illegal migrants and rejected asylum seekers.

India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Somalia, Egypt and Gabon have been identified as resistant to taking back illegal migrants and could face sanctions.

Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said roughly 7,000 applications for asylum came from Eritreans, about 8% of the total.

About 84% were successful on first application and more would be successful on appeal, she said.

“There are different types of threats that can be made such as stopping student visas, or stopping visit visas. It will be interesting to see what kind of impact this has on the number of returns.”

Reacting to Mahmood’s announcement, one Eritrean asylum seeker said any returnees would “be put in prison and may never be able to get out”.

The advocacy group Justice for Eritreans condemned the announcement. “Many Eritreans have fled indefinite national service, arbitrary detention and severe human rights abuses,” it said. “These risks cannot be ignored for the sake of immigration targets. Refugee protection is a legal responsibility, not a political bargaining tool.”

UN experts say the human rights situation in Eritrea continues to be dire. Mohamed Abdelsalam Babiker, the special rapporteur on human rights in Eritrea, said there were no signs of meaningful improvement in the country’s human rights situation.

“There remain reasonable grounds to believe that crimes against humanity continue in Eritrea,” he said when launching a report this year into the human rights situation.

“Regrettably, the core human rights issues that prompted the creation of this mandate 14 years ago remain mostly unresolved.

“The ongoing systematic, and widespread enforced disappearance and prolonged incommunicado detention without charge or trial, torture, and the persecution of political opponents, journalists, and members of religious communities remain central features of governance in Eritrea.”

Steve Valdez-Symonds, Amnesty International’s policy lead on refugee and migrant rights, said: “As Amnesty and others have documented, Eritrea has an appalling human rights record.

“It has not become any less unsafe following the election in this country of a Labour government in 2024 or Shabana Mahmood beginning her term at the Home Office in 2025.”

Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “Severe political repression and widespread human rights abuses are the reason people are forced to flee Eritrea, and are, in the vast majority of cases, recognised by our government as in need of support.

“It’s imperative that this policy only targets the Eritrean authorities, and does not undermine the UK’s moral and legal duty to provide protection to those who need it.”

The one that got away: Tom Willis back to show what England are missing

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 16:19:01 GMT

Bordeaux No 8 takes on Gloucester in Champions Cup to underline hole he will leave Borthwick for the World Cup

Swines are swirling above Twickenham, the cows have returned to their roots and hell is an icy sub-zero. Steve Borthwick has been given a free pass to pick one player based outside England. The consensus is that Jack Willis – Toulouse captain and two‑time Top 14 player of the season – would be the obvious choice. The smart money, however, would be on Borthwick picking brother Tom in a flash.

For clarity, this is not going to happen. It is not World Cup season without a cause celebre but the reality is that you, dear reader, have more chance of selection. Still, the story of the younger Willis warrants re-examining. Firstly because his decision to head for France after receiving an enhanced contract was unprecedented. Secondly because for Bordeaux he is pulling up trees, forests and anything else in his way this season. England’s No 8 depth is shallow and Willis is the type of player Borthwick would give his right arm for. After Bordeaux have begun their Champions Cup defence at Gloucester on Friday, chances are his left too.

“He’s an incredible competitor,” Bordeaux’s attack coach Noel McNamara says. “You can talk all you want about the technical and tactical but sometimes it’s just about desire. He won an aerial battle a couple weeks ago that I showed to the backs. Tom just wanted that ball, he’s an unbelievable competitor more than anything else. The Top 14 is incredibly competitive, because of relegation, because of the JIFF rule [which limits the number of foreign players]. That adds its own pressure and it’s not for everybody. We knew what we were getting, not just the player, he’s a fantastic human being.”

Willis’s decision will not have been easy but by the time he informed Borthwick, shortly before the 2025 autumn internationals, his mind was made up despite having received the enhanced contract worth £150,000 a couple of months earlier. As someone who could offer ball-carrying heft, hard yards, Willis was a dead cert for the plane to Australia in 2027. Borthwick’s decision to leave him out immediately was equally difficult but he felt there was no choice with less than two years until the World Cup. What message would he have sent had he not?

“I understand both sides, I understand the benefits for the [Prem], and I knew the rules before making my choice. I have no problem with it,” Willis told Midi Olympique last week when asked about England’s selection policy. “There are strong arguments on both sides. Some say it’s bad, others that it’s necessary. I could have stayed in England to remain eligible, but I decided to leave.”

It is clear Willis felt a strong draw to Bordeaux and there are obvious reasons why. After Wasps went bust he joined the club on a short‑term deal in November 2022 before moving to Saracens the following summer. He arrived in France just after the head coach, Christophe Urios, had left, did not speak French and had never lived alone before. The personal growth those circumstances precipitated meant that Willis had a deep-rooted connection with the club. It helps, too, they are one of Europe’s leading lights, the money is good and the lifestyle appeals. The opportunity to be close to Jack was an enormous factor too. The Willis family is exceptionally tight-knit.

It is less clear precisely when in 2025 Bordeaux planted the seed. Saracens, for their part, were desperate to keep him. His first season in north London was disrupted by a knee injury but his second was mightily impressive. One performance against the Bulls in December 2024 stood out. Willis had been challenged to perform at “an elevated level” after being overlooked for the autumn Tests. Against the Bulls, he knocked a few Springboks around like they were nine-pins.

By the 2025 Six Nations, Borthwick had been convinced. Willis had one cap in a World Cup warm-up match against Wales but returned to the fold initially as a replacement against Ireland. “I felt like I had not had a proper crack at playing for England and that is really what I wanted to do,” he said at the time. Starts followed in victories over France, Scotland and Italy but while Willis did little wrong, there was a feeling he wasn’t quite reaching his best at Test level. He was back on the bench against Wales and while a regular in the matchday 23, he had not managed to force his way into the British & Irish Lions conversation.

Then came the 2025 tour of Argentina and the USA. With Tom Curry, Ben Earl and Henry Pollock away, with less spotlight on England, Willis shone. His performances against the Pumas were emphatic and a few months later, Borthwick rewarded him with an enhanced deal. Willis had made strides when some of the bigger fish were away, when the pond was a little smaller.

The suggestion is Willis does not possess self-belief by the bucketload as someone like Earl does, that he needs the odd reminder of his talents. Maybe the environment in Argentina was perfect for him then, particularly with the presence of Lee Blackett on the coaching staff. But speak to those who know him well and they reject any sense of timidity wholeheartedly. There may be a hint of shyness but “deep-thinking” and “diligent” are the words that come up. That he was spotted at Bordeaux’s base finishing a French lesson at 5pm recently bears that out.

It also says much about Willis that in his third and final season with Saracens, despite his impending move, he was named Prem player of the year, producing more carries and beating more defenders than anyone in the league. Bordeaux evidently know how to harness those talents but McNamara cautions against pigeon-holing. “Jack is perceived as more of a defensive player and Tom as offensive but we can be very reductive,” says McNamara. “Against Clermont recently Tom had four turnovers. He’s a very smart player, he’s got leadership capabilities. He is doing that with his actions and he’s learning the language diligently so he can express himself.”

The way Willis is performing does not suggest any regrets but if there is a tinge of sadness it is that we cannot be sure if he knew or understood quite how highly Borthwick regarded him at the very point Bordeaux turned his head. That is neither’s fault, it merely shows the importance of timing. The upshot is one of the most talented English players of his generation will not grace the World Cup stage next year. It is a testament to Willis’ character, however, that he left little open to interpretation when recently asked if he did not get a fair crack of the whip. “I did get the opportunities, and I was delighted to have them,” he said. “I have no issue with the coaching staff. I simply chose something different.”

John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 16:17:05 GMT

Exclusive: Chancellor to target sector in his first budget, to help offset Iran war’s damage to public finances

John Healey is poised to tax Britain’s banks in his 28 October budget, to help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, the Guardian understands.

The chancellor is in Bangkok, where the International Monetary Fund has praised the UK’s progress towards balancing the books, urging him to “stay the course”.

To keep the Treasury’s deficit reduction plans on track in the face of rising government borrowing costs, the Guardian understands Healey has decided to tap the financial sector for additional revenue.

One option understood to be under discussion – reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt – would raise upwards of £2bn a year.

Lenders have been logging strong earnings on the back of rising interest rates, with the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds Banking Group – alone having generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years.

Thinktanks and trade unions have repeatedly urged Healey to tax Britain’s banks more heavily, an option considered but rejected by his predecessor Rachel Reeves, who was wary of deterring future investment.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), said: “Britain’s big four banks are making a billion pounds a week, while bonuses have hit a post-crash record. These are bumper profits, driven by high interest rates and households’ mortgage misery. It’s time to make sure banks pay their fair share.”

Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, Healey praised the banks as crucial to supporting economic growth. “People too often see them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects,” he said.

But he is nevertheless believed to be minded to increase the surcharge banks pay on their profits, over and above corporation tax. Industry figures believe that will probably mean raising the surcharge back to 8%, from 3% at present.

The UK’s cost of borrowing has risen sharply in recent weeks, alongside that of other big economies, as bond markets have responded to the prospect of higher inflation as a result of the Middle East conflict.

Analysts have suggested that could as much as halve the £24bn cushion Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules at the time of the spring forecast in March.

Healey is understood to be willing to accept a narrower “headroom”, but is also keen to convince bond markets he is wedded to deficit reduction.

Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against tax rises since narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget. UK bosses of lenders including HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest, Barclays and Santander met Healey last week but were given no reassurance that bank tax hikes had been ruled out. Their lobby groups – including UK Finance and TheCityUK – wrote to Healey days later, saying that on top of “weakening investors confidence and damaging UK attractiveness”, higher taxes would force them to move staff and business out of the country. That echoed warnings by the chief executive of JP Morgan, Jamie Dimon, who said in May he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile towards banks. News of the tower – which will house more than half of the US investment bank’s 23,000 UK staff – was came days after Reeves spared the sector further tax rises in her 2025 autumn budget.

One industry source said banks were resigned to a rise in the surcharge. They believe Healey is minded to reverse Hunt’s cut – taking it back to 8% – but not go further. Such a move would raise £2.25bn a year, according to analysis by the TUC.

Another industry source said they were caught off guard by the change in messaging, having come just hours after Healey hailed banks as a “jewel” in the crown of the British economy. “We’re surprised to see this following earlier comments which appeared to be more supportive of the sector.”

When asked about how much the banking industry might be able to absorb in terms of tax rises, the head of policy at TheCityUK, John Godfrey, said banks “do not want to get into debating the menu of taxation. The fact is that we don’t want to eat in that restaurant.”

Healey has also been “listening to representations” from specialist banks, including Revolut and Shawbrook, that want the profit threshold at which the surcharge kicks in to be raised from £100m to £500m.

One government source said Labour was mindful of the UK needing to offer a positive environment for startup banks, especially the lending they offered to small businesses.

The TUC has lobbied for a much more punitive increase, to 16%, saying that could raise £24bn in tax revenues over the next four years.

Healey said he wanted his first budget as chancellor to give “breathing space” to both consumers and businesses in the face of rising energy prices.

There will be little additional funding for other Whitehall departments, however, which he stressed would have to stick to the budgets Reeves set out at her spending review in June 2025.

“It’s important that they do manage within what they’ve got, and it’s part of the job,” Healey said. “You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things, or more.”

The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said Reeves’s plans could result in real-terms spending cuts for some departments in the later years of the spending review period.

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, used a visit to a financial services firm in Edinburgh on Thursday to caution against further banking tax rises, saying the sector already faced a higher effective tax rate than in many other big global financial centres.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Britain needs growth. But a raid on the financial services sector will stifle it. Labour should be backing businesses and wealth-creators, not making their lives even harder. Rather than hiking taxes yet again, Labour should cut spending.”

As well as an energy support package for households and businesses, Healey’s first budget is expected to set out more details of plans to devolve income tax to mayoralties, and explain how the government will fully fund the four-year defence investment plan announced by Keir Starmer before he stepped down as prime minister.

Healey is expected to duck the longer-term question of when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence, the issue over which he resigned as defence secretary in June, contributing to Starmer’s downfall.

How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 16:16:10 GMT

International delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of years

After decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour.

Delegates from 69 countries cast their votes on Thursday at a conference in France of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which ensures the world sticks to the same standards of time, weight, distance and more.

The decision to adopt the leap hour from next year aims to reduce the risk of computers and other technical systems tripping over as their software grapples with minutes lasting 61 seconds – and, worse, 59 seconds – instead of a round 60.

“After 30 years of debate, the leap second is making way for the leap hour,” said Dr Setnam Shemar, principal scientist in the time and frequency department at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL). “This will reduce the risks to the systems and national infrastructure that depend on accurate time while still preserving the fundamental link between our global time system and the rotation of the Earth.”

The vote at Versailles means that coordinated universal time (UTC) can drift up to an hour from astronomical time before a leap hour is needed, but that is unlikely to happen for thousands of years.

“We already have daylight saving where we change by an hour and no one gets bothered about that, apart from losing sleep or getting an extra hour’s sleep,” said Shemar, who sat on the international timekeeping expert committee that proposed the leap hour.

The more familiar leap year was introduced more than 2,000 years ago to ensure that the calendar year did not fall out of step with the time that the Earth takes to circle the sun. Adding a day to the end of February every four or so years does the job, because Earth orbits the sun every 365 and a quarter days.

Leap seconds are a much more modern invention. In 1955, Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the NPL built the world’s first practical, high-precision caesium atomic clock. The device revolutionised timekeeping, and in 1967 the astronomical definition of a second, based on the rotation of the Earth, was abandoned. Ever since, the formal definition of one second has been 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the caesium atom.

Atomic clocks are exceptionally stable and precise. Their timekeeping has become critical for modern computer systems, communications, satellites, trading systems and electricity grids. But the Earth’s rotation is far less reliable. Its spin is affected by the planet’s molten core, the shift of the oceans, global jet streams and other natural forces.

Broadly, Earth’s rotation is slowing down: when an asteroid doomed the dinosaurs, a day lasted about 23 and a half hours. Because of this, officials have added 27 leap seconds since 1972 to ensure UTC is aligned with astronomical time.

The strategy endured for more than 50 years until scientists spotted a fresh reason to fear technological mayhem. In the past decade, Earth’s rotation has sped up, meaning officials might have needed to add the first negative leap second, equivalent to lopping a second off UTC. The 30% probability of a negative leap second in the next decade brought the Versailles vote forward.

“Leap seconds can be tricky enough to deal with,” said Shemar. Telecommunications, electricity grids and navigation systems used high-accuracy timing, he explained, but software updates could apply leap seconds at the wrong time, knocking networks out of sync.

Sign up to TechScape

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

“After the leap second applied in 2012, there were some computer systems whose operating systems couldn’t cope with 61 seconds in a minute. The servers froze, they seized up. Systems went offline. And those are the sorts of failures that can happen with positive leap seconds,” Shemar said.

Among the crashed websites were Reddit and LinkedIn. Separately, Qantas flights were hit with delays. Negative leap seconds come with even greater risks. “There could be software out there that hasn’t been tested on negative leap seconds because we’ve never had to apply one before,” Shemar said.

To test all the computer systems that talk to one another around the world would cost companies a fortune. It was this concern that swung the vote.

Historically, the UK has grumbled about canning leap seconds because of the link with Greenwich mean time. Russia has also opposed the move, citing concerns of the impact on its Glonass satellite navigation system.

The IERS Earth Orientation Centre, in Paris, tracks changes in the Earth’s rotation and other movements that feed into UTC. The centre also issues notices when leap seconds must be added.

Dr Christian Bizouard, the director of the centre, approved of the vote, but said it passed the decision to people far in the future. “It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” he said. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”
