‘A powerful act of imagination and self-affirmation’: experts on how to start writing a book

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 16:00:36 GMT

Thinking about writing a book and doing it are two very different things – so how to get started and follow through?

At some point in their lives, many people are confronted with a big question: what if I wrote a book?

Writing a memoir, murder mystery or steamy romance is an accomplishment. Like running a marathon or successfully filing your taxes, it speaks to grit, determination and hours of research and effort.

But thinking about writing a book and actually doing it are two very different things. According to a 2021 survey by ThriftBooks, more than half of respondents thought they had a good idea for a novel, but only 15% had started writing, and only 8% had finished.

So how does one get started and follow through? We asked experts.

“So many reasons”, says Jami Attenberg, bestselling author and founder of the annual writing project 1000 Words of Summer.

For some, it’s a necessary form of artistic expression. “They’re born writers, and this is how they communicate with the world,” Attenberg says.

For others, she says, there’s a story in them that’s dying to get out, and writing provides “that cathartic release”.

Still others are motivated by the difficulty of the task.

“Writing a book is a powerful act of imagination and self-affirmation,” says Marita Golden, novelist and co-founder of the Zora Neale Hurston/Richard Wright Foundation, which fosters and celebrates Black writers. “It is demanding, scary and the kind of personal challenge that many people find irresistible.”

That there are so many different reasons for so many different people is encouraging, Attenberg says: “It means people still read, love and value books.”

And yet, lots of people who talk about writing books don’t actually do it – or they start, and never finish. (For example, without naming any names: me.)

For a lot of people, “it’s difficult and they don’t know how to do it”, says novelist Christopher Moore. “Once you’ve written one, it’s difficult, but you know how to do it,” he adds.

Often, Golden says, aspiring writers are stopped by their own negative self-talk. Perhaps others have questioned their abilities, or they feel writing a book is only for “certain types of people”, she says.

Some fret that they won’t accomplish what they set out to do. “People fear that if they begin the process, they won’t complete it, and that will reinforce their insecurity or open them to criticism and judgment,” Golden says.

And, Attenberg says: “Life can get in the way.”

Read. While everyone’s writing process is different, experts agree one practice is non-negotiable: reading. A lot. This allows you to figure out what you like and don’t like, identify the different tools authors use, and get inspired.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

“Figure out who your influences are, what kind of books you want to be writing, what genre, what length, what kind of vibe,” says Attenberg, adding that she starts every workday by reading someone else’s writing. “Literature, to me, is a big, beautiful, noisy conversation, and we can all learn from and be inspired by other people’s work.”

Figure out why you want to write. “Having something to say is important,” says Moore. Even if you’re not writing a polemic, Moore says, in the process of writing a book, you should regularly be asking yourself: “What am I saying here?”

“It doesn’t have to be profound,” he says. “It might be showing your unique perspective on a topic that’s been covered.”

Research. “Some kind of research is where I start,” says Moore. This is more than looking up dates and places, he explains – it is finding out “what has been written before on the subject I’m interested in”, and then “creating characters to carry the story”.

More from How to start:

How to start weightlifting

How to start budgeting

How to start running

Set a start date. It’s easy to slip into a trap of endlessly preparing to write – telling yourself you’re just going to do a little more reading or add further detail to your outline before you start. To escape this, Moore suggests setting a start date. “On that date, I begin,” he says. Sometimes, all he writes that first day is a paragraph: “And that’s OK.”

Take a writing class. In addition to learning the basics of the craft, taking a writing class can help you meet other writers who can support you on your journey, Golden says.

Write yourself a letter. “Try to recall what your intentions were when you began this project,” Attenberg suggests. “Think about why it’s important to you to finish it. What would it mean for you to complete this project?”

Then, she says, set a reasonable but firm timeline for yourself and get going.

Write a scene. Even if it’s not in order, even if it’s a hundred pages from where you last stopped writing, “giving your characters a chance to talk to each other or make decisions will give you guidance for where to go next”, says Moore.

Don’t rewrite. “People get stopped because their expectation for themselves is too high,” says Moore. Allow yourself to write until you have a full first draft, and only then go back and edit. “Once you have a thing that vaguely resembles a book, you can always go back and shape and polish it until it’s what you want,” he says. “No one will ever know that, for a while, your masterpiece was absolute shit.”

Repressive, secretive and highly militarised: Eritrea, the east African country facing UK visa ban threat

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 15:52:19 GMT

Country has not had an election in 33 years and has withdrawn cooperation with UK on migrant returns

Eritrea, the east African country embroiled in a row with the UK over its refusal to accept the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals, is considered one of world’s most secretive and repressive states, with reports of arbitrary detention and severe restrictions on freedom of expression, opinion and religion.

Situated in the Horn of Africa and bordering Sudan, Ethiopia and Djibouti, it became a sovereign state after gaining independence from Ethiopia in 1993 following a 30-year war.

The country is run by an authoritarian regime under Isaias Afwerki, who led separatist forces to defeat Ethiopian forces in 1991 and became president in 1993. He has served as president since independence and heads the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice, the country’s only legal political party.

Eritrea has not held a national election since independence. A constitution that was ratified in 1997 by the constituent assembly has still not been implemented nearly three decades later.

In 2001, the government shut down all independent newspapers after the publishing of an open letter by senior ruling party officials calling on the government to implement the constitution and hold elections.

A highly militarised state, Eritrea runs a compulsory national service system that requires students to study at a military training centre in their final year of secondary school. They undergo military training and political education before working in either military units or civilian national service roles that can last decades.

The repression and conscription has forced many Eritreans to risk harsh punishment for evading, deserting or escaping the military by fleeing the country. It is estimated that up to one-third of the Eritrean-born population lives abroad.

Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat to the UK in the year ending June 2026. Earlier this year, Eritrea abruptly withdrew cooperation with the UK on migrant returns, and on Thursday the UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said all Eritreans could be stopped from coming to the UK unless the country agreed to accept more rejected asylum seekers and criminals.

Eritrea’s political, economic and social framework has been defined by a doctrine of economic self-reliance, with the country notably rejecting foreign aid.

It was an Italian colony and parts of the country feature early to mid-20th-century Italian modernist architecture. The capital, Asmara, was inscribed as a world heritage site in 2017, with Unesco describing it as “an exceptional example of early modernist urbanism at the beginning of the 20th century and its application in an African context”.

A multi-ethnic country, Eritrea is mainly made up of the Tigrinya people. Its extensive Red Sea coastline (1,388 miles) gives it a strategic position along the Red Sea corridor.

The country has been in the spotlight in recent weeks because of fears of war with Ethiopia. Both countries have accused each other of aggression. Ethiopia has claimed Eritrean troops crossed up to 60km (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, while Eritrea has said the accusation is a fabrication to create a pretext for war.

The escalation is linked to renewed fighting between Ethiopian government forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), an armed opposition group, in Tigray, which borders Eritrea.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, a claim that Eritrea has denied. On Tuesday, Ethiopian forces advanced to Zalambessa, ​a town on the border with Eritrea that was under Tigrayan rebel control.

Top health official urged to recuse herself from private ADHD crackdown over ties to industry

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 15:35:21 GMT

Exclusive: Four MPs raise conflict of interest concerns over Samantha Jones’s past links to a big provider of ADHD assessments

A senior civil servant should play no part in ministers’ crackdown on private attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism clinics because of her recent ties to the industry, MPs have said.

Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs are demanding that Samantha Jones, the permanent secretary at the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), steps away from any role in plans to toughen regulation of the booming market in private neurodiversity assessments.

They say Jones should not be involved because of her links to a company that is one of the biggest providers of NHS-funded neurodiversity assessments, which earned it £26m from the health service in England over the past six years.

Ministers are drawing up plans for how to better regulate the “wild west” of private clinics offering assessment, diagnosis and treatment of ADHD and autism that has grown rapidly in recent years as people have struggled to access care via the NHS.

The push comes after the government last week accepted the findings of a review by Prof Peter Fonagy, which raised concerns about the “consistency and quality” of assessments by private providers of neurodiversity services that had inbuilt “financial incentives” to diagnose and treat people.

Jones is responsible for overseeing the implementation of government decisions on health policy. She would therefore be expected to advise ministers on how best to strengthen the regulation of private providers of ADHD and autism services. Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, has vowed to introduce a much tougher regime.

Four MPs have called for Jones to recuse herself from any role in those decisions because of her previous ties to ADHD360, a provider of neurodiversity services. Her links to the private ADHD sector represent a serious conflict of interest, they claim.

Jones was appointed as the permanent secretary on 22 April 2025. A month later, she was still the chair of and a director of and shareholder in the private care provider Keys Group when, on 16 May, it bought ADHD360, a clinic that has increased its NHS income considerably in recent years.

At the time of the £22.5m purchase, Jones was also an operating partner in G Square Capital, the private equity company that owns Keys Group.

She sold her shares in Keys Group and resigned her roles there and at G Square Capital before she started at the DHSC on 16 June. Jones has already recused herself from involvement in the department’s decision over whether to extend Palantir’s £330m, seven-year contract with the NHS because of her past work for the lobbyists Carnall Farrar, which advised Palantir regarding the contract.

MPs believe her tenure at Keys Group could represent a conflict of interest. Ben Coleman, a Labour MP on the health and social care committee, said: “People will want to feel reassured that future regulation of private ADHD and autism assessments is beyond reproach. Given her recent close involvement with ADHD360, I would encourage Ms Jones to recuse herself from that work, as she has done over Palantir, to avoid any perception of a conflict of interest.”

In June, Jones apologised after she was reprimanded by the Civil Service Commission for breaching lobbying rules by failing to ask the (now defunct) Advisory Committee on Business Appointments for prior approval before undertaking work for four healthcare companies.

Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrats’ health spokesperson, said: “Given Sam Jones oversaw the multimillion-pound acquisition of ADHD360 just weeks before entering the Department of Health, ministers must ensure she recuses herself immediately, just as she has over Palantir.”

Jones, 55, was widely admired in the NHS when she ran West Hertfordshire NHS trust in 2013-15. After a role with NHS England, she began working in private healthcare. Boris Johnson as prime minister handed her a key role in Downing Street in 2021. She returned to private health in 2023 and by 2023-24 had paid roles or shareholdings in 13 health or consultancy organisations.

Clive Lewis, the Labour MP for Norwich South, said Jones’s deep involvement in private healthcare meant she should not have been made DHSC permanent secretary in the first place, saying: “It just defies logic that anyone thought it was a good idea. Surely this must have come up during her recruitment process?”

Jones did not answer questions put by the Guardian. The NHS has paid ADHD360 just over £26m for its services since 2020, according to figures supplied by the Tussell public expenditure database. “When it comes to the government’s response to the [Fonagy] review, there should be no suggestion that the top NHS official is being influenced by any past or current links to a major private provider of NHS ADHD services,” said Stella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow. “This issue is too sensitive and complex to permit any conflicts of interest. As a result the permanent secretary should recuse herself from this area of policy.”

David Rowland, the director of the Centre for Health and the Public Interest thinktank, said: “The permanent secretary at the department which has responsibility for regulating private ADHD providers appears to have a conflict of interest in this area and so may struggle to remain impartial when it comes to implementing the recommendations made by Prof Fonagy.”

A DHSC spokesperson said: “There is no conflict of interest. The permanent secretary has appropriately declared all interests, in this post and when she was a non-executive director [of the DHSC]. She resigned from all her private sector posts before taking on the permanent secretary role at the department.”

Just as Saint Nige thought it was safe to reappear, along comes pesky ITV

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 15:11:28 GMT

How dare the channel reveal more racism and bigotry within Reform just as he was planning a press conference?

Sometimes the world can be very unfair. As though life is just one cruel joke. How else to make sense of everything? For when the history books come to be written, Nigel Farage will go down as one of the century’s unluckiest politicians.

Poor Nige. All he has ever wanted is a better Britain. A country united in a shared vision where everyone gets along with one another. Where people of all faiths and none look out for each other. Where men and women of all colours are treated as equals. Where Nige can teach the world to sing in perfect harmony.

So why do so many bad things keep happening to such a good person? Where’s the justice in that? How come Nige has been given a lead role in the rewrite of Little Britain’s Book of Job. Nige as a latter day Old Testament prophet put on Earth to show us all the value of eternal suffering. Because Nige is a decent man. The very best of us. And yet time and again he is made to feel pain. No more so than in the last few months.

First there was the money. Few would have batted an eyelid if he had been given £5m by the RNLI. For all he has done to support the work that unpaid volunteers do in rescuing all people in trouble on the sea. Let’s face it, a modern day ministry doesn’t pay for itself and no demigod-like politician can expect to get by on less than £1m a year. Those houses and bottles of champagne aren’t going to pay for themselves. Yet because the £5m came from a Thai crypto-billionaire, suddenly everyone was asking difficult questions. Anyone would think Reform might have crypto-friendly policies.

Then there was the Channel 4 sting. And yet again our Messiah was the innocent victim of an establishment plot. Compared to Nige, Jesus had it easy in Holy Week. How could he be expected to realise that two associates whom he had barely known for years might allegedly be trying to secure an illegal donation from overseas? And what were the chances that Nige might be caught on camera giving considered responses as part of a conversation he hadn’t even been listening to? Some days you just can’t buy a break.

On Thursday morning, Farage had been scheduled to host a press conference near Southend where we were promised he would spread goodwill to all men with yet another major policy announcement. Only for the event to be cancelled late on Wednesday evening. The official reason given was that Reform didn’t want to clash with the fifth anniversary of the murder of the former Southend MP David Amess. Yet more bad luck for Nige. Imagine only being given five years’ notice to plan your schedule.

Or perhaps there was another reason for the cancellation. One related to another sting, this time by ITV, that had sent undercover journalists into the Reform operations room and uncovered the only bad apples in the entire organisation. Again, what were the chances of finding racists and misogynists attracted to a party that loved women and people of all colours?

How could this ever have happened? The chances were slimmer than winning the EuroMillions lottery. And surely had nothing to do with Nige’s would-be chancellor, Honest Bob Jenrick, saying he would consider allowing soldiers to be able to blow up migrants in small boats in the Channel. What’s wrong with killing a few thousand people for the sake of a greater good? The country is just too woke for its own good sometimes. Then there’s the wannabe home secretary Zia Yusuf, who is on a one-man mission to round up all immigrants – even women and children – and send them back to countries where they may be killed. So again we are left with the question. Why are so many racists attracted to Reform?

Let’s take Dean Miller. A vetted Reform councillor from Bromley who was filmed campaigning during the Makerfield byelection. Quite how extensive the vetting process was is anyone’s guess. “Tell us, Dean. Are you in any way prejudiced against people of colour?”. “Absolutely not. I just don’t want them anywhere near me.” “That’s great. Thanks Dean. Welcome to Reform.”

Anyway, Dean was caught on camera saying that it was kill or be killed with illegal immigrants. “They’re all fucking black and they’re like animals,” he said. “I’m not a racist, but you know what I mean.” Yes, Dean. We know exactly what you mean. And he couldn’t have been clearer about his intentions towards the king. Charles was a Muslim and deserved to be beheaded. It’s a view.

When Miller was asked for a comment before the film is aired this weekend, his defence was that he had been on heavy medication at the time. And suddenly that all made sense. Because I too am on regular medication both for my psyche and for my heart. So I chose to reread the common known side effects of one of my drugs. And there among the small print about causing faster breathing, fever, muscle stiffness and drowsiness, one thing stood out. “Never take in the presence of a black person or royalty. Can make you prone to racist outbursts and in extreme cases can provoke urges to kill the monarch.” I guess I must just have been extremely lucky so far.

Miller was not the only one to have been caught out this way. Others – also apparently vetted – declared that all foreigners were parasites, that the UK should have a 1% limit on all immigrants and made disgusting comments about a female Reform councillor. Raymond Dunning said he was so far-far right it was unbelievable. Then there were those who thought it best to try to sound moderate until after they had been elected. Then the gloves would come off and they could give foreigners hell.

And in the middle of all this we have the saintly Nige. Scratching his head and wondering why all this was happening to him again. He hadn’t come in to politics to stir grievance and division. He was the god of love, the man of peace. Others among the Reform elite knew exactly where the blame lay. And it wasn’t with the innocent men who had been caught saying the only racist and sexist words they had ever said. Dicky Tice and the former Tory MP Ben Bradley were pointing the finger at ITV for daring to do its job properly. It was outrageous they had recorded Reform councillors going about their everyday jobs. Every man and woman was entitled to be as racist as they like in the comfort of their workplace.

For now, Nige was determined to rise above it. He would survive. He was doing God’s work. Just a shame that God didn’t seem to like him much.

The Amol Rajan Connection review – another wrong move after lasting one night in The Celebrity Traitors?

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 15:05:39 GMT

The broadcaster has bullet-proof confidence as he departs the BBC. But his first YouTube show with Gareth Southgate is nowhere near as radical as you’d expect – and he sounds like yet another tech guru

Whatever you think of Amol Rajan, he can’t be accused of not dreaming big. In the clip trailing the launch of his YouTube project The Amol Rajan Connection, he acknowledges the seismic volatility of our times but locates himself firmly at the heart of them. “We are about to get 100 years of change in a single decade,” he says. “And that’s scary. But maybe I can help.” Big talk for someone who somehow managed the singular feat of being outlasted by Richard E Grant in The Celebrity Traitors. But joking aside, Rajan’s bulletproof self-confidence remains titanium-tough.

The branding of The Amol Rajan Connection features a mock-up of the poster from The Harder They Come, a Jamaican film about a renegade insurgent whose reckless defiance of the establishment’s rules culminates in him dying in a hail of bullets. But however he might see himself, it’s impossible to regard Rajan as an outsider. From his editorship of a national newspaper, via University Challenge and Today, he has shown an uncanny facility for arriving, briskly, at the very heart of one national institution after another. The sponsors of this show are two world-bestriding tech corporations, one of Britain’s largest banks and an upmarket supermarket chain. He soft-launched with an appearance on former Tory chancellor George Osborne’s podcast. Rajan’s connections are clearly being worked very efficiently.

In the course of the conversation with Osborne, he explained himself thus: “The BBC, and BBC News, is going to get smaller at an accelerating rate. And I want to go to where the action is.” But what constitutes the action in this context? The long-form, one-on-one video podcast (which, essentially, this is) has become a crowded field. In fact, co-presenting Today on Radio 4 remains a much more influential position for a media operative to occupy.

Since leaving Today, Rajan has hinted at certain low-key beefs with the limitations of the BBC, mainly revolving around the sense of being unable to say what he really thinks. Unpromisingly, these feelings were initially articulated in an article in the Spectator, and the piece contained, more unpromisingly still, an expression of agreement with some of the ideas of Dominic Cummings. Rajan is an undeniably fluent communicator but there’s a sense that his quickness can devolve into something slightly less palatable. There is a touch of the tech guru about him – his self-belief sometimes borders on the messianic. Can he listen to an expert? Or, in keeping with the current affairs interlocutor he has recently been, does he interrupt?

Perhaps his first guest can be seen as reassuring. Gareth Southgate is arguably the anti-Amol. He is unflashy, measured and occasionally even a little ponderous. Rajan reads the room: like most right-thinking people, he’s clearly full of admiration and fondness for the former England manager, and so he allows himself to be incorporated into his steady, sometimes mildly soporific rhythm. The result is a very traditional piece of broadcasting.

Initially, it wanders at length down some well-trodden paths. Rejection by Southampton, a second chance at Crystal Palace, captaincy, England, that penalty miss, club management – and then back to England; this time in a waistcoat, searching for footballing redemption but finding himself, at a sensitive time, forced to take the lead in cultural areas, too. It’s gently enjoyable, like a lulling, familiar bedtime story.

In the second of the conversation’s two hours, the pair navigate choppier waters, talking about Fifa governance, the Manchester City situation and, eventually, Southgate’s pet subject: his heartfelt concerns about the problems afflicting young men.

None of this is dull, exactly. In fact, much of it is engaging and worthwhile. It just doesn’t feel particularly dynamic or radical. If this interview is “where the action is”, it’s hard to see how it provides proof of concept for the venture as a whole.

Obviously, tone and mood will vary with the guests – the version of Rajan we see here is certainly more thoughtful than usual, and that’s refreshing. But at first glance, The Amol Rajan Connection plays things safe. Maybe something more reflective of the times that spawned it will emerge. For the time being, though, this isn’t it.

The Amol Rajan Connection is on YouTube now

Alex Scott, the former Football Focus host, has left her role as a presenter of the Women’s Champions League coverage on Disney+.

It is understood it was Scott’s decision to walk away and focus on other projects, including her new show, One More Word WSL, with her fellow former England internationals Anita Asante and Fara Williams.

Scott had fronted the streaming platform’s coverage of the elite women’s European club competition since it obtained the rights in 2025. However, Disney’s production levels were criticised after the opening round following a series of technical problems. These included an unscheduled advert break that interrupted the second half of Arsenal’s 1-0 win over HB Køge for more than three minutes.

A spokesperson for Disney+ told the Guardian: “We would like to extend our sincere thanks to Alex Scott for her contribution to our coverage of the Uefa Women’s Champions League on Disney+. Her passion for the women’s game and the competition shone through throughout her time with us, and we are grateful for all she contributed. We wish her every success.”

Scott, a former England and Arsenal defender and former contestant on the BBC’s Strictly Come Dancing and ITV’s I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, has also presented major sports shows for the BBC, including coverage of the 2020 Olympics. Scott’s representatives said: “Alex is grateful for the opportunities she has had to work with the team at Disney+ and hopes that they continue to work together in the future.”

Scott presented the BBC’s Football Focus show for five seasons before its closure this year. At the start of this season’s Women’s Super League campaign she launched One More Word through her own production company, First Cap Productions, and has previously explained that show was createdin response to the BBC cancelling its weekly WSL highlights show.

Scott, who turned 42 on Wednesday, told the Observer, this month: “I feel like there’s always an excuse about women’s football shows not working because of the viewership or needing to save money. Whereas I think if they are done right, they can work, if things are given a fresh idea or a fresh format, they can work.”

In the same interview, discussing some of the criticism aimed at Disney’s Women’s Champions League coverage this term, Scott said: “Ultimately, do I agree with all the decisions that were made? Absolutely not. Did I try and advise? Yes, but I can only do so much.

after newsletter promotion

“But nobody sees the conversations, the fights I have behind the scenes. But I can hold my head up and know that I’ve always tried my best for the greater good of women’s sport.”

Sources have told the Guardian the presenter’s relationship with Disney remains positive. Disney, whose coverage is produced by ESPN, secured an exclusive five-year deal to broadcast the Women’s Champions League across European broadcast territories in 2025. It is understood its presenting team will continue to include Shebahn Aherne, Nedum Onuoha and Lianne Sanderson. The lineup includes commentators such as Vicki Sparks and Jacqui Oatley. The competition resumes on 28 October.

‘Stranger than stranger-than-fiction’: how Lance Oppenheim made the year’s two buzziest films

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 14:55:54 GMT

Primetime and You Can See Everything are both clammy, audacious awards contenders that challenge our sense of reality. Ahead of the release of his drama starring Robert Pattinson as a TV vigilante, the 30-year-old director talks crime, punishment and South Park

To direct one movie that is on everyone’s lips in awards season is remarkable. To make two begins to look like sorcery. That is the position in which the 30-year-old Florida-born film-maker Lance Oppenheim now finds himself. Next month brings the release of You Can See Everything, the three-hour documentary which he co-directed with faux-naif deadpan prankster Nathan Fielder, in which they spend a month living with the disgraced health-tech mogul Elizabeth Holmes before she begins her 11-year prison sentence for fraud and conspiracy. The film, described by Oppenheim as “head-spinning” and so shrouded in secrecy that Variety magazine’s list of Oscar predictions identifies one of its cast members only as “[Redacted]”, is expected to become the first documentary nominated for best picture.

When I meet Oppenheim in a London hotel, it is to discuss his other hot ticket, Primetime, for which Robert Pattinson is the one attracting Oscar buzz. The Batman actor gives a high-wire performance as Chris Hansen, the sensationalist US television vigilante renowned for ambushing paedophiles on To Catch a Predator, which was a disreputable and highly addictive segment of the current affairs show Dateline NBC between 2004 and 2007. Hansen later parlayed the idea, and his crusading shtick, into a succession of spin-offs. Some, including Hansen Vs Predators, had the same sleazy catnip quality. Others, such as a sting to collar bicycle thieves, did not.

The format of To Catch a Predator is simple. A volunteer from the website Perverted-Justice enters an online chatroom pretending to be underage. Once a paedophile takes the bait, chats with the supposed teen and then pitches up at the agreed location (which is in fact a “sting house” rigged with cameras), he is met by an actor posing as the adolescent. Suddenly, Hansen slinks out of the shadows and calmly invites the offender to “have a seat,” an offer which quickly became his catchphrase. He then reads aloud excerpts from the incriminating online chat as the guilty party squirms and panics. Reality television this may be, but it is also a theatrical performance with its own unvarying props from one sting to the next: cookies and pizza the pre-sex snacks, a table or kitchen island Hansen’s equivalent of a CEO’s desk or judge’s bench.

“The show is so tonally strange,” marvels Oppenheim. “It feels like an alien object beamed in from Mars. You’re seeing this horrific situation where someone who’s sick in the head has shown up to do a terrible thing. Then they’re confronted by Chris Hansen, who has these catchphrases and one-liners. He’s a crime-stopper but he’s also there to make a TV show out of their miserable state. It oscillated between making me nauseated and making me laugh. The challenge for me was how to create something that’s even stranger than stranger-than-fiction.”

In person, you would never take this boyish chatterbox for a zeitgeist-surfing A24 auteur whose fanclub includes Ari Aster, Darren Aronofsky and the Safdie brothers. In fact, you might think twice before serving him alcohol, at least without ID. His mini pompadour gives him an Eraserhead Jr look; his black, round-framed glasses might have been felt-tipped on to his face by a classmate. A black-and-white striped shirt worn under his suit jacket lends him the appearance of a well-dressed humbug.

Though based in fact, Primetime is Oppenheim’s first non-documentary feature. His haunting 2020 debut, Some Kind of Heaven, was set in a Florida retirement community where happiness becomes oppressive and tyrannical. Its 2024 follow-up, Spermworld, delved into the private lives of men who donate sperm, including one who has fathered more than a hundred children.

“I’ve always wanted my documentaries to feel like Hollywood dramas,” the director explains. “With Primetime, I was curious about what it would be like to make an actual Hollywood drama with actors.” The resulting character study is almost as kaleidoscopic and overripe as Ren Faire, Oppenheim’s masterful 2024 HBO “docu-fantasia” featuring a mercurial, Viagra-popping elderly theme-park despot, his back-stabbing underlings and a giant talking lizard.

The film-maker’s own introduction to Chris Hansen came as a child when he saw him spoofed on an episode of South Park, in which Cartman is strong-armed by the presenter into appearing on a TV special about Tourette syndrome; a group of paedophiles inadvertently come to his rescue by shooting themselves en masse. From there, Oppenheim became hooked on To Catch a Predator and its derivatives. A few years ago, his girlfriend (now wife) even bought him a personalised Cameo video message from Hansen. He scoots forward now to play it to me on his phone. In the video, the silver-haired paedophile-hunter cheekily invites Oppenheim to “have a seat … not because I suspect you of anything predator-like,” before plugging his own upcoming shows.

It is this confusion between righteous avenger and meretricious huckster that makes Hansen such an irresistible subject. “I think he started off with noble intentions, but he turned serious reporting into entertainment and willingly transformed himself into a meme. He’s on Cameo presenting what he does as a service you can pay for; then he puts his whole project into this moral register where he talks about good and evil. What happens to you psychologically when you believe you’re doing something good for the world? Does that turn you into a superhero?” He grins: “And now we’ve got the guy who plays Batman as Chris Hansen.”

It was Pattinson, already a diehard Hansen fan, who brought the project to Oppenheim intending only to produce rather than star in it. “Rob’s quite possibly the actor of our time,” the director says. “Every movie he’s done this year has been a defining cultural moment.” Primetime follows The Drama, his prickly black comedy with Zendaya, and The Odyssey; Dune: Part Three arrives in December. “As I’ve gotten to know him, I feel like he also stitched some very human and vulnerable parts of himself into Primetime. Rob became an overnight celebrity when he went to Comic-Con with Twilight in 2008. He was instantly a public figure with expectations about how he should behave. That’s part of what Chris Hansen goes through in the movie.”

The special alchemy of Primetime lies in the way it renders Hansen’s story in the clammy style of To Catch a Predator so that we are simultaneously inside the show, with its churning moral tumult, and outside, looking on in appalled and impotent horror. “It is very much not a biopic,” agrees Oppenheim. “I wanted it to be experiential and phantasmagorical. I was wondering what would happen if you took Billy Wilder’s Ace in the Hole, Oliver Stone’s JFK and Brian De Palma’s Body Double, then threw them in a blender with the real-life events of To Catch a Predator. Would it taste weird or delicious? Maybe you sprinkle a little Sexy Beast in there, too, and it’s, like, ‘Boom!’”

Boom, indeed. Hansen, who has griped bitterly about not being consulted or even informed about the film, has accused Primetime of “weaponised empathy”, “[making] audiences feel sorry for the predators” and portraying him and his staff “as ratings-obsessed, maniacal people”. On the other hand, he has insinuated himself enthusiastically into the Primetime experience, booking trailers for his own true-crime streaming platform, TruBlu, to run immediately before screenings of the movie in US cinemas.

Oppenheim is full of admiration. “The way he has created a media circus around his reaction to the film is on a par with what we’ve seen of him on television. He contains multitudes. He is a journalist but also an entertainer, a circus ringleader and maybe a compulsive performer.” Are there parallels with the current US president? “Well, they were both on television around the same time and both on shows which were made or green-lit by Jeff Zucker, who plays himself in the film.” He stops short, though, of calling them kindred spirits.

Perhaps Hansen’s persona is too closely intertwined with the development of Oppenheim’s own sensibility for him to make any such damning judgment. “I saw To Catch a Predator long before I saw Abbas Kiarostami’s Close-Up or Orson Welles’s F For Fake,” he says, citing two films in which documentary and drama form an unstable concoction. “But I feel the show has a lot in common with them because it’s such a reality bender. It has short adult actors pretending to be children in a house that looks like a set from Blue Velvet.” He shakes his head as if experiencing afresh the insanity of To Catch a Predator. “I don’t think I’d be making nonfiction films the way I do if I hadn’t seen that show as a kid.”

Primetime is in UK cinemas from 30 October. You Can See Everything is in UK cinemas from 20 November

‘Don’t do this!’ Why Paul McCartney cares about looking shorter than John Lennon in Sam Mendes’ Beatles films

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 13:30:13 GMT

You’re Paul McCartney. So how come you’re still getting het up at a fictional version of you being marginally smaller than a fictional version of John Lennon?

There has been a lot of discourse and conjecture surrounding Sam Mendes’s forthcoming Beatles biopics. Some of this is logical (will people really turn out to see four near-identical films on the same day?), some creative (what animal did they have to shave to make John Lennon’s Abbey Road beard?). At every turn the film has been examined and factchecked and cross-referenced against testimonies from the band’s actual hairdresser.

But until now the remaining Beatles have managed to keep fairly quiet about the whole thing. Last year Ringo Starr mentioned that he’d sat down with Mendes to rework a scene he wasn’t happy with, and Paul McCartney has praised the guitar playing of Paul Mescal, but it appeared that no real red lines had been crossed. Until now.

On the most recent episode of Amy Poehler’s podcast, McCartney hinted at one underlying tension that might just rip the whole project apart: under no circumstances should he be seen to be shorter than John Lennon.

Informing Poehler that he, Lennon and George Harrison were all roughly equal height – with Starr slightly smaller – McCartney revealed that he was moved to text Mendes after shots of the actors recreating the Abbey Road album cover were published. In them, it looked an awful lot like Harris Dickinson (playing Lennon) loomed above Mescal’s McCartney. As per McCartney’s retelling, the text read “Sam! Smaller? Don’t do this! You said you wouldn’t do it!”

While he was quick to point out that Mendes’s reply assured him that this was simply down to their respective strides in the shot, even going as far as sending another one that showed them both equally tall, you can understand his dismay here. By his own admission, McCartney is still sore about 2009’s Nowhere Boy, which depicted him as Lennon’s slighter and weedier sidekick.

But this has always persisted. In the 1960s, the official and now genuinely bewildering Beatles cartoon series similarly depicted McCartney as a relative pixie compared with the strapping Lennon and, even though the Yellow Submarine film fastidiously kept Lennon and McCartney at the same height, there’s still a perception that McCartney was the smaller half of the partnership.

In a sense, you can feel his pain. McCartney is a man who has spent the last couple of decades fastidiously building a counterargument to the once-prevalent claim that he was simply the sappy hanger-on to Lennon’s towering genius. Remember in 2002, when he released the live album Back in the US and changed the credits of 19 of its songs from “Lennon-McCartney” to “Paul McCartney and John Lennon” to better show the world that he had been in the driving seat?

This ended up with threats of legal action from Yoko Ono and subsequent editions were released with the credits reverted. But McCartney was more successful recently with both Peter Jackson’s Get Back (which recontextualised the Let It Be film from “Paul McCartney irritates everyone into leaving the Beatles” to “Paul McCartney singlehandedly keeps the Beatles afloat”) and the Now and Then single (which had been vetoed by Harrison on the basis that it was “fucking rubbish” and then released anyway after his death). Slowly but surely, McCartney has won the war. His undoubted talent is now recognised at every turn, to the point where you have to do some searching to find any recent interview that doesn’t end with the interviewer tearily thanking McCartney for his genius. So physical height is the final hurdle. Making sure that Harris Dickinson never looks taller than Paul Mescal is the last T that McCartney has to cross to secure his legacy for ever. And, sure, it might seem a little petty – it is the biopic equivalent of the contracts in the Fast and Furious films that stipulate The Rock must never be seen to lose a fight, even if that means inventing a bizarre contrivance to render it a draw – but this is important.

If these films do as well as they’re likely to, then these four actors, with their weird wigs and pubey faces, may well become a generation’s lasting depictions of the band. The slightest inaccuracy could rewrite all of history as we know it. Nobody, especially the man himself, wants Paul McCartney’s gravestone inscription to be “Composer and musician (slightly shorter than John Lennon)”.

‘A guy held a knife to my throat and said: play something normal!’ Richard Thompson on crazy crowds, his beloved beret and Sandy Denny’s driving skills

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 12:30:12 GMT

As he releases new album Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the 77-year-old British folk legend answers your questions about Billy Connolly, Californian fish and chips and whether he nearly joined the Eagles

Billy Connolly recalled being in a room with you, Sandy Denny, Nick Drake and John Martyn. Did you feel you were collectively doing something special? poscopy That might have been at the Royal Festival Hall [in 1969], where Fairport Convention had Nick and John as openers and Billy must have been backstage. He’d have been in the Humblebums with Gerry Rafferty, before he evolved from a banjo player who told jokes into a comedian who played a bit of banjo. He was always a fantastic bloke and we’ve been friends for a long time.

There was a great camaraderie between the stable of acts Joe Boyd produced: Fairport, the Incredible String Band, John Martyn, Chris McGregor. We felt different, not special, and didn’t feel successful because we weren’t. None of these people really sold many records in their lifetimes, but people are still discovering them now. This album is my latest attempt to sell some units.

Have you ever been on a 1952 Vincent Black Lightning and did that inspire the song? llamapaca I’ve never ridden a Vincent Black Lightning. There’s only about 15 left, but when I was a kid one of the neighbours had a Vincent Black Shadow – a very similar motorcycle – and us kids thought it was one of the most beautiful things we’d ever seen. I was casting around for a British equivalent to American romantic imagery, so thought it would be a good object to build a drama around. Boy, girl, motorcycle, armed robbery …

The narrator in your song Cold Kisses is one of the most chilling characters I’ve ever met in a song. How much of that rogue is you? If it’s none, where did you summon him up from? LeroyDeSwoon He wants to compare himself with her old boyfriends. Some of us have been there – not necessarily going through someone’s drawers, but looking at someone’s diary or emails, trying to find out more about a new partner. It’s a sneaky thing to do, obviously, but in the guise of entertainment songwriting can dig below the surface of what’s considered civilised and into an area that’s slightly uncomfortable. I love that.

On the new album, the song Cocaine Walking, Booze Talking is based on people I met in the psychedelic era who were a bit edgy or violent. Then acid came along and they suddenly went all peace and love, but it wouldn’t last. So the last verse asks: “Who’ll win the battle before the nurse pulls the plug? The Kings Road hippy or the Sauchiehall thug?” Conflicted human beings. I thought John Lennon was a bit like that.

Could you tell a nice – not sad – story that I haven’t heard about Sandy Denny or Nick Drake? katstu Nick was so taciturn and hard to know that I couldn’t say a lot of uplifting stuff about him. Sandy was a terrible passenger, hypersensitive. In a car, she’d be going: “What was that noise?” “Why did you put the brakes on?” Eventually, our tour manager [in Fairport Convention] had to teach her about the internal combustion engine: “I’m now changing gear.” On an airplane, she was impossible. Flying to Los Angeles, she spilled a gin and tonic in my lap in the first hour, although on a boat she was totally at ease, in her element, hence so many of her songs about the sea. From what I’ve heard, when she finally got a licence, she was driving into ditches and all sorts. Bless her.

Who is the inspiration behind Beeswing? EddieHaskell People say: “Oh, what a beautiful song about [the folk singer] Anne Briggs,” but it’s more complicated. When I lived in Suffolk in the 1970s, a tramp used to come looking for odd jobs. He’d do a bit of gardening, we’d wash his clothes and feed him and he’d tell extraordinary stories about his life. So his stories were part of the song, but also Sandy and Anne were great friends and it was really Sandy’s sense of Anne being this free spirit. But I need credit as a writer of fiction, too, because it’s not about anybody.

Do you have a favourite cover of any of your songs? Mine is Wall of Death by REM. MrsGRafferty Wall of Death was a memo to myself: take risks, go to the edge, don’t be complacent. But my favourite cover is The Great Valerio by Swan Arcade, a vocal trio around the folk scene in the 60s and 70s. They did a fantastic job of getting all the dissonant, unusual harmony that exists in the guitar arrangement and ended up with a wonderful piece of music. [Swan Arcade’s] Dave Brady had one arm. The story was that he’d been on his motorcycle and was hurtling towards a brick wall, so stuck his arm out to grab a lamp-post. But he managed to shape a chord with his left hand and strum with his little finger. A great character.

Would you have liked to have worked more closely with John Martyn – at least before he became “difficult” and his music moved in a different direction? archiebargie “Difficult” is a bit cheeky. John was one of those guitar players, like Martin Carthy, who cover all bases. I’m a bit like that myself, so if you put us together there’s a lot of treading on each other’s toes, but we were neighbours for a while in the late 60s and early 70s and used to jam together. Once, we were in Olympic Studios for one of John’s sessions and he played acoustic and I played electric. We jammed for about 20 minutes and it was just wonderful and joyous, but they didn’t have the machine running. We should have done more of that.

How did the offer to join Eagles come about? BobinDay Offers would come through lawyers or management. I don’t think it was ever someone from a band phoning up saying: “We’d love to have you.” When I was on tour with Sandy in ’71, I did get a firm approach to join Linda Ronstadt’s band because four of them had left to form Eagles. I thought: I can’t jump ship. Sandy would kill me … and do I wanna live and work with a bunch of Californians? I wanted to do my Anglo-Celtic thing and sing in my own accent. I was asked to join a later incarnation of the Animals when they wanted to dump [the guitarist] Hilton Valentine. Shocking stuff. I was asked to join the Band twice, but I thought they were gonna drink themselves to death.

You were originally a fervent enthusiast for all things British and yet now you live in the US, which seems at odds with everything the UK stands for. Why? DozyDanny For the last 40 years, I’ve had a place in London and a place in America. I lived in Santa Monica for a long time, but you’re surrounded by Brits in the music and film business. You can’t go 10 or 20 yards without a pub screening Premier League games or a fish and chip shop. Plus, when I open up my computer, the Guardian is my homepage. You can be connected anywhere in the world, but I’ve never felt connected with American culture. I’m not going to sing Jan and Dean songs about surfing. My inner landscape is London, Scotland or some dark moor in Brontë country.

What was it like being on stage with Bob Dylan at the Guitar Legends festival in Seville in 1991? You looked on high alert, or anxious. Was there any rehearsal beforehand? MaskedTortilla I was on the road with [the American singer-songwriter] Bonnie Raitt when I got a call from [the guitarist] Phil Manzanera. Word was Bob wanted to do some acoustic numbers together, which was great. We did rehearse in the dressing room, and rehearsed All Along the Watchtower with his band. When we went on stage, the acoustic guitars had gone out of tune, so I spent the first song trying to tune up – that was probably high alert – but once things settled down it was great fun; a great honour to work with Bob.

Your first band was Emil and the Detectives, with Hugh Cornwell, later of the Stranglers. Did you cross paths again? Haigin88 We had the band in school, but by 16 I was playing with Fairport Convention, so I didn’t see Hugh for 40 years. Then, in the 2000s, we were both playing a festival in Spain and picked up the conversation where we left it. Since then, we’ve done some musical things and gigs together and a splendid version of Tobacco Road for charity.

What has been your most improbable backing role as a guitarist? thoughtwhacker In the band with Hugh, we backed Helen Shapiro, but I’ve played unlikely places like care homes, funerals, weddings and schools. Singing at my own mum’s funeral was the toughest gig. I played a girls’ school in Connecticut because we knew the teacher. The kids knew a bit of Chaucer, so I could do something like Sumer Is Icumen In plus a Britney Spears song or something. The kids went nuts. Best audience ever.

Bono spent a small fortune having his favourite hat flown in first class for a gig in Italy. How far would you go to ensure your trademark beret [a Balmoral] was in place come showtime? SalfordianBlue That must have cost Bono £20,000. For the price of a stapler, I have someone staple it to my head before I go to the airport. I sometimes forget to pack any shoes, but people don’t notice ’cause I wear black socks.

The last time I saw you, a fire alarm cleared the theatre. What’s your best, worst or most memorable moment playing live? RobFrampton In the 70s, I did a solo tour of Sweden and played somewhere in the Arctic Circle where I was singing my precious little folk-rock numbers between the disco. A guy held a knife to my throat and said: “Why don’t you play something normal?” I wasn’t afraid; I was wondering: what’s normal? I might have done a Buddy Holly cover. At school, when I deputised for some local poppy covers band, there was a real fight in the audience, kids throwing chairs; hang on to your equipment and get off stage.

At one point, you became an antiques dealer. Why was this and how did you acquire the expertise? rjoncas A friend of mine took over an antique shop in Marylebone. I knew a bit, but I was too nice to the old ladies, too honest: I’d tell them we’d offer £1,000, but they’d get double that at auction. I sold a couple of porcelain Ming dynasty lions for £60, thinking they were fakes. They were worth thousands. I soon went back to music, but I still annoy my family by watching Antiques Roadshow and correctly guessing what something’s worth, so they look at me like I’m some sort of genius.

Hippies, Thugs and Heroes by Richard Thompson is released on 16 October on New West Records. He tours North America until 18 February, then Europe and the UK from 15 April to 7 May

Sally Rooney’s stand on Palestine is brave and humane

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 10:56:22 GMT

The Normal People author’s determination to support Palestine Action, even if it means that her books are withdrawn from sale in the UK, makes a mockery of Britain’s terrorism laws

It’s hard to think of a published author in living memory who risked arrest in the UK for their political beliefs, hard to think of one whose books could be published anywhere but here. Sally Rooney went into this debacle with her eyes open: she said last July that royalties from her books, and their BBC adaptations, would be used to support Palestine Action.

Rooney’s courage is not so much in risking imprisonment, since there is a fix for that, which is what she’s doing – avoiding the UK. Rather, she has chosen the thorniest possible path for this cause. Authors can write essays and sign letters in support of the Palestinian people; actors can voice it in interviews, musicians can say it from the stage, and there is always a cost to it, whether it’s in plain sight and they’ve been kicked off a global tour, or it’s behind closed doors and they are simply excluded from opportunities. But such actions, even if they logically suggest support for a proscribed organisation, don’t entail actively breaking the terrorism laws. Rooney had taken a financial hit anyway, by pledging support for Palestine Action with her royalties; but that’s a price at least you can count. The lost sales and opportunities that ripple out from being effectively both barred from and banned in the UK are innumerable.

Yet, speaking as not-her-accountant, but as someone living in the culture she also inhabits and has made such an impact describing, the value of her stand is similarly hard to put a price on. Her authorial voice and body of work makes this intervention distinctive in its reach. She’s never been an apolitical author. Normal People was razor sharp on class, Conversations With Friends wasn’t shy of a Marxist analysis. But the work is also intimate, often domestic, I mean, the clue’s in the name – these were always normal people. It was from a reputation of delicately challenging but everyday subtlety that Rooney assumed her outrider position, and in so doing, took on the idea that caring about Gaza is somehow a crank’s life choice; insisted that it is a human response, as natural and quotidian, as passionate and important, as friendship.

It also, come on – surely at some point we’re allowed to say this – makes an absolute mockery of the terrorism legislation thus applied. Nobody anywhere thinks Sally Rooney poses a danger to the British state, or any state, just as nobody anywhere thinks a 94-year-old human rights barrister who was a friend of Ed Miliband’s late mother does. Keir Starmer, paradoxically, given that the two things in his favour were his caution and his legal hinterland, painted himself into an absurd corner, where terrorism arrests went up between 2024 and 2025 from 250 to nearly 3,000. On demos where anyone crunched the numbers, more of them were over 80 than under 20.

The history and particularity of Irish solidarity with the Palestinian cause have been discussed a lot since the painful Ed Sheeran tour, in which the singer thought a support act could be quietly ditched over a pro-Palestine song, without losing his backing band – Beoga, founder members of Irish Artists for Palestine. More broadly, Ireland has a vibrant tradition of young women with no reason to think they have the right to opine on geopolitics sticking their oar in anyway. The Dunnes Stores strike of 1984 kicked off when 21-year-old Mary Manning refused to handle some South African grapefruit, leading to her receiving only £21 a week in strike pay for two years and nine months. It reached its political crescendo less than three years later, when Ireland banned South African goods altogether in protest at apartheid. In between, though, in 1985, Desmond Tutu met Manning and her fellow strikers on his way to get the Nobel peace prize, extending as he did an invitation to visit him in South Africa – which they took him up on, only to be turned away at the border. There’s an instant echo, here, of a state showing its might at customs only to draw attention to its weakness; and of an author who, as well as that, is an ordinary citizen, whose forgone royalties are almost the least of the sacrifice, but are still a powerful emblem.

This article was amended on 15 October 2026. An earlier version said that the Dunnes Stores strike of 1984 “cost [Mary Manning] £21 a week”. In fact, this was her weekly strike pay for the two years and nine months of industrial action.

Trump should fear the BBC. Instead he’s picked a fight – and he seems to be losing

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 10:00:09 GMT

The president is used to bullying his media targets. The quagmire that is his libel actions shows the broadcaster is working to a different script

For the greatest account of the BBC’s finest hour, one must turn to Penelope Fitzgerald’s novel, Human Voices, written in 1980 and set 40 years earlier, at the corporation’s Portland Place wartime HQ. Flanked by sandbags and infused with a smell of cooking “from the deep hold that suggested more strongly than ever a cruise on the Queen Mary”, the organisation that Fitzgerald describes is at once noble and deeply eccentric. “Broadcasting House stood headed on a fixed course south,” she writes. “With the best engineers in the world, and a crew varying between the intensely respectable and barely sane, it looked ready to scorn any disaster.”

In other words, a formidable foe, one that in the spring of 1940, in the face of anticipated Nazi invasion, decided “without prompting, that truth was more important than consolation, and, in the long run, would be more effective”. I bring this up in respect to the gathering storm of Donald Trump versus the BBC, a fight triggered by the US president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit – $10bn! It’s a wonder he didn’t go for $10 gazillion – brought against the corporation at the end of last year in response to a poorly edited episode of Panorama. The BBC was at fault, editing together comments made by the US president at a rally on 6 January 2021 to give, as the corporation’s apology put it, “the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action”. But it is fighting the lawsuit.

This will have come as a surprise to the president, who in his own country has had great success frightening media companies into craven submission. This week, as news broke that the BBC has been cleared by a judge to serve legal papers on Trump’s children, while still seeking judicial intervention to force him to show up to his own deposition, the president must be wondering what’s going on. In August last year, Trump applied to the court to block the BBC from deposing Donald Trump Jr and Ivanka Trump, and yet … the corporation simply ignored him and ploughed on with its mission.

Well. Welcome to the British Broadcasting Corporation, Mr President, let me give you a little insight into what you’re up against. There is no institutional power in the world to rival the BBC’s ability to drone on, a constant background hum for the nation. We all, at some level, consist of an interior mix-tape made up of Melvyn Bragg saying, “Hello. In the 13th century …” and Libby Purves opening an episode of Midweek with, “all my guests this week are time travellers, in a way”. The US president simply has no idea of the effect on this country’s nervous system of the opening bars of EastEnders, or a BBC newsreader interrupting normal programming with the line, “This is BBC television from London.”

Nor will he have encountered that very particular BBC mindset, which, unlike the workforce at Google, doesn’t run on can-do energy and corporate good cheer, but rather on toxic gas released by an underpaid, overworked labour force, seething with resentment and, as Fitzgerald put it, “bitterly loyal” to its employers – which, as it happens, is a very high standard of loyalty indeed. You don’t get that at Fox News.

Or indeed at ABC News, which in December 2024, agreed to pay Trump $15m in an uncontested defamation suit. And while CNN, MS Now and Politico are all suing the White House for banning them, CBS rolled over like a dog, announcing it would be axing Stephen Colbert’s highly critical show days after settling another defamation suit with the president. Meanwhile the Federal Communications Commission, the regulatory body run by arch-conservative Brendan Carr, threatened to review the licences of misbehaving broadcasters. A day after the president called for Trump-mocking Jimmy Kimmel’s dismissal from his late night ABC show, Carr ordered an early licence review of all eight of Disney’s ABC television stations.

The BBC isn’t bound by these forces. There are financial pressures on it to settle, of course, but in public broadcasting money is never the be-all and end-all, and I would bet Trump has never come up against a force so stubborn, so irrational, so inexplicable to the American corporate or political mindset as his opponents at Langham Place. If the president prizes his own unpredictability as a key weapon in his arsenal, I’d like to introduce him to the people who brought us Noel’s House Party and Grandstand.

Yes, the BBC loves nothing more than to don a hair shirt and report on its own failings. Yes, it could do with relying a bit less on Clare Balding. And yes, the corporation is a lunatic in so many ways. But it’s our lunatic and if you come for it, you come for us all. In the BBC’s long history of standing up to tyranny, it has seen off bigger enemies than Trump. I would bet the Shipping Forecast it will come out victorious.

Apologetic Infantino ‘not fit’ to lead Fifa, claim European FA heads after meeting

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 09:00:16 GMT

Infantino failed to provide answers to questions

European leaders expect someone will stand against him

European football leaders are increasingly confident they will find a candidate to stand against Gianni Infantino in next year’s Fifa presidential election, with the heads of the English and German football associations questioning his fitness to govern after a three-and-a-half-hour council meeting.

Infantino began the long-awaited gathering of Fifa’s 37-strong executive board by apologising for failing to consult them over his abandoned World Cup sell-off plan but failed to provide answers to dozens of questions posed by the European FAs on a range of subjects including the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, Donald Trump’s Fifa peace prize and the Folarin Balogun affair, when the USA striker’s World Cup suspension was overturned after lobbying from the US president.

Infantino’s apology was followed by a 30-minute presentation on FFE from two American lawyers, who described the $20bn (£15.1bn) valuation and proposed sale of a 20% stake to Thrive Capital as a good deal for Fifa. At the insistence of some attenders, the lawyers were asked to leave the meeting after they had presented. When questioned, one of them confirmed he had been commissioned and paid by Fifa to produce a review of FFE.

“The main objective for Gianni was to survive this meeting and nothing more,” one council member told the Guardian.

Council members succeeded in deferring, until they receive more information on Balogun, a Fifa proposal to amend its disciplinary regulations by removing the scope for players shown a straight red card to have it rescinded. Infantino pledged to provide that information by their next meeting in Doha on 16 December, after nominations close on 18 November for March’s presidential election.

The issue of whether the Fifa peace prize will be revived this year or Trump left as a standalone winner has been referred to Fifa’s social responsibility committee, and the Asian Football Confederation president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, has been appointed to chair a new committee examining governance reform. But otherwise the meeting broke up without tangible answers, to the frustration of the English FA’s chair, Debbie Hewitt.

“We didn’t get answers to anything that we had specifically requested,” Hewitt said. “I think the man [Infantino] has to answer those questions, and if he doesn’t answer those questions, he’s not fit to be Fifa president. That was what was shared in the meeting.”

The German FA’s president, Bernd Neuendorf, went further by calling for wholesale reforms of Fifa’s administration, which he hopes will fall within the purview of Sheikh Salman’s governance committee.

“The whole administration has to be reformed and the whole governance has to be reformed,” Neuendorf said. “But I’m pretty clear here that this is not possible with Gianni as the responsible person at Fifa. So we need a complete restart, I think, a political restart of persons who represent Fifa.

“Yes he apologised, but I didn’t have the feeling that this apology was because of the FFE project in total. My impression was it was just because it wasn’t brought forward to the council and no one was involved.”

Neuendorf also said he was “very confident” that an alternative candidate would be found to stand against Infantino, a view shared by senior figures at Uefa, who expect a late declaration to limit the amount of time for Fifa to scupper the nomination.

Can Lena Dunham’s new Girls do for 40-year-olds what she did for 23-year-olds? I know it can

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 07:00:25 GMT

I was in my early 20s when the classic series debuted and I recognised so much. I can’t wait to see how the reboot takes on a new – equally messy – stage of life

HBO’s Girls is coming back, Lena Dunham and her fellow cast members announced this week, and the internet is already abuzz. Women of a certain age, myself included – approaching, turning or having turned 40 – are genuinely thrilled, if also slightly trepidatious. When you’ve loved, loathed and most importantly grown with characters in the way many of us did with Girls, you feel protective of a show’s legacy. But with Dunham, I’m confident it is in good hands.

Girls means a lot to me, in part because it was the topic of my first ever column for this newspaper: in 2012, shortly after the show premiered, it was already generating a bananas amount of internet discourse and I was on work experience. I was in my early 20s and not long off the dole. I didn’t share the privilege of Dunham’s characters, which is perhaps why I so enjoyed how she skewered it. (I never understood the criticism that the show was about spoilt rich girls. So many people missed the satire.) Yet there were aspects of it that I related to, as I wrote at the time:

“The experiences of Dunham’s characters, where they languish in unpaid jobs and have emotionless, awkward sex in grotty flats with pretentious males, resonate … with my experience and that of my friends.”

It’s not the finest piece of journalism I’ve ever produced (and my God, I would never make reference to my sex life in print these days), but I feel as though history has vindicated me. The series has aged spectacularly well, and in the past few years has been discovered and appreciated anew by younger women. There are popular rewatch podcasts; it’s been big on TikTok. Without all the surrounding noise that constituted 2010s Twitterstorm hell, the quality of the writing, direction and acting has been allowed to speak for itself.

What will Hannah, Jessa, Marnie and Shoshanna’s lives look like now they are more women than girls? When we left them, Hannah had just had a baby who would now be approaching tweenagehood. Will she have made it as “the voice of her generation”? Shoshanna had cut them all out of her life (in a prescient nod to the cult of going “no contact”) and was engaged to a man called Byron: will she be back in touch? Marnie was already divorced – Dunham has jokingly imagined she’d be on her third divorce by now – and Jessa was single in New York. How will we meet them again? And most importantly: will Elijah have become a Broadway star, and will he still have the bitchiest lines?

I can’t wait to find out because, as Dunham wrote in a post announcing the new series, there are so many ways to be 40: “You can live with roommates and get drunk every night, or you can be a parent of four keeping a bustling household in check. You can proudly sleep around, or be in perimenopause and never want to be touched again. I have friends who are in marriage crises but think they’re too old to move on, and still others switching careers for the ninth time.”

It’s true. Of the women I know and love, our lives all look quite different – from each other’s, and also from what we imagined in our 20s. Some marriages are imploding while others are just getting started. Some have tiny babies, some have teenagers and some are child-free. The sandwich years of caring for both offspring and elderly parents are beginning for some, while others don’t yet have those responsibilities. Some own huge houses and others are still renting. Many of us are grappling with our careers – whether that’s realising our ambitions and being given more power, or struggling with the juggle and paying the motherhood penalty (sometimes all of these at once). There are affairs. Perhaps most poignantly, there are the dreams that were never realised – and now may never be. There are the people we have loved and lost.

Dunham won’t be the first screenwriter to pay homage to this complicated stage of life, but she will be one of the first to be exactly of our generation, just as she was the first time around. It’s always cathartic to see art that speaks so directly to your experience, especially when it’s so, so funny.

Reading that first column, I cringe a little at my younger, wide-eyed self, but mostly I think about just how lost I was, how unsure of what my future would look like. That article helped convince my then editors that my perspective was worth sharing, that readers were interested in writing by young women. It still feels like an absurd stroke of luck and I’ll always be grateful to Dunham for saving me from the traditional nine to five. To quote Jessa: “You know what the weirdest part about having a job is? You have to be there every day. Even on the days you don’t feel like it.”

after newsletter promotion

Will this new, short run of episodes generate similar levels of controversy? I expect not. We have all grown up, examined the bruises left by those years and moved on. Girls is widely accepted to be one of the finest, funniest works about female experience that has ever been made for television. Will Dunham do for perimenopause, divorce, fertility issues, care work and postpartum what she did then for abortion, HPV, one-night stands and unpaid internships? I have a feeling she will, and I can’t wait.

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist

Martínez has drawn back the curtain on Manchester United’s ruinous ownership

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 05:00:23 GMT

Defender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the club

Heartbreaking: the worst defender you know just made a great point. And no, nobody would describe Lisandro Martínez as the ideal person to scrutinise Manchester United’s indifferent start to the season, given that his high-profile defensive errors against Fulham and Tottenham are partly responsible for it. “We’re all trying to find the guy who did this,” Martínez burbles on Amazon Prime after United’s 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid on Tuesday night, dressed in a hot dog costume and throwing his arms out in mock innocence.

For those with no interest in engaging with what Martínez actually had to say, this alone will be sufficient grounds to ignore him. Already you can sense the squeamishness of former players for whom the violation of an omertà is the real cardinal sin here, a phantom limb that still tingles years after they last stepped into a dressing room. “Disrespectful,” reckoned Wayne Rooney. “I don’t feel like he’s got the right,” agreed Ashley Young. “These things don’t end well, man,” Rio Ferdinand observed on his podcast.

But traducing the messenger will always be easier than hearing the message, even if Martínez’s views are widely shared within the United dressing room. If the fallout from the Manchester City legal case has demonstrated anything, it is English football’s ingrained reluctance to scrutinise the owners and executives who hold more influence over the sport than anybody else. Men in boots, not men in suits. Hey, watch the ball. It’s going to move!

All the same, it’s worth parsing exactly what Martínez was complaining about, because it’s a good deal more complex than it may appear on first viewing. Player calls out board – and specifically “technical director” Jason Wilcox – for failing to invest sufficiently in the squad over the summer. This was a summer in which United brought in three midfielders (Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans, Carlos Baleba), a reserve goalkeeper (Karl Darlow), nobody up front and nobody in defence. So far, so simple.

But let’s begin to unpick the threads. Why did United not buy a defender in the summer, despite pursuing deals for Lewis Hall and Myles Lewis-Skelly? Because they were unable to sell a defender. There was no interest in Diogo Dalot or Noussair Mazraoui, nor in Harry Maguire, nor in Luke Shaw or Martínez, whose contracts are up next summer in any case. This is the product of recruitment decisions made and deals signed years ago. But why do United, one of the world’s most lucrative clubs, need to sell to buy in the first place?

Perhaps for the same reason they baulked at the asking price for Elliot Anderson and decided to sign the inconsistent Santos and the adequate but overpromoted Tielemans instead: this is a club in austerity measures, whose part-owner Jim Ratcliffe has been furiously cutting costs and raising ticket prices, determined to curb the years of excess that preceded him, where mediocre players were signed on ridiculous money, where failing coaches were paid to leave. But why would United, one of the most commercially successful clubs in footballing history, ever need to cut costs?

Perhaps as a result of the more than £1bn drained out of the club by the Glazers in their 21 years of ownership, not just in dividends but share sales and interest payments on the debt they undertook to buy the club, while neglecting the maintenance of Old Trafford and the training ground at Carrington. Whether he knows it or not, when Martínez is criticising the lack of investment he is in effect holding the Glazers accountable for more than two decades of avarice and mismanagement.

All of which lends a certain significance to Martínez’s intervention that goes beyond the churn of the weekly news cycle. Has any serving United player spoken out so frankly about the ruins of the Glazer ownership? Ole Gunnar Solskjær made a minor stand in early 2005, before they had arrived at the club. Cristiano Ronaldo threw some hand grenades over his shoulder a few days before he left for the second time in 2022. Countless others waited for the safety of retirement, when their disgruntlement could be monetised for personal gain, rather than used to stigmatise them, as Martínez will doubtless be stigmatised in the coming days.

Does any of this help United to win games in the short term? Almost certainly not. Martínez attempted to clarify his comments in a social media post on Wednesday night. He may still be dispatched to the bomb squad anyway, for the crime of pointing out that the emperor secured his throne almost entirely through the use of payment-in-kind loans.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Inevitably Michael Carrick too will be gone before long, away to the great Overlap podcast in the sky. A few months ago I wrote hopefully that Carrick might be the ideal man to cut through the noise and nonsense. I was wrong. The noise has beaten him; the nonsense always wins; any accumulated credit from last season has long since evaporated.

Of course it’s not Carrick’s fault that United haven’t signed a new defender in almost two years, that Bruno Fernandes is so clearly playing through discomfort, that Joshua Zirkzee is still somehow hanging around the place, that the ownership decided to embark on a purge of season-ticket holders in the summer, generating a huge wave of ill-feeling and apathy that can be felt at Old Trafford on matchdays: an entire fanbase trying to work out whether they actually still care about this.

But accountability is for the little people, and far easier to replace a coach on a modest 20-month contract than to oust Ineos or the Glazers, to replace Wilcox or Omar Berrada, even if we now know they partly built their reputations on the success of a club that has been found to have serially cheated. Bumper returns for the owners, price hikes for the fans, corners cut on the pitch; this is the story of the modern Manchester United, which by no coincidence is also the story of modern football.
