How Gaza changed Europe, exposing cracks that grow bigger by the week

The Guardian Thu, 15 Oct 2026 04:00:21 GMT

Solidarity with Palestine’s suffering is punished but MEPs allow a witch-hunt of European Muslims

For three painful years, Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, in retaliation for the Hamas terror attacks on 7 October 2023, has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, wounded thousands more and reduced most of the territory to rubble. It has changed views of Israel across the world, increased support for Palestine and raised questions about US power.

Europe’s failure to hold Israel’s government to account has cost it global credibility and influence. But I fear something even more consequential than that: Gaza is changing Europe itself.

European governments did nothing to try to stop the genocide; there have been no collective sanctions, no trade restrictions or ending of arms sales to Israel. The EU sanctions Russia over its war in Ukraine but retains almost-business-as-usual ties with Israel, a blatant double standard.

Gaza has exposed how Europe’s supposedly universal commitment to human rights is now conditional on whose suffering is recognised, whose resistance is considered legitimate and whose demands for justice are considered worthy of attention. EU policymakers are selective even in the groups of women they choose to celebrate as heroic in struggles against occupation and the children whose right to life they defend.

After these three years I am convinced that the question of Palestine has become a stress test for European democracy itself. Democratic societies can only thrive when there is space for dissent, including dissent that is uncomfortable, disruptive and politically inconvenient. Yet today, across Europe, governments – which speak up against undemocratic conduct abroad – are now unapologetic in imposing restrictions on free expression and peaceful protest at home. Police violence at pro-Palestinian demonstrations has become the norm, and those whose only crime is to speak up publicly for Palestinian rights are increasingly criminalised or made the target of suspicion.

When this happens repeatedly it undermines public trust in the legitimacy of democratic governments and institutions. As Rabin Baldewsingh, the Netherlands’ national coordinator against discrimination and racism tells me: “Governments and public institutions have a responsibility not to reinforce polarisation when society is deeply divided.” Sadly, the opposite appears to be happening.

Many societal fractures existed before Gaza, but they have received new oxygen and traction over the past three years. The EU’s Fundamental Rights Agency has long warned of both anti-Muslim racism and antisemitism. What has become increasingly troubling over the past three years is the political framing under which antisemitism in connection with Gaza is rightly treated as a threat to democracy, while Islamophobia is viewed through a security and anti-terrorism lens.

This can’t all be blamed on the far right, either. True, some extremist groups hide their age-old prejudices behind accusations that it is Muslims and refugees who have “imported” antisemitism into Europe. But the European People’s party (EPP) – the EU’s largest political “family” for pro-European centre-right and conservative politicians, including Ursula von der Leyen and Magnus Brunner, the EU’s most senior official for migration – is also giving old and debunked Islamophobic tropes a new and dangerous lease of life.

The party backed a resolution in June condemning the “interference of political Islam” in European democratic processes. If “political Islam” was interfering in European democracy, the resolution may have some validity. But there is no evidence for the claim, and certainly none advanced in this document, which merely echoes French conspiracy theories about “Islamist entryism” and calls for a crackdown on alleged members of Muslim Brotherhood networks. It claims to make a distinction between “political Islam” and the Islamic faith itself but it reads more like the start of a witch-hunt of European Muslims.

An even tougher EPP resolution, backed by a majority in the European parliament on 8 October, goes a step further by casting suspicion on Muslim civil society groups’ loyalty, activity and participation in European democracy.

Hiba Latreche, president of Femyso, a pan-European network of young Muslim organisations that is explicitly mentioned in the EPP’s attack, points out the double bind of such unfounded allegations. “When we are not active we are accused of communitarianism, separatism and lack of integration. When we engage and exercise active citizenship we are accused of having a hidden agenda.”

Such an environment demands even stronger anti-discrimination action. Yet Europe’s most powerful pro-equality body, the European Network Against Racism (ENAR), has just lost European Commission funding. Worried that this could mean it has to cease operations by the end of the year, ENAR has launched a legal challenge against the decision at the EU’s general court.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Beyond the visible, there are many unwritten post-Gaza codes being applied inside the EU’s corridors of power that are harder to measure and challenge. Islamophobia has become “quite blatant”, EU officials tell me, with micro‑aggressions and remarks about Muslims’ supposedly “irrational and emotional” behaviour. Like von der Leyen in her recent “state of the union” speech, many now talk about Gaza as a humanitarian emergency, but not as a human-made genocide. There is agreement on the need for action against settler violence and illegal settlement in the West Bank, which is framed as the work of “extremists”, but confronting the Israeli government remains difficult.

For many, it has also been a time of uncomfortable conversations, ruptured personal relationships and disillusionment. But there are also moments of intense solidarity, as across Europe pro‑Palestinian movements have extended to include trade unions, faith groups – including Jewish activists – students, celebrities and senior politicians. Every Thursday, members of the EU Staff for Peace gather for a vigil outside the commission and the EU Council. Former EU commissioners, ambassadors and senior staff continue to write to their bosses urging stronger action against Israel.

So all hope is not lost. But Gaza has stripped away a great deal of self-soothing assumptions that many of us harboured about Europe. As the far right becomes more influential, too many have forgotten that democratic freedoms rarely disappear all at once. They begin to erode when some voices are silenced, some suffering is ignored and the rights of some citizens are treated as less deserving than others.

Shada Islam is a Brussels-based commentator on EU affairs. She runs New Horizons project, a strategy, analysis and advisory company

Trump Cancels Planned Livestream of Fort Hood Shooter’s Execution

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Fort Hood Shooter’s Execution

Advertisement

Supported by

The president said only immediate families of the victims of the mass shooting in 2009 would witness the execution of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan.

By Tyler Pager

Reporting from Kalispell, Montana

President Trump on Thursday canceled the Pentagon’s planned livestream of the execution of the Army officer who was convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting.

Pentagon officials said last week that the execution of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others on the grounds of Fort Hood, Texas, would be broadcast via livestream. But Mr. Trump said Thursday that only immediate families of Mr. Hasan’s victims will be able to watch the execution in person.

“Many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” he wrote on social media. “He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.”

Democrats and Republicans in Congress panned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the shooting, and even Vice President JD Vance expressed doubt about the plan.

“I’m not going to be watching it,” he said. He added: “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.”

In an interview with Real America’s Voice, Mr. Hegseth said he supported the public execution of Mr. Hasan “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

Mr. Trump, in his post on social media, acknowledged that streaming the execution “might have been a strong deterrent” to show how “America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan,” but he said it would not go forward.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Defying Trump, Zelensky Says Ukraine Will Resume Russian Refinery Strikes

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed overt frustration with the United States in an interview with The Financial Times. He had paused the strikes to comply with a demand from the United States.

By Cassandra Vinograd and Francesca Regalado

President Zelensky’s anger with the Trump administration burst into view on Thursday when he said he would no longer abide by President Trump’s demand to stop striking Russian oil refineries. It was a remarkably vocal expression by the Ukrainian leader of frustration with the United States, as Kyiv grapples with what it sees as a betrayal by Washington.

Mr. Zelensky’s remarks, in an interview with The Financial Times published on Thursday, brought to a head days of mounting tensions with the Trump administration. It drew expressions of support from European allies in Brussels, but could be a risky move for a country that has depended heavily on U. S. support.

The Trump administration has long blown hot and cold when it comes to Ukraine. But a new round of frictions emerged last week, when Mr. Trump said he had reached an agreement to immediately import Russian diesel fuel to the U. S. market. Ukraine panned the move, saying it would help fund Moscow’s war effort.

Mr. Trump upped the ante on Sunday, unilaterally declaring an energy cease-fire between the two warring sides and calling for Mr. Zelensky to be replaced. While Ukraine shrugged that idea off, it stopped striking Russian refineries. But Mr. Zelensky’s public expressions of frustration became more pointed amid concerns that Washington might cut off intelligence sharing that helps Ukraine detect Russian attacks.

Then Ukraine said on Wednesday that its military had lost some critical access to a military-grade version of Starlink, a pillar of its battlefield communications that the Pentagon pays for.

Mr. Zelensky now appears to have had enough.

“That’s it. The block is out,” Mr. Zelensky said when asked by The Financial Times how much longer Ukraine would maintain the pause on targeting refineries. He did not say what had tipped his decision or when the strikes would resume.

On Thursday, Pavel Malkov, the governor of Ryazan, a Russian region southeast of Moscow, said on social media that a fire had broken out at an oil refinery after a drone strike overnight. Those details could not be independently confirmed.

In his interview, Mr. Zelensky appeared baffled by Mr. Trump’s decisions, criticizing him for making deals with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, and for openly admiring dictators who have clung to power. Mr. Putin, the Ukrainian leader said, is “real evil.”

“How can Trump be friends with him?” Mr. Zelensky added. “I think it’s a mistake.”

Questions about U. S. support for Ukraine in the war against Russia grew after a meeting this month between Ukrainian officials and top U. S. negotiators in which some present thought the Americans made a veiled threat about curbing intelligence sharing.

U. S. officials said this week that Washington had not cut back on intelligence sharing with Ukraine, and denied any threat to withhold such support.

But Mr. Zelensky said in his interview that U. S. military officials had threatened to withhold intelligence if Ukraine did not stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure. He also reiterated that Ukraine had not received advance warning about Russian ballistic missile launches this week, including overnight on Wednesday.

Russia launched dozens of ballistic missiles in that assault, hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and leaving 600,000 people in Kyiv without power. Reports that the use of the military version of Starlink had been restricted for devices traveling faster than 100 miles per hour came later that day.

On Thursday, officials from Ukraine’s defense ministry said they were working to verify whether Starshield’s connectivity for devices in motion had been restored.

The restrictions were seen in Ukraine as part of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to limit the fighting ability of Ukrainian forces. Mr. Trump has pushed Kyiv to stop attacking Russia’s oil refineries so that Moscow can send more diesel to global markets, as high prices threaten the Republican Party’s prospects in the midterm elections.

“Business is interesting between the United States and Russia,” Mr. Zelensky said in the Financial Times interview. “I think that they want to have energy projects. This, politically, is not simple, because everybody will want to ask how it can be when some people are surviving, fighting, dying.”

European leaders entering a meeting in Brussels on Thursday mostly expressed support for Mr. Zelensky’s decision to resume attacks on Russian refineries.

“The faster all the Russian refineries and ability to sell energy will be blown to smithereens the better, because Russia is funding the war with that,” Prime Minister Kristen Michal of Estonia told reporters.

That backing, however, wasn’t unanimous. “I don’t support strikes on any refineries,” Prime Minister Rumen Radev of Bulgaria told reporters.

With the exception of Mr. Radev, many also criticized the Trump administration’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel.

“This ridiculous diesel deal won’t do anything at all for prices on the world market,” said Rob Jetten, the prime minister of the Netherlands. “It does, however, fill Putin’s war chest, so it’s really a very bad choice on Trump’s part, and he’d be better off abandoning it.”

Constant Méheut contributed reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine and Koba Ryckewaert from Brussels.

Francesca Regalado is a Times reporter covering breaking news.

Trump Administration Sues California Over Voter Rolls

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The lawsuit seeks to temporarily block the state from counting mail ballots of voters it claims are likely noncitizens, opening a new front in the administration’s legal fights with election officials.

By Devlin Barrett and Laurel Rosenhall

Devlin Barrett reported from Washington, and Laurel Rosenhall from Sacramento.

The Trump administration on Thursday sued the state of California and a Los Angeles County official, seeking to temporarily block the state from counting mail ballots submitted by voters it suspects are noncitizens.

The suit, which would apply to some 20,000 people in the state the administration has cast as “likely noncitizens,” is a long shot. But it opens a new front in the administration’s legal battles with local election officials weeks before the midterm elections.

Over the past 18 months, the Trump administration has sued California and other states over voter rolls, and has lost resoundingly in court. This time, the Justice Department is trying a new strategy, seeking a court order to prevent the counting of votes from the 20,000 people in the state identified by the Department of Homeland Security “until their citizenship status can be determined.”

Similar past claims of thousands of illegal voters have fallen apart under scrutiny. Last month, election officials in Nevada said that they had examined a list provided by homeland security officials of 185 names of supposed noncitizens who had been improperly registered to vote, and found that every person on the list was a lawful citizen.

In recent months, President Trump has claimed that hundreds of thousands of people have voted illegally. Reviews by election officials and criminal investigators have found small numbers of people who have been caught voting illegally every election cycle — but not in quantities that would come close to deciding the winners of major races.

California officials vowed to fight the administration’s effort.

“This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day,” Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, a Democrat, said on social media. “Courts have made clear the federal government has no role in running state elections.”

Rob Bonta, the attorney general of California, said that the state would not comply with the administration’s demands and instead would respond in court.

“This is nothing more than their ongoing, dangerous, reckless, scorched-earth, widespread attempt to advance conspiracy theories about widespread voter fraud that doesn’t exist,” he said.

U. S. elections are administered and supervised by state and local authorities, and the federal government plays a limited role. The Trump administration, however, has pushed to assume far greater authority over the management of state voter rolls, with little success.

Earlier this year, Justice Department officials sent letters to state and local election officials warning that they could be prosecuted if they did not take sufficient steps to remove noncitizen voters from the rolls.

The administration has escalated its fight with California over the last week.

Days earlier, federal authorities sent a thumb drive of roughly 20,000 names they suspected were noncitizens registered to vote in California to election officials in Los Angeles County, demanding they act within 48 hours.

In a blistering letter, Shirley N. Weber, California’s secretary of state, said the data sent by the administration “lacks both the detail and function to be of any investigative use.” She added that “nowhere has the federal government clarified the basis for suspecting — not even confirming with any level of certainty — the listed individuals are noncitizens.”

The administration’s demands and deadline, she said, “threaten thousands of Californians’ right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide.”

The election officials in Los Angeles County said they had not opened the thumb drive “because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols.”

Dean Logan, the registrar in Los Angeles, said in a statement that “we do not consider the device a secure medium.”

Devlin Barrett covers the Justice Department and the F. B. I. for The Times.

Laurel Rosenhall is a Sacramento-based reporter covering California politics and government for The Times.

Trump’s Attacks on Voting Raise Fears He Will Try to Challenge Midterm Results

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Election officials say they worry the administration could use its own unsubstantiated claims to contest the vote in November.

By Zolan Kanno-Youngs

Zolan Kanno-Youngs, who covers the White House, has been chronicling President Trump’s efforts to reshape the rules governing elections.

President Trump has warned that the country’s election systems are vulnerable to foreign meddling. Federal agents are scouring state rolls and federal databases to try to find noncitizen voters. And the homeland security chief has asked the Justice Department to examine whether a commonly used voting machine can be trusted.

Just weeks away from the midterm elections, Mr. Trump’s longstanding attacks on the integrity of voting systems are crystallizing into what many election officials and Democrats fear is an attempt to lay the groundwork to challenge the results in November.

So far, the president has been stymied in his efforts to directly assert federal control over elections, which under the Constitution are administered by the states. Last month, the Supreme Court blocked Mr. Trump’s effort to have the U. S. Postal Service screen mail ballots.

Instead, Mr. Trump and his allies across the government have intensified another tactic: systematically laying out unsubstantiated and false claims in an effort to sow doubts about the safety of the country’s decentralized election system.

The result, election officials fear, could be an effort by administration officials to try to contest results that do not favor Republicans by citing their own findings that the vote is tainted.

Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said he had grown increasingly worried that Mr. Trump may claim foreign interference in the election as a reason to seize voting machines, noting that the president made dubious claims about the country’s election defenses in a speech in July.

“President Trump will use any tool, legal or not, to try and make sure he gets the results he wants this year,” Mr. Warner said in an interview, adding that he had reached out to business leaders, former military leaders and veteran federal law enforcement officials to ask them to stand up to Mr. Trump if he contests the results.

“Good people of both parties and independents are going to have to say, ‘No, we’re not going to allow this to take place,’” he added.

White House officials maintain that the administration’s efforts are designed to ensure a fair election. When asked if the president will accept the outcome of the midterms, Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, referred to his recent response to that question.

“Of course I will,” Mr. Trump said earlier this month. “But we don’t want cheating.”

Nearly every day, the president questions the reliability of the vote. At a rally Wednesday in Arizona, a state that was a major focus of his effort to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election, Mr. Trump once again made false assertions about voting machines that year.

“The damn machines were broken in Republican areas,” Mr. Trump said, repeating his lie that the election was stolen from him.

The administration’s intense focus on potential election issues comes as Mr. Trump has been conferring with outside supporters urging him to consider drastic actions. Last week, Mr. Trump met in the White House with Tina Peters, a former Colorado county clerk who was convicted of tampering with voting machines after the 2020 election, according to two people familiar with their meeting, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation.

Ms. Peters has long pushed the unsubstantiated claim that voting machines are vulnerable to foreign interference and has called for the Trump administration to inspect or take them into custody — a move legal experts say would be an overreach of federal authority.

Ed Martin, a former senior Justice Department official, told Real America’s Voice that Ms. Peters and the president had discussed “election integrity,” saying both are concerned that foreign actors could exploit election vulnerabilities to change votes. That unsubstantiated claim was echoed this summer by Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary.

Ms. Bis declined to comment on the meeting, as did Peter Ticktin, a lawyer who has represented both the president and Ms. Peters.

Despite all the inflammatory rhetoric, it is unclear that Mr. Trump would actually pursue the extreme measures his supporters are seeking. And election experts note that the administration’s attempts to assert more federal control over voting have been repeatedly blocked by the courts.

“There’s been a lot of posturing,” said Lawrence Norden, who oversees the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice at New York University, noting that election workers across the country are committed to ensuring a fair vote. “I think mostly election officials are tuning this out. They have elections to run.”

Still, some state and local officials say they are now taking preparations to defend their elections against what used to be a reliable ally: the federal government.

Deidre Henderson, the Republican lieutenant governor of Utah, said that for the first time her state had planned for a situation involving such potential interference, including the prospect of a federal agent showing up to a polling station with a warrant.

“We have had to figure out how to handle some measure of maybe interference from federal officials,” Ms. Henderson said during a George Washington University panel this month. “I don’t think we’ve ever had to think about that before and I don’t necessarily expect it, but right now it would be foolish to not at least think through some scenarios.”

Some voting rights advocates are also worried that a longstanding program by the Justice Department to deploy federal monitors to the polls to protect the civil rights of voters could instead be used to interfere with the elections.

During Wyoming’s primaries in August, two Justice Department monitors tried to interview voters and examine voting machines at polling places, local officials said. Gov. Mark Gordon, a Republican, called their actions “aggressive, unexpected, disruptive,” saying it “certainly didn’t seem to show respect for the state.”

In an expansion of past efforts, the department plans to have 1,000 monitors in all 50 states this year. The N. A. A. C. P. has sued, seeking information about the deployment. “This administration has made clear its intent to disrupt and interfere with the way elections are run in our country,” said Kristen Clarke, the group’s general counsel.

Attorney General Todd Blanche has defended the program, telling Fox News earlier this month that the monitors “are making sure federal law is being enforced appropriately.”

Mr. Trump has been relentless in his efforts to sow doubts about the integrity of American elections, singling out a variety of issues that he claims are suspicious, whether voting by mail or California’s slow vote counting.

At a rally in Alaska this week, Trump took aim at the state’s ranked-choice voting system, calling it a “way to cheat.” He said he had instructed the U. S. attorney in Alaska to closely monitor vote tallies there.

Over the last year, his administration has pushed to find evidence to support his claims. Mr. Trump and Mr. Mullin asserted this summer that 278,000 noncitizens were registered to vote across multiple states, a claim that the government has not been able to substantiate. Homeland security officials have mobilized hundreds of agents to try to find noncitizen voters.

Ms. Bis said Mr. Trump’s actions were meant to ensure the country had “free and fair elections.”

“Every American should be asking why the radical left continues to fight against common-sense election integrity measures, like voter ID and citizenship verification, to make sure only Americans decide our elections,” she said.

Mr. Trump has also left open the possibility of taking more extreme steps. He has refused to rule out invoking the Insurrection Act to deploy the military in connection with the elections, a move encouraged by some of his supporters.

“You have the right to declare a national security emergency for elections,” Wayne Allyn Root, a conservative TV and radio host, told Mr. Trump during an interview in August, referring to a legally dubious theory popular among right-wing election activists.

“Let me just say that stranger things have happened,” Mr. Trump responded. “I’ll leave it at that.”

Mr. Ticktin, who took part in the June meeting with the president and Ms. Peters and says he maintains “pretty direct” communication with Mr. Trump, said he believes the president would consider deploying the military in connection with the midterms.

If many Republicans lose their seats “and we can show that there’s something that was wrong with the election, then it could lead to a serious situation such as martial law or something,” he said.

In late August, the president’s top military adviser, Gen. Dan Caine, said there were no plans for the armed forces to deploy troops in relation to the elections.

The president also said earlier this year that he regretted not seizing voting machines in the 2020 election. Ms. Peters, who also met with Mr. Trump in June, has said she has urged Mr. Trump to take possession of voting machines she claims were constructed with foreign-made equipment.

“I said, ‘We are going to lose this country if we don’t get rid of these machines before the midterms,’” she told the pro-Trump outlet Lindell TV. Ms. Peters also said she had urged him to fire members of an independent, bipartisan commission that supports states in administering their elections.

Mr. Trump forced out the panel’s members in July.

The lobbying efforts by election denialists echo the lead-up to the assault by Mr. Trump’s supporters on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, to try to stop the certification of the 2020 election. At the time, a number of conspiracy theorists pressed Mr. Trump on novel ways to try to overturn that election.

Mr. Trump was flanked then by advisers who were willing to push back on such moves. He is now surrounded by loyalists who are judged not so much on their legal assessments, but rather their ability to turn the president’s wishes into action.

They include top policy adviser Stephen Miller, who has been heavily involved in the efforts to assert more federal control over elections, according to people with knowledge of his efforts.

Mr. Miller, who did not return requests for comment, circulated a draft of an executive order to limit mail voting months before Mr. Trump signed a similar version in March. Some of Mr. Trump’s aides initially pushed back on the order because they felt it was too draconian, according to the people familiar with the events.

But Mr. Trump decided to sign the order, which was ultimately blocked by the Supreme Court, once it became clear that his efforts to have the Senate pass legislation that would restrict mail voting were futile.

Maggie Haberman, Devlin Barrett and Julian E. Barnes contributed reporting.

Zolan Kanno-Youngs is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Democrats Worry That a Few Senate Races in Bluer States Aren’t Slam Dunks

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Despite hopes for a blue wave, Democratic candidates in Minnesota, Maine and Michigan are facing local political headwinds and have struggled to open up clear daylight in the polls.

By Reid J. Epstein

Reporting from Minnesota, with stops in Minneapolis, St. Paul, St. Louis Park and West St. Paul.

President Trump’s low approval ratings have given Democrats a chance to win Senate races in red states like Alaska, Iowa, Texas and Kansas for the first time in a generation.

But at the same time, Democrats in blue states like Minnesota and Maine, and in battlegrounds like Michigan, remain locked in close races where the party’s nominees could jeopardize a Senate majority if they falter in winnable contests.

These too-close-for-comfort races for Democrats are all in states where the party, in varying ways, has created its own political headwinds. All three also feature progressive Democrats who won their nominations over the objections of party leaders who backed more moderate rivals.

“I hope they win — we want them to win,” said Matt Bennett, a co-founder of Third Way, a moderate Democratic think tank. “But they are weaker nominees than we had hoped there would be and it means we have to spend money and time, and there are all kinds of things we have to do that we would not if we had stronger nominees.”

In Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed still faces vocal resistance from some moderate and Jewish voters in his race against former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, after one of this year’s most hostile Democratic primaries. In Maine, Troy Jackson, who was subbed in as the Democratic nominee in July after the implosion of Graham Platner’s campaign, trailed Senator Susan Collins in the most recent New York Times/Siena University poll.

And in Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is being dogged by the state’s major fraud scandal in her contest against Michele Tafoya, a Republican former sports broadcaster. Ms. Tafoya is trying to appeal to the political middle by running TV ads that declare herself to be “a pro-choice Republican” and feature a parade of Democrats who say they are voting for her.

“This election is coming down to this reality,” said former Gov. Tim Pawlenty, whose 2006 re-election was the last time a Republican won a statewide election in Minnesota. “Democrats want to make it a referendum on Trump, and Republicans want to make it a referendum on fraud, which happened under Democrats’ watch. It’s the ‘Trump versus fraud’ election.”

The Minnesota fraud scandal has dominated state politics for more than a year. It was the reason the Trump administration gave for flooding Minneapolis with immigration enforcement agents in January, which led to the killings of two people protesting their actions.

The scandal also forced Gov. Tim Walz to drop his re-election bid in January. And now, even as Democrats in other states run ads talking about high prices and their opposition to Mr. Trump, the party’s down-ballot candidates in Minnesota are talking about fraud and saying they “stood up to Tim Walz.”

This awkwardness for Democrats was evident in separate interviews this week with Ms. Flanagan and Ms. Tafoya. Ms. Flanagan, who has had a rocky relationship with Mr. Walz since his turn as the Democratic nominee for vice president in 2024, would not say whether the governor’s standing was hurting her campaign.

“People have been used to Walz-Flanagan,” she said in an interview Monday, referring to her role as Mr. Walz’s lieutenant governor. “This campaign has been about Peggy Flanagan and my name on the door. And that’s what I’ve tried to focus on.”

Ms. Tafoya said questions about how she would grade Mr. Trump’s performance in office were unfair, and sought to focus on the fraud scandal.

“You’re sounding a little bit like my opponent,” she said in an interview on Tuesday at the Minnesota State Capitol. “Trump, Trump, Trump, Trump, Trump. There are only two of us running for United States Senate, and only one of us let $9 billion walk out the door.”

Mr. Walz, for his part, said the responsibility for not stopping the fraud belonged to him and not to Ms. Flanagan.

“Look, this stuff happened,” he said in an interview at the governor’s residence in St. Paul. “We were on it early, did what we could do to stop it. It doesn’t excuse it. And that’s why I said I took full responsibility for it. I think most people know that’s not the lieutenant governor’s job.”

Despite the problems for Minnesota Democrats, Ms. Flanagan is still considered the favorite.

Even in a Republican-friendly year, Vice President Kamala Harris won the state in 2024 by four percentage points. And this year’s Senate race has yet to draw significant investment from either party’s top super PACs — a sign of limited Republican hopes and Democratic worries about the contest.

When asked about her lack of support from national Republicans, Ms. Tafoya laughed and said, “We will work with what we’ve got.”

Like other Republicans in electoral battlegrounds, Ms. Tafoya faces the challenge of carefully distancing herself from Mr. Trump. As Mr. Rogers in Michigan and Ms. Collins in Maine have done, she has expressed disagreements with him without criticizing him by name.

On Tuesday she called the immigration raids on Minneapolis “abysmal” and said “no president should have a blank check to wage war without the consent of Congress or the buy-in of the American people.”

Ms. Tafoya’s name recognition and moderate politics, along with the effects of the fraud scandal, have some of Ms. Flanagan’s Democratic allies nervous.

Gary Wertish, the president of the Minnesota Farmers Union, said the race was “a little closer than I would hope,” pointing to the fraud scandal fallout.

Other Democrats — especially more moderate ones — quietly worry about Ms. Flanagan’s progressive politics and lack of experience in competitive general elections. She has not been in such a race since her first contest for the Minneapolis school board in 2004.

In the Senate primary race in August, Ms. Flanagan defeated Representative Angie Craig, a moderate who had the backing of party leaders including Representatives Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader, and Gwen Walz, the governor’s wife. Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader, did not endorse a candidate, but his allies made clear they preferred Ms. Craig.

If she wins, Ms. Flanagan could become the first Native American woman to serve in the Senate (Mary Peltola, who is running in Alaska, could also reach that milestone). She said she hoped to emulate liberal senators like Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Elizabeth Warren and Ed Markey of Massachusetts. She has endorsed an array of progressive policies, including “Medicare for all” and said in the interview that she would seek to expand the Supreme Court to “at least 12 or 13” justices.

The winner of the Senate race will replace Senator Tina Smith, a Democrat who did not seek re-election. Public polling suggests a competitive contest, with a survey this week from The Minnesota Star Tribune showing Ms. Flanagan with a four-point lead.

Democrats must flip at least four Republican-held Senate seats to win a majority in the chamber. Losing in Minnesota would imperil the party’s hopes of doing so.

As in Minnesota, polls show Democrats with comfortable leads in the governor’s races in Maine and Michigan.

But in those state’s Senate contests, where there is far more outside spending, Dr. El-Sayed and Mr. Jackson, like Ms. Flanagan, are only narrowly ahead or are tied. After winning their primaries (or, in Mr. Jackson’s case, a last-minute convention) by embracing their left-wing politics, they are now vying to win over voters in the middle.

It has not always gone well.

In Michigan, a faction of Democrats has refused to come around to Dr. El-Sayed. A group of rabbis who described themselves as loyal Democrats urged him last month to change his tone and position on Israel, of which he is a fierce critic.

Dr. El-Sayed has sought to build a new type of coalition. He has campaigned in rural, more conservative counties and is planning a bus tour this week of the state’s Upper Peninsula with Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.

Yet he faces some Democratic resistance. Representative Hillary Scholten, a Michigan Democrat, has withheld an endorsement, and Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Senate primary to Dr. El-Sayed in August, said in an interview on Wednesday that many of her constituents remained unhappy with him.

“I have a constituency group that has always supported me that is horrified,” Ms. Stevens said. “My goal here is to back the car into the garage. It’s a tossup election. It’s just straight-up a tossup election and it is going to come down to Election Day.”

The concerns about Dr. El-Sayed from fellow Democrats come after the party’s primary voters largely rejected concerns about his electability.

At the same time, Mr. Jackson emerged in Maine after a fellow progressive candidate, Mr. Platner, won the Democratic primary, only to withdraw in the wake of a rape allegation that he denied. Mr. Platner, upon leaving the race, made a public call for a like-minded candidate to replace him on the ballot.

Mr. Jackson, a former logger and longtime state legislator, had a short runway to get up to speed, is a rougher political messenger and has not been as active on the campaign trail as Mr. Platner was. And Ms. Collins has sought to use her experience and seniority in the Senate to argue that she can do more for the state than Mr. Jackson would if he replaces her in January.

Ms. Flanagan, Dr. El-Sayed and Mr. Jackson have all said they would not support Mr. Schumer for majority leader. Mr. Schumer said in an interview with The New York Times last week that he remained confident they would all prevail.

Democratic Senate candidates are running strong races in red states like Alaska, Kansas, Ohio and Texas. But in blue states like Maine, Michigan and especially Minnesota, the party’s candidates are locked in tight races, a function of local headwinds and left-wing nominees who are struggling to put distance between themselves and their Republican opponents. What do you think it means that the Democrats who told primary voters they wanted to shake up the party’s establishment are now in tight races in states where more moderate candidates for governor are far ahead in the polls?

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

Hegseth’s Plan to Livestream Execution Drew Opposition From Many

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

A retired general, a Catholic archbishop for the military and one of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan’s victims were among those who had spoken out.

By John Ismay

Reporting from Washington

A retired general who approved the death sentence for Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, the Army psychiatrist convicted of a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood in Texas.

An archbishop who ministers to Catholics in the Defense Department.

A sergeant who was shot seven times in the rampage, including once in his face.

All of them opposed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the execution of Mr. Hasan, who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others. Their reasons varied, but their conclusions were similar.

On Thursday, President Trump said the execution would not be broadcast. “Many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” he wrote on social media. “He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.”

It is a rebuke of his defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, who had said the killing of Mr. Hasan would be made public “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

Mr. Hegseth’s decision, however, violated Army regulations that prohibit anyone younger than 18 from witnessing an execution.

If all else goes to plan, Mr. Hasan will be shot to death on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, the Army post where the massacre took place.

Sean B. MacFarland, who served as commanding general of Fort Hood five years after the shooting, approved the death sentence for Mr. Hasan following his conviction by courts-martial.

He said that Mr. Hasan deserved to die for his crimes. But the general said he was against streaming the execution.

“By livestreaming this at a U. S. Army installation in the United States of America, it seems to me that not only are we inspiring or encouraging future enemy combatants, but we’re also making Fort Hood a potential target for retribution in the future,” he said in an interview on Tuesday.

General MacFarland, who commanded Fort Hood from 2014 to 2017, said there was an important distinction.

“We are not executing an enemy combatant,” he said. “We are executing a member of our own Army who betrayed his oath as an American soldier and his own oath as a physician. And he was tried and he will be executed under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. That’s completely different than the Geneva Conventions and the laws of armed conflict that govern the treatment of enemy prisoners of war.”

“But I don’t think that our future opponents around the world are going to make that fine distinction, and that’s a real source of concern for me,” he added.

The plan to execute Major Hasan in public also drew rare criticism from the Archdiocese for the Military Services, USA, which oversees all Catholic priests serving in uniform as military chaplains, and ministers to members of the church serving in the Defense Department.

On Monday, Archbishop Timothy P. Broglio, who leads the archdiocese, issued a public statement that reiterated the Catholic Church’s opposition to capital punishment in all circumstances. He added that streaming such an act was a violation of Mr. Hasan’s innate dignity as a human being.

“In general, I avoid making public statements about public policy,” Archbishop Broglio said on Wednesday. “However, I felt this was such an egregious affront to the dignity of the human person that I really had to take a public stance — as I did, of course, also when they approved other anti-life measures under the previous administration permitting abortions on military medical facilities.”

“I think it would be disastrous for young children” to view the execution, the archbishop said. “I mean, I realize we live in a violent society, but to see something like that orchestrated before their very eyes, I think it would be detrimental.”

In his statement on Monday, Archbishop Broglio issued a call that Catholics be excused from participating in Mr. Hasan’s execution.

A spokeswoman for Mr. Hegseth declined to comment on the archbishop’s statement.

On that day in 2009, Sgt. Alonzo M. Lunsford Jr., a combat medic, was working in an office that assessed the physical and emotional fitness of Fort Hood soldiers deploying to or returning home from combat deployments.

Major Hasan shot him just above his left eye, then returned to shoot him six times in his torso.

In an interview, Sergeant Lunsford, who had been promoted to staff sergeant before his medical retirement from the military, said those additional gunshot wounds resulted in devastating internal injuries.

Sergeant Lunsford believes that Major Hasan should die for his crimes and plans to attend his execution. But he was against broadcasting it.

“The thing about it is that I don’t think that it should be displayed to kids and adolescents,” he said on Wednesday. “And the other thing is, I don’t think this should be displayed like it’s a damn spectacle, like it’s a pay-per-view event where we’re going to have a tailgate for his execution.”

“We’re better than that as a country, and as a people — we don’t have public executions. Those days are long gone,” he added.

In conversations with other surviving victims, Sergeant Lunsford said that “for the most part, they just wanted it to be over with and they want their privacy to be respected. They don’t want a spectacle to be made of this, because the true heroes are the ones who are no longer here.”

On Wednesday, dozens of retired admirals and generals and other officers published an open letter opposing Mr. Hegseth’s plan to broadcast the execution.

“Livestreaming this execution would clearly violate the basic human dignity of the condemned prisoner,” they wrote. “It turns what should be the solemn and grave punishment of a member of our society for committing the most serious crimes into a carnival for the enjoyment of voyeurs and spectators.”

“This type of exploitative broadcasting — that debases human dignity — will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it,” they added.

Some members of Congress also welcomed Mr. Trump’s decision to cancel the livestream.

They included Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee.

Mr. Reed, who graduated from West Point and served in the Army, said in a statement that Mr. Trump “was right to backtrack and ultimately reached the correct conclusion.”

But the senator added: “Still, this episode highlights the impulsive and dysfunctional civilian leadership from the White House and U. S. Department of Defense.”

A few Republicans had also criticized the plan.

Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who is retiring and has become increasingly critical of the Trump administration, said the decision to broadcast the execution was “beyond disgusting.”

He likened it to the actions of some of the United States’ most brutal adversaries.

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

John Ismay is a reporter covering the Pentagon for The Times. He served as an explosive ordnance disposal officer in the U. S. Navy.

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Advertisement
