Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Isabel Wilkerson remembers covering a flood powerful enough to disrupt the dead.

Credit... Matt Dorfman

Supported by

By Isabel Wilkerson

Isabel Wilkerson, a Pulitzer Prize winner and a former Chicago bureau chief for The Times, is the author of “The Warmth of Other Suns” and “Caste: The Origins of Our Discontents.”

All spring and into the summer of 1993, beyond the notice of the outside world, the heavens opened up above the central United States, a steady stream at first and then biblical torrents that drowned the soil and forced the Mississippi River to climb over its banks and to defy the will of man. This was not the flash flood of a single storm but the slow, steady rise of a makeshift sea that over the weeks and months would drape itself over entire towns, or threaten to, in nine Midwestern states.

By that June, the Father of Waters and its tributaries — the Missouri, the Minnesota, the Iowa, the Cedar, the Wisconsin and the rest — had all run out of room and were returning to where they had been before highways and subdivisions displaced them on the primordial plains that had once been theirs. They re-established residence and would linger for as many as 200 days. They drove uncountable numbers of townspeople from their homes and paid no heed to the sandbags that tried to coax the rivers back into the channels that humans had assigned them.

I was The New York Times’s Chicago bureau chief at the time, responsible for the 12 states of the Midwest, and was coming off a monthslong immersion in the life of a 10-year-old boy on Chicago’s South Side at the height of a different calamity — the 1990s crack cocaine epidemic. I was anticipating a quiet re-entry into my everyday world, when reports began to surface of river crests beyond anything ever recorded and futile attempts to prop up failing levees.

By the time the city of Des Moines was shut down after the Des Moines and Raccoon rivers overran their dikes, engulfing the municipal water treatment station, forcing highways and bridges to close, and leaving the city without running water even to put out fires, I was on a plane to Iowa.

From the window seat I could see the roof caps of houses poking up from the river water like buoys and rafts out to sea. I wrote on the back of a napkin that it looked as if someone had spilled gallons and gallons of coffee on a patchwork quilt that happened to be farms and towns. I would tuck that note into my bag to save for an overview that would end up, as it turned out, in that Sunday’s paper. For now, I had to get to Des Moines.

Covering disasters requires a certain kind of accelerated metabolism, a nimbleness and stamina you might not need until you are suddenly heading to the airport into the middle of an unfolding catastrophe. Your life is now suspended for the duration. Overnight, you have to get up to speed on the inner workings of a place you may never have been to, and on whatever field of expertise applies to the crisis at hand.

There were few cellphones back then, no GPS and no laptops as we currently know them, but, instead, for us, hulking processors with DOS screens and clunky paraphernalia, all told weighing in at close to 15 pounds, with no guarantee that whatever you wrote on them would get to the editors, given the temperamental nature of dial-up. Thus I arrived with pens, notebooks and instinct.

The year before, I had been dispatched to South Florida to cover Hurricane Andrew, at the time the most damaging hurricane in U. S. history. I drove through the barren no man’s land of denuded palm trees, abandoned highways and empty tollbooths, and saw, as never before, the power of nature. I walked up to one of the many shellshocked homeowners as he stood in front of what was left of his house, awaiting the arrival of an overworked claims adjuster. He was surrounded by the rubble of the hurricane — matted mounds of clothing, broken table legs and torn-up chairs on their sides, a refrigerator.

“How is it possible,” I asked the man, “that the wind could pick up your refrigerator and blow it all the way out to your front yard? It is unbelievable.”

He shook his head at the enormity of it all and corrected me. “That’s not my refrigerator.”

So I considered myself prepared for whatever the summer had in store. But the Great Midwest Flood was not merely a disaster. It was a siege that would become the worst flood in modern U. S. history. So many records broken, so many levees breached, so many residents evacuated, so many houses and farmers’ soybean fields ruined and sodden over the course of five months that the term “flood stage” lost all meaning, and I and the other Times correspondents scattered over the region were running out of synonyms for “flood” and “water.”

Then a news brief came over the wires about the unimaginable: The flood had washed away most of the cemetery in a tiny town in northwestern Missouri. Caskets were floating down the Missouri River or had come to rest along railroad tracks and in soybean fields. It seemed like a scene out of the Old Testament. By the time I arrived, townspeople let me know that reporters had come and gone and had already written about the caskets, which were by now attracting gawkers from other states.

That was not why I had flown all the way to Kansas City and then driven 45 miles to the town of Hardin, in rural Ray County. The story was not about caskets. The stories that touch the soul are those that reveal themselves on multiple frequencies and are never only about what they seem on the surface. The caskets might have gotten a reader’s attention, but it was the human response to the unthinkable that would hold it.

In that farm town of 598 people, the Ray County coroner, Dean Snow, was leading the recovery effort for a pre-Civil War cemetery where nearly everyone who had ever lived and died in Hardin had been buried. The townspeople who had lost everything to the flood were now worried sick over what had become of their loved ones. It was as if the people had “died all over again and the survivors must grieve anew,” I wrote.

Every day they gathered at the fairgrounds to scour the bulletin board where the names of the dead who had been recovered and identified were posted. It was a painful task, more akin to a plane crash than a flood, that required survivors to give volunteers any descriptions they could recall of their departed relatives, like the man who was wearing a Timex watch and had a slide rule in his shirt pocket, or another who had “a tattoo on his right arm that said ‘Irene.’”

One woman, distraught and near tears as she stood there, searched the list close because she had two husbands in the cemetery and was beside herself at the thought that the wrong one might have been carried off. “You don’t feel the same way about every husband,” she told me.

Later, because I was by myself and not with a gaggle, the coroner let me accompany him past the barricades to what was left of the cemetery. He waved along Ed Wolfe, a friend who was so heartsick over the stillborn son he had buried years before that he beseeched the coroner to let him come with us. The two of them walked the cemetery reminiscing about the people beneath the headstones as if they were at a reunion.

“That’s Della’s husband,” Wolfe said, pointing to the surviving headstone of a World War II veteran.

“Yeah, Bob’s dad,” Snow said, looking down. “He was working on his car, and it fell on him.”

Wolfe had been pacing the cemetery the whole time, in search of his father and stillborn son. Soon we got to the edge of the cliff that had been gouged by the river, and he sank when he saw that the earth had vanished where their caskets had once been.

“My baby and my dad are gone,” he said, his eyes red and watery. “We’ve been hoping for five weeks they were safe. The way things are broken up down there, I don’t know if they’ll ever be recovered.”

This was not the time for questions but for empathy. In the finished piece, I ended with: “He wiped his eyes and headed back to the road, walking over dead corn shucks and wheat stubble, to break the news to his wife.”

I wrote the story in longhand back at a hotel in Kansas City and called it into the dictation desk, which passed it on to the editors. We had no concept of email or high-speed Wi-Fi back then because they did not exist for the general public.

As I look back, I am in awe of what all of us did with seemingly so little compared to now. We could not Google the length of the Mississippi River. There was no internet on which to search an oblique scientific reference, just finger-crossed calls to researchers that you hoped you could get on the phone before deadline, and the rushed clippings faxed to the front desk of your hotel from the newspaper’s librarians in what we used to call the morgue.

In a pinch, after all the offices had closed, I phoned my civil engineer father, who, though he built bridges and not hydraulics, relished — in fact, had been waiting all my life for — the chance to talk theory and terminology, as it was going to be the closest glimmer he would ever get to seeing me as the engineer he had once wanted me to be.

The rivers did not fully recede until that October. The catastrophe had crept along unnoticed until it was beyond the dominion of man, and it only ended when the rivers said so. It was an early sign of the earthly trials to come in the current century — the sudden flooding in Nepal and Tibet from a collapsing glacier this summer, the record-setting heat and drought in Europe, extreme enough to expose a Nazi warship at the bottom of the Danube, and the wildfires in Canada that sent smoke a thousand miles from the original flames, all reflections of the unheeded forewarnings of history.

What people came to realize during the Great Flood was that a river is not what we can see on any given day. A river is wherever it has been and could return to again. Which is why, by the fourth month of the flood and after twice being submerged by the Mississippi, the village of Valmeyer, Ill., surrendered to the forces of nature. The people voted to move the town from the rich lowland that Swiss immigrants first settled during the previous century, to a bluff a mile and a half inland and 400 feet higher. The people of Valmeyer gave the river back to itself. They decided they couldn’t trust it anymore.

As for the mourners in Hardin, Mo., sadly most did not get their wish. While more than 600 caskets were recovered from what the Missouri River carried away, only 120 remains could be identified. So the town reburied most of them in a mass grave for the unknown. One hundred and forty-eight of the departed were never found and were effectively lost at sea for all time.

That summer’s anguish was recounted without the technology we now take for granted, which affirms, in case we ever doubted, that technology cannot speak for the human heart. We may be covering a region or a country or a beat. We may think we are writing about elections, hurricanes, famine, poverty. But what I think we are always actually writing about is the ancient story of humans battling, and somehow surviving, the odds against them, whether the foe is others of our own species, systems of our own making, injustice, greed, war, or, in this case, the power of nature itself.

Once the storms were over and the river had collected itself, traffic at last came back to life after months of impassibility. This allowed me to make a six-day journey down the Mississippi on barges and towboats and every possible conveyance. There I ran into an engineer from Washington, Mo., named Bill Scholl, on the deck of a gambling boat, the Alton Belle. Beyond the tree line, a gray silt veil still clung to collapsed houses and grain bins, to deserted farm towns and to cornfields laid to waste. The river was quiet and composed now, as if nothing at all had happened that summer. Scholl leaned on the railing as he fixed his gaze on the deceptively still waters before us. Then he turned to me. “The river always wins,” he said. “God always wins.”

Rising Mortgage Rates Risk Plunging Housing Further Into Crisis

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Mortgage rates have pushed above 7 percent and home prices remain elevated, hurting the prospects of would-be buyers.

By Sydney Ember

In late February, would-be home buyers and sellers rejoiced.

For the first time in more than three years, the average interest on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage had dropped below 6 percent. Finally, it seemed, the languid housing market might perk up.

That glimmer of hope has flamed out.

Mortgage rates have rocketed back up, hovering at 7.4 percent as of Thursday. And it appears unlikely that rates will decline significantly anytime soon. Mortgage rates are tied to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which has soared because of concerns about persistent inflation, ballooning national debt and optimism around growth driven by artificial intelligence.

“Unless you get a recession, it’s really hard to bring down rates,” said Josh Hirt, an economist at Vanguard.

The surge in mortgage rates could further depress housing activity and plunge the country deeper into a housing crisis. The United States had 3.7 million fewer homes than it needed in late 2024, according to Freddie Mac.

Homeowners who secured ultralow mortgages during the pandemic, when borrowing costs plummeted, will be less willing to move, limiting already sluggish sales. Prospective buyers might instead live with their parents or remain renters, pushing up rents. Builders could be more reluctant to invest in construction, exacerbating a national housing shortage.

The era of rock-bottom mortgage rates may be over, but higher rates are historically more common. During the 1980s, the average interest on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage surpassed 18 percent. The difference now is that home prices are sky-high as well, a combination that is putting home buying out of reach for many Americans, especially first-time purchasers.

Alex LeForestier and his wife started thinking seriously about buying a house last month. They were contemplating moving from Stockton, Calif., to nearby Sacramento and wanted to see what kind of mortgage they could get.

After speaking with a loan officer and perusing home prices in the area, they concluded their monthly payment would far exceed the $2,400 they paid in rent for their 2-bedroom, one-bath home.

“It’s really hard to imagine buying a house during this period of time,” said Mr. LeForestier, 27, who works at a local university.

“The interest rates really scared us,” he added.

Owning a home is as unaffordable as it was in the years before the financial crisis, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta’s homeownership affordability monitor, which takes into account the median household income and the median home price.

The result is that more people could remain in the rental market, said Daryl Fairweather, the chief economist at Redfin, an online real estate brokerage. An increase in the pool of renters, combined with slower construction of apartment buildings, could push up rents.

Rents have risen modestly in recent years but they could start to accelerate in a year or two, Ms. Fairweather said. Rental housing costs increased 0.2 percent in September and 2.8 percent over the year, according to the most recent Consumer Price Index report.

“Rents have been stable because there was all this new construction of apartments during the pandemic that added to inventory,” she said. “But that’s over, and that’s going to be slowing down as more people go to the rental market.”

Higher rents could lift overall inflation, which could be a challenge for the Federal Reserve as it tries to tamp down persistent price increases.

Another way higher mortgage rates could dampen housing is by curtailing the housing supply. The home building sector has been languishing for years because of labor shortages, rising material prices brought on by supply chain trouble and tariffs, regulatory hurdles and a lack of land.

As mortgage rates rise, home builders will have to weigh the cost of construction with the likelihood that their homes will find ready buyers. Many home builders have had to offer concessions to entice potential homeowners, including price cuts, which decrease their profit. Builders are also facing higher borrowing costs, making financing their projects more expensive.

The National Association of Home Builders forecasts that single-family home building will decline by 4 percent this year and another 3 percent next year. Multifamily construction will also fall.

“We’re not talking about the bottom falling out,” said Robert Dietz, the trade group’s chief economist. But, he added, “it’s a hard slog.”

Christian Albright, a project manager at Titan Design Build, a home builder in the Denver area that replaces derelict houses and structures with new homes, said higher mortgage rates have changed the company’s calculations.

In addition to reducing prices, it is advertising its duplexes, triplexes and townhouses before they are finished in an attempt to sell them quickly and avoid paying carrying costs like heating and electric bills.

“Interest rates really are the determining factor of how quickly sales move,” he said.

Although the company has not reined in its building, Mr. Albright said rising rates could limit its property acquisitions.

A slowdown in building raises the possibility that there will not be enough houses later if mortgage rates fall, even slightly, and buyers rush back into the housing market. That could drive up housing prices and make it even harder to buy a home.

Earlier this year, Congress passed a bill that aims to make it easier and cheaper for developers to build houses. The measure, which became law in July, could make housing more affordable in the long term.

Fed officials will be watching how much the housing market and home building slow in response to higher rates. Housing, while highly sensitive to interest rates, may not have much room to slacken given its already slow pace. That could make it harder for the Fed to bring inflation back to its 2 percent target. The Fed, which increased rates by a quarter of a percentage point last month, is expected to raise rates at least once more in the coming months.

One question is whether sellers will reduce prices to woo buyers while rates are high, which could improve the number of sales. Home prices nationally were up 1.9 percent in July from the year earlier, slightly faster than the previous month, according to a widely followed index from S&P.

Some research suggests that home prices actually rise during periods of high interest rates because they are correlated with a stronger economy and higher inflation.

“Higher rates don’t necessarily mean home prices fall,” said Laurie Goodman, a fellow at the Urban Institute, a nonprofit research group.

Mr. Hirt, the Vanguard economist, said the housing market has been less susceptible to interest rate hikes because the housing shortage prevents prices from falling considerably. After the Fed started raising interest rates in 2022 in response to skyrocketing inflation, he noted, housing prices did not drop as much as they might have because demand for homes outweighed supply.

As a result, he said, the housing market should only marginally worsen as long as interest rates do not climb much higher.

“Maybe it doesn’t weaken a lot more,” he said, “but it certainly would be somewhat weaker tomorrow than it is today.”

New York Times economics reporters want to understand how Americans are navigating employment and the rising cost of living. We may want to use your experience in a story, but we would only do so with your permission.

Sydney Ember covers the U. S. economy for The Times.

Why Does Saudi Arabia Struggle to Stop Houthi Attacks?

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Houthi-Saudi War

Advertisement

Supported by

The Saudi military has expensive equipment, but the missiles and drones used by the Yemeni militia are difficult to detect and stop.

By Neil MacFarquhar

Neil MacFarquhar has long reported about the Middle East, including assignments in Saudi Arabia during previous wars.

Over decades, Saudi Arabia has invested hundreds of billions of dollars in building an advanced military, putting the kingdom among the top 10 nations in terms of arms spending.

Still, the country has stumbled in response to deadly attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi militia, with the fighting in recent months reigniting a war that the kingdom began in 2015.

The problem in part is that Saudi Arabia invested heavily in weapons having what some military analysts call a “glitter factor” — things like high-tech fighter jets and the latest missile interceptors. But the Houthi guerrillas often deploy cheap drones or low-flying cruise missiles that Saudi forces struggle to detect.

In addition, Saudi defenses were built assuming that the biggest threat would come from the east or northeast, from Iran or Iraq, not from Yemen to the southwest. So the country was left somewhat exposed, analysts said.

Finally, the kingdom only recently started to address longstanding systemic problems. To inoculate the Saud dynasty against the military coups that plagued most Arab states, the military was built as two competing branches. Each suffers from highly centralized decision-making, which limits flexibility, analysts said.

“It’s a hugely rattling moment for Riyadh, humiliating on a number of fronts,” said Burcu Ozcelik, an expert on Middle East security issues at the Royal United Services Institute, a defense research organization in London.

“There has been a very substantial, longstanding investment in building up hard military capabilities,” she added. “But the issue is preparedness. How ready were the Saudis for this kind of lightning-speed offensive, as it is being called by the Houthis?”

For days, the Houthis have launched repeated attacks on infrastructure, energy and military targets deep within Saudi Arabia. This week, they struck the Saudi energy giant Aramco, setting a building on fire in Dhahran in the east of the country. On Thursday, the Saudi authorities said a drone was intercepted and destroyed in the eastern province, as well as a cruise missile in the Medina region, though the Houthis denied targeting Medina.

On Saturday, a cruise missile struck a domestic airport terminal in Riyadh, the capital, killing at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others. It was the worst attack on the kingdom in over a decade.

Note: Houthi-controlled areas as of Oct. 13 Sources: Saudi and Houthi officials; Institute for the Study of War and Critical Threats Project at the American Enterprise Institute (Houthi-controlled areas). Samuel Granados/The New York Times

The military spokesman for the Houthis issued a statement on social media on Sunday detailing multiple sites targeted by drones and missiles.

“The Yemeni armed forces will continue their operations in an escalating manner toward the Saudi interior,” the Houthi spokesman, Yahya Saree, said, adding that the strikes would continue until the kingdom stopped attacking Yemen. Houthi forces are also blocking Saudi oil shipments to Asia through the Bab al-Mandab Strait between Yemen and Africa.

Saudi Arabia vowed retaliation. “The events of recent weeks are serious,” Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, the energy minister, said at an international conference in Riyadh soon after the attack on the airport. “Our response must be equally serious.”

In 2015, Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, then defense minister, ignited the war against the Houthis, a Shiite Muslim millenarian sect seeking to unseat the Yemeni government. Routing them would take weeks, said Prince Mohammed, who became crown prince in 2017 and is now Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler.

Instead the war became a quagmire. The United Nations brokered a cease-fire in 2022, but the conflict flared anew amid tensions over the United States and Israel attacking Iran.

Given that the Houthis fired hundreds of missiles at Saudi Arabia during the initial war starting in 2015, the Royal Saudi Air Defense Force, the separate military wing that protects Saudi airspace, gained unique experience firing Patriot missiles, said David Des Roches, a professor and former Pentagon policy director for the Persian Gulf.

Patriots are expensive, mobile, surface-to-air defense systems sold by the United States and consisting of advanced radar and interceptor missiles.

Since 2020, Washington has sold Saudi Arabia at least 730 Patriot interceptors, according to figures from the U. S. State Department.

But Patriot missiles are designed to knock down ballistic missiles, which follow a high, fixed trajectory that can be tracked. THAAD interceptors, which Saudi Arabia has also purchased from the United States, are meant to hit missiles flying even higher.

So the fight against the Houthis is asymmetrical. Using a Patriot missile bought for over $3 million to shoot down a drone costing $15,000 to $25,000 is akin to trying to swat a mosquito with a hammer, analysts said.

Also, because of the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, there is an interceptor supply shortage worldwide.

Since the Houthis began fighting, their arsenal has become more robust, with the militia now manufacturing some weapons and diversifying supplies away from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran, according to a U. N. Security Council report.

Radar is also a key issue for Saudi Arabia. Drones and cruise missiles that the Houthis use — with a lighter payload still capable of decimating civilian targets — fly at low altitudes and can change direction. “It can be tough to find them at long range if you don’t have radar coverage,” said Kenneth M. Pollack, author of “Armies of Sand,” a book about Arab military effectiveness.

Saudi Arabia is immense and hard to protect. Since the kingdom has long feared attacks against the Eastern Province, the heart of its oil resources along the Persian Gulf, it has concentrated there the most sophisticated air defenses, including layers of radar installations and missile interceptors, analysts said.

Complex radar installations are not mobile, and although some face Yemen, they are ground-based. Their lack of reach over the horizon means they often do not detect projectiles zipping low through Yemen’s mountainous terrain until they are already over Saudi Arabia, leading to erratic warnings to civilians. The kingdom requires more airborne radar to identify them earlier.

Although jet fighters are designed to confront other jet fighters, they can be used against drones and missiles. But they need to be alerted to their trajectory, analysts said. (Ukraine uses acoustic sensors to help detect drones.) Saudi Arabia has several hundred fighter jets — mostly F-15s from the United States plus Eurofighter Typhoons.

In April 2024, when Iran launched more than 300 projectiles at once against Israel, Israel and the United States, along with Britain, France and Jordan, intercepted most of them. Wide, overlapping radar coverage pinpointed the projectiles, with fighter jets shooting down the smaller threats including drones while Israel’s ground-based interceptors handled missiles at higher altitudes. Even so, not everything was intercepted.

Aside from drone warfare, the Saudi military has been grappling with structural problems.

Its current annual military budget is more than $82 billion, according to the independent Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, but the force remains divided into two silos. The regular military has around 250,000 troops, while the Saudi Arabian National Guard includes about 125,000. The National Guard has long recruited from tribes loyal to the Saud dynasty, and trains against possible domestic insurgency.

Princes dominate both forces, analysts said, and the rigid, top-down command structure thwarts initiative in the field.

Prince Mohammed made streamlining the military part of his Vision 2030 plan for developing the kingdom, which included the firing of several senior commanders in 2018. He also established a joint operational command in Riyadh to coordinate military decisions, but analysts called the overall changes slow. For example, they said, the military still struggles with maintaining high-tech weapons, a job often done by Western contractors.

In confronting the Houthis, Saudi Arabia is not expected to mount a ground invasion that would require a bloody slog to try to dislodge the guerrillas from their mountain redoubts. Inside Yemen, division and disorganization mar the anti-Houthi coalition backed by the Saudis.

With President Trump denying Riyadh’s recent requests for help, Saudi Arabia invoked a mutual defense pact that it signed with Pakistan and Turkey last August. Those countries are expected to aid matters like intelligence and communications, analysts said.

A renewed air campaign alone would probably be insufficient to defeat the Houthis. “There is nothing really that the Saudis did not already try,” said Jean-Loup Samaan, a Middle East expert at the National University of Singapore. Mainly, there is no viable alternative to the Houthis inside Yemen, he added.

A negotiated political solution anytime soon seems unlikely. Amid a war against Iran inaugurated by Mr. Trump, the Iranians want the Houthis to ratchet up the cost of the conflict for both Washington and Riyadh, a crucial U. S. ally. The Houthis, who seek more power, are emerging as the strongest force in the region among the Iranian proxies, which Tehran calls “the axis of resistance.”

The United States fought the Houthis to a standstill for four months in 2025, and Mr. Trump has shown little appetite to resume. Still, the Houthis represent a strategic dilemma.

“Saudi Arabia’s increasingly difficult position cannot simply be ignored,” Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli military analyst, wrote on social media. “Riyadh is a critical American partner, and a Houthi victory, or a political settlement imposed on Saudi Arabia under military pressure and largely on Houthi terms, would represent an enormous strategic achievement for Iran and the broader Axis of Resistance.”

Neil MacFarquhar has been a Times reporter since 1995, writing about a range of topics from war to politics to the arts, both internationally and in the United States.

To Inflict Economic Pain, Russia and Ukraine Strike at Data Centers

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Military forces have sought to damage the computing hubs that power online services and artificial intelligence systems.

By Ryan Mac and Ivan Nechepurenko

The war between Russia and Ukraine has come for data centers.

Forces from both sides have recently ramped up attacks on infrastructure that serves as the backbone to web-connected services and artificial intelligence systems.

The Russian military hit a data center in Kyiv and other telecommunications sites, while Ukraine struck back by damaging three major data centers operated by the technology giant Yandex, often referred to as Russia’s Google, and a data center run by Sberbank, Russia’s largest bank.

The targeting of data centers is a relatively new phenomenon in the war, now in its fifth year since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said in a speech on Monday that the targeting of Yandex was “responding to Russia’s operation against our data centers.”

The strikes on digital infrastructure have come on top of intensifying attacks on energy installations, including a recent Russian barrage of dozens of ballistic missiles that cut power to 600,000 people in Kyiv, Ukraine’s capital. Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries, one of the factors pushing global diesel prices to record highs, have drawn a rebuke from President Trump, who has pushed for Ukraine to limit its strikes as energy-driven inflation accelerates ahead of the U. S. midterm elections.

Since the boom in artificial intelligence has generated a seemingly insatiable demand for computing power, data centers have emerged as increasingly important economic hubs. That makes these installations high-value targets for the drones that now define modern warfare, and not only in Russia and Ukraine. Shortly after the start of the U. S.-Israeli war on Iran, Iranian drones struck Amazon data centers in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates, disrupting computing services for users around the region.

The disruptions to daily life and business after the strikes on data centers have varied in Russia and Ukraine, said Vili Lehdonvirta, a technology policy professor at Finland’s Aalto University. Ukraine’s data centers are important to enabling remote work in a country under regular bombardment, but the country had shifted much of its government and banking data to American and European facilities at the start of the war, he said.

Russia’s government and private-sector systems are “mostly hosted in domestic data centers,” Mr. Lehdonvirta said. The government passed legislation requiring companies, including tech firms, to store personal data on servers inside the country, prompting many businesses to invest millions of dollars to build local data centers. Cross-border sanctions also make it hard for Russia to rely on internet services hosted outside its borders.

“In that sense, Russia is probably more vulnerable to data center warfare than Ukraine is,” Mr. Lehdonvirta said.

Ukraine’s attacks resulted in some of the largest internet service disruptions in Russian history. Yandex runs the country’s dominant ride-hailing app, popular streaming platforms and extensive payment processing services. It also provides cloud computing services to more than 50,000 Russian businesses that form the backbone of the country’s internet economy. Across central Russia, Yandex operates at least six large data centers, which also house its three A. I. supercomputers.

Over the past week, since Ukraine began striking Yandex’s data centers, several of the company’s apps have stopped working. Users were unable to order food and taxis and download files from their cloud accounts. Street-level images in the mapping app were blurred, and the Yandex Pay system, which many Russians use to store money in digital wallets, suspended operations, leaving users with the ability to view their balances but not transfer money.

Yandex’s cloud-computing platform was “still operating in a limited mode,” the company said in an update to customers on Wednesday. “Our specialists continue the restoration work around the clock.”

Customers of Sberbank on Wednesday reported disruptions among many services, including the bank’s A. I. assistant, website and app, after a drone attack on a data center used by the bank.

Service outages also spread to Cian, the leading real estate listings platform in Russia. The website of Pulkovo, the airport serving St. Petersburg, was also knocked offline.

Mr. Zelensky has suggested that Ukraine’s strikes on Yandex’s infrastructure also took out “bots” used by the Russian government to sow discord and spread misinformation on social networks around the world.

“When our strikes reached Yandex’s data centers, it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms,” he said in his speech on Monday. “A lot of people noticed it. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations.”

On social media, some politicians, political consultants and commentators seized on the idea, noting that apparent drops in engagement for right-wing accounts including those associated with Elon Musk and the Alternative for Germany political party were due to damage to Russian data centers. Some cited a chart from the internet services company Cloudflare that showed that “bot traffic” from Yandex had collapsed.

In the Cloudflare context, however, bot traffic refers to so-called crawlers, or software programs that run automated tasks on the web, a company spokeswoman said, not automated accounts run by influence operations that post on social media. Many observers conflated the two in online posts.

“Across Cloudflare’s network, there was no evidence that the strikes knocked social media manipulation offline or otherwise disrupted malicious activity on the internet,” the company wrote in a blog post on Wednesday.

What is not in dispute is the lasting damage that attacks on data centers can do. Experts said it could take months for Yandex to fully repair the damage. In the Emirates, some six months after its data centers were hit, Amazon said in a blog post that customers there would be unable to restore access to some of the data it had hosted in the country.

Mr. Lehdonvirta anticipates that this may be the start of a new way of waging war. “I would unfortunately expect data centers to continue to be a target,” he said.

Ryan Mac is a Times reporter who covers corporate accountability across the global technology industry.

Ivan Nechepurenko covers Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, the countries of the Caucasus and Central Asia. He divides his reporting time between Moscow and Tbilisi, Georgia.

Mortgage Rates Hover at 7.4%, Highest Since 2023

The New York Times October 15, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

The average 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage has steadily risen in recent weeks, compounding affordability challenges for many Americans.

Source: Freddie Mac.

The New York Times

By Gregory Schmidt

Mortgage rates remained elevated for the eighth straight week, further straining affordability for many Americans already struggling with everyday expenses.

The average rate for the 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage, the most popular home loan in the United States, held steady at 7.4 percent, the highest in three years, the mortgage finance giant Freddie Mac said on Thursday. Mortgage rates were 6.27 percent at this time last year.

The war in Iran has crimped the world’s oil supply, pushing up energy prices for consumers and businesses. Higher costs for gasoline, diesel fuel and heating oil have begun to spread to the wider economy. Overall inflation jumped to 3.7 percent in September from the year before, higher than economists had expected.

Investors’ inflation fears have pushed up the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which influences consumer and business borrowing costs, including mortgage rates.

The rise in mortgage rates has sent home sales tumbling. Existing-home sales fell 2.2 percent in September from the year before, the National Association of Realtors reported Tuesday. “Further increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home,” Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist, said in a statement.

The affordability crunch is hurting first-time buyers in particular, said Nancy Vanden Houten, senior economist at Oxford Economics, because “more income is being eaten up by essentials.”

Activity in the housing market is not likely to pick up until after inflation eases, she said, adding, “We see things will begin to bounce back maybe next year or 2028.”

Gregory Schmidt is a senior staff editor who has covered real estate since 2022.

Why Russia Sees a Window to Bomb Ukraine Into Submission

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

Moscow is not winning on the battlefield. Instead, it is seizing an opening to inflict immense human suffering in Ukrainian cities.

By Constant Méheut

Reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine

It’s almost impossible to force a country to surrender solely through a conventional air campaign in war.

Russia seems determined to try.

With Ukraine’s air defenses diminished and its infrastructure weakened after years of Russian strikes, Moscow appears to see an opening to pound Kyiv into total submission this winter. Under this new theory of victory, Russia would be wagering that its missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities can inflict so much human misery that they will succeed where its troops have failed on the front.

Since the summer, Russia has used its growing arsenal to unleash wave after wave of strikes on ammunition depots, gas stations, book warehouses, steel factories, power plants, data centers and commercial ships. Many of the attacks have been carried out with fast new jet-powered drones that have added a frightening new element to round-the-clock Russian onslaughts.

The result is a sense of increased pressure in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, as the economy teeters under the strain and as the energy system, which keeps homes heated and toilets flushing, faces potential collapse in the coming months. Adding to the strain is a new clash between Ukraine and the Trump administration that has come to a head this week.

“The Russians are inflicting a lot of damage in an effort to terrify Ukrainians ahead of winter into giving up,” said Harry Nedelcu, a senior director at Rasmussen Global, a European political advisory firm. “Essentially, into capitulating.”

History — and any understanding of the Ukrainian people — suggests that the effort will fail.

In Vietnam, the Persian Gulf and, more recently, the U. S.-Israeli war against Iran, bombing campaigns that wrecked economies and civilian life failed to force a surrender. Russia’s own air campaign, now in its fifth year, has yielded limited results as Ukraine has found inventive ways to shoot down missiles and as its people adapted to bombardments.

“Punishing the adversaries’ civilian population and trying to break its will has a very poor historical track record for coercing it to concede defeat,” said Seth G. Jones, a military expert at the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Ukraine has waged its own air campaign, using drones to hit Russian oil refineries that help finance the Kremlin war effort. President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine had recently halted the strikes to comply with President Trump’s demand that Russian oil flow back onto global markets.

But with nothing offered in return except more American restrictions on Ukraine’s ability to fight, including a throttling this week of Starlink’s military-grade sister satellite internet service, a visibly angry Mr. Zelensky said on Wednesday that the refinery strikes would resume.

Still, Ukrainian officials and analysts acknowledge that such strikes cannot inflict as much damage on the Russian economy as Russia’s strikes on Ukraine. And they fear that Moscow is now better positioned to succeed in its air campaign than at any other moment in the war.

They point to three main factors. Ukraine’s air defenses have been depleted by years of attacks and a drop in American military assistance. Russia’s arsenal of missiles and drones has grown in both size and effectiveness. And Ukraine’s energy infrastructure is now so fragile that a single hit can inflict as much damage as several strikes once did.

Russia’s confidence that it can knock out Ukraine’s energy system is laid bare in an intercepted attack plan that Kyiv presented to European officials last month, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times.

The plan estimates that Russia would need some 70 ballistic missiles, 720 long-range drones and 150 guided bombs to cut off the cities of Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa from water, power and heating. That is roughly the number of ballistic missiles and drones that break through Ukraine’s air defenses each month on average, according to a Times analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data.

Essentially, that means Moscow thinks that one month of strikes could do what four winters of attacks never did: wreck Ukraine’s energy system.

The grid’s vulnerability was evident after attacks earlier this month. The strikes forced the authorities to introduce scheduled power outages in Kyiv, even as mild autumn temperatures and long daylight hours have kept electricity demand relatively low. Last year, scheduled outages did not begin until late October.

Energy experts say the problem stems partly from Kyiv’s reliance on three combined heat-and-power plants in the capital. Years of attacks have left them unable to operate at full capacity, and each new strike knocks them offline quickly.

Before the war, the three plants had a generating capacity of about 1.3 gigawatts, enough to cover roughly three-quarters of Kyiv’s power needs during winter. That capacity was reduced to about 500 megawatts by this fall, said Maria Tsaturian, an energy analyst at the research group Ukraine Facility Platform.

On Wednesday, Russia struck all three plants with ballistic missiles, further reducing their outputs — at least temporarily.

As a result, Kyiv is likely to enter the winter with very limited electricity generating capacity of its own, according to a Ukrainian government official and a European diplomat in Kyiv, both of whom requested anonymity to discuss a sensitive subject.

That leaves Kyiv dependent on electricity from facilities outside the city, which include a thermal power plant to its south, nuclear plants to the west and three hydroelectric stations. Russia has struck the thermal plant and a number of substations that carry power from the other plants into the capital this month.

Ms. Tsaturian called it a “scorched-earth tactic” designed to cut Kyiv off entirely from power.

If Russia’s attack plan is successful, Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa would lose 90 percent of their electrical capacity, have their heating supplies fall by 90 percent, and suffer severe disruptions to their water and sewage systems.

Russia’s confidence largely derives from Ukraine’s shortage of air defenses, above all the U. S.-made Patriot interceptors that are its best protection against ballistic missiles. On Wednesday, Ukraine said it shot down only four of 39 ballistic missiles that Russia launched, most of which were aimed at the country’s energy infrastructure. That assault was one of Russia’s largest of the entire war.

While Ukraine has learned how to intercept many of Russia’s long-range drones, the new class of jet-powered ones, which fly at hundreds of miles an hour, are slipping through. Kyiv is racing to build new interceptors and pressing Western allies for conventional weapons that can bring them down.

Alyona Getmanchuk, Ukraine’s ambassador to NATO, said her list of requests to partners now included air-to-air missiles that fighter jets could fire to down jet-powered drones, along with medium-range surface-to-air systems that have also proved effective.

Russia’s air campaign has also inflicted severe damage on Ukraine’s industrial backbone. Oleksandr Myronenko, chief operating officer of Metinvest, Ukraine’s largest steel producer, said this month that the company had been forced to close its biggest plant after Russia fired 17 ballistic missiles at it.

Metinvest, which employs more than 36,000 people, is one of Ukraine’s largest private taxpayers. The factory shutdown means less money for the state budget and, ultimately, for the war effort. Serhii Marchenko, Ukraine’s finance minister, told Parliament this week that the shortfall in annual tax revenue could reach about $1.7 billion this year.

Ukraine has repeatedly called for a limited cease-fire focused on energy facilities or port infrastructure, arguing that one would be in both sides’ interest. But Mr. Nedelcu, from Rasmussen, said he did not see why Russia would agree to stop its air attacks now, especially before winter.

“The only card they have to pressure the Ukrainians are these air attacks,” he said. “They don’t have anything else.”

Kim Barker contributed reporting.

Constant Méheut is a Times correspondent covering the war in Ukraine.

Could Embracing Sprawl Ease California’s Housing Crunch?

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Among the measures up for a vote in November is one that would amend the state’s landmark environmental law and make it easier to build large housing developments outside cities.

The company that owns Tejon Ranch has spend two decades trying, and failing, to build developments there. Proposition 45 could speed the process up. Credit... Mark Abramson for The New York Times

Supported by

By Conor Dougherty

In the foothills above Los Angeles sits a yellow field with a cement plant in the distance. It looks like the middle of nowhere but lies at the center of a debate about the cause of California’s housing crisis and whether more suburbs can help solve it.

The company that owns the field, the Tejon Ranch Company, has spent the past two decades trying and failing to turn the plot into housing, part of a larger plan to build what would amount to three new towns with some 40,000 homes across them. The development has been stymied by lawsuits arguing it would increase wildfire risk and lead to more carbon emissions that cause climate change.

To fight back, Tejon Ranch is backing a ballot initiative, Proposition 45, that would curtail the length of environmental reviews on large projects, including housing, roads, power and other infrastructure. Proposition 45 would also make it harder to challenge development.

If passed by voters on Nov. 3, the measure could shift the state’s development pattern by reigniting the kind of edge-city growth that built the modern California but is now derisively known as “sprawl.” Proposition 45 is backed by the California Chamber of Commerce and supported by a long list of homebuilders whose vision for California’s future comes from the past.

“This is the Chamber of Commerce saying, ‘We need to bring back the kinds of growth that California had in the 1960s,’” said Christopher Elmendorf, a law professor at the University of California, Davis, who studies land-use regulations.

It is not much of an exaggeration to say housing is the only issue Californians care about. The state’s median home price sits around $750,000, and home buyers in Los Angeles and San Francisco consider themselves lucky to find a teardown for twice that. More than a decade’s worth of surveys place the cost of housing atop the list of issues state voters are most concerned about and the reason a steady stream of U-Hauls continues to leave California for cheaper states.

The root cause of high home prices is a longstanding housing shortage. For the past decade, California legislators have tried to increase supply by passing dozens of laws that relax zoning rules, streamline permitting and curb environmental regulations.

But most of these efforts have focused on building more housing in existing cities, usually by allowing more density or punishing local governments that drag out permit approvals. The idea that the state should also make it easier to add subdivisions on the urban outskirts — which is what Tejon Ranch wants to do — has been largely absent from the policy agenda.

Proposition 45 would change that by expanding the kinds of projects that qualify for streamlining. If passed, the law would narrow the scope of environmental reviews on large projects, making it harder to sue to stop them and setting timelines to prevent the lawsuits that do come up from dragging out. That is the briefest of summaries: Proposition 45 would add 41 pages to the novel-length California Environmental Quality Act, CEQA, known colloquially as “See Qua.”

As with most everything that touches environmental law, there is a chasm of disagreement about Proposition 45’s potential impact. Depending on whom you talk to, the measure is either a wholesale gutting of CEQA or a needed update that will help create the kinds of housing and energy projects the state’s voters say they want.

“For decades, anti-housing activists have used the environment as a shield,” said Jason Elliott, a political consultant who helped write the measure. “We’re saying enough is enough.”

Proposition 45’s opponents argue that the campaign is using the housing crisis as a smoke screen. The measure would apply to a catalog of projects that, in addition to housing, includes transportation, water, energy, hospitals and broadband. Opponents say the broadband piece could apply to the warehouse-size data centers that voters around the country have risen up against, while the measure’s backers say it applies only to projects like connecting rural communities to the internet with broadband fiber.

“The proponents are talking a lot about housing, but that is hiding the full scale of projects,” said Aruna Prabhala, a senior attorney and urban wildlands director at the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental advocacy group that has filed multiple lawsuits accusing Tejon Ranch of violating CEQA.

CEQA was passed in 1970 and signed by Ronald Reagan, then the governor, months after the federal government enacted the National Environmental Policy Act. For all the fear CEQA inspires in developers, the law only rarely kills developments outright. What it can do, however, is drag projects out and keep many others from being proposed in the first place.

The way it usually works is that developers of large projects have to complete a report detailing the impact of their development on the environment and how they can mitigate it. Advocacy groups can sue to challenge the findings, creating yearslong court battles that add tens of millions of dollars in lost time and extra costs — which is what happened at Tejon Ranch.

Tejon Ranch is a 270,000-acre spread at the junction of Los Angeles and Kern Counties. The Ranch began as a series of land grants from Mexico shortly before California joined the United States. In the nearly two centuries since, its rolling mountains and grassy valleys have been central to the idea of California as a contiguous state. The land connects the Central Valley and Southern California via the Grapevine, a 4,100-foot pass that snakes through the Tehachapi Mountains.

Aside from a commercial center with gas stations, outlet stores and warehouse space, most of Tejon’s land is undeveloped. In the early 2000s, as growth from Los Angeles began pushing farther outward, the company proposed three developments. In the decades since, the projects have run into legal challenges raised through CEQA. Environmentalists do not deny that CEQA can delay projects, but they say the process makes development better by reducing their impact or moving them to places that are better suited for them.

Jordan Grimes, legislative director at the Greenbelt Alliance, said his group opposed Proposition 45 while also supporting proposals to curb environmental regulations in urban areas. The group’s logic is that cities are already so full of cars and concrete that it is hard to see how another building will harm the ecosystem. But that analysis changes when a project encroaches on sparsely populated land.

“The changes that Proposition 45 makes to CEQA will create an explosion of sprawl across California,” Mr. Grimes said.

In an interview, Matthew Walker, chief executive of the Tejon Ranch Company, said that while focusing on urban development sounded good in theory, home buyers continued to favor single-family houses in suburban environments. That is the kind of housing Californians are leaving the state to find, so while the state needs more apartments and condominiums, he said, it needs more suburbs, too.

“There is still a strong desire from many people to live in detached single-family homes,” he said. “We sit in a growth corridor and can be a solution to the housing problem.”

Until recently, changes to CEQA were a sensitive subject for California’s Democratic leaders, who were wary of crossing powerful environmental and labor groups that line up against major changes. But the housing crisis has upended that calculation as voters have grown increasingly frustrated about housing costs. In September, a survey by the Public Policy Institute of California found that Proposition 45 was neck and neck in polling, but the measure has already created cross-party alliances. Proposition 45 is endorsed by California’s Republican Party and opposed by the state Democratic Party, but there are cross-party alliances on either side.

“CEQA is being weaponized to stop projects of all shapes and sizes in their tracks,” said Buffy Wicks, a Democrat in the California State Assembly from Oakland who supports Proposition 45. “We need homes across the board.”

Conor Dougherty covers housing and development, focusing on the rising costs of homeownership. He is based in Los Angeles.

Trump’s Democracy-for-Diesel Deal Shames Us All

The New York Times October 15, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Thomas L. Friedman

By Thomas L. Friedman

Opinion Columnist

If President Trump does not understand what will happen to him if he proceeds with his plan to trade away support for Ukraine’s democracy for Russian diesel, let me spell it out: He will enter the history books in the chapter on leaders who sold out their country’s democratic values to appease a dictator.

Donald Trump, meet Neville Chamberlain. When future students search online for “sellout,” “appeaser” or “traitor to his country’s core values,” their two pictures will come up first, side by side. And deservedly so. At least Chamberlain was trying, in what proved to be lethally misguided fashion, to avoid a world war. Trump is trying to avoid losing a few seats in Congress — and is likely to be no more successful in achieving his goal than Chamberlain was in achieving his.

I have never believed that Trump was somehow an agent of Russia’s leader, Vladimir Putin, or in his pay. It is much worse. He simply does not cherish democracy. He cherishes money. And he has no problem selling the first for the second. When he acts in his own commercial interests, that’s his personal business. When he uses the American presidency to make a buck, it is our collective shame.

There is simply no core American value Trump will not sell. Desperate to lower diesel prices, which are hurting Republicans in the midterms, Trump actually made a deal to import diesel fuel from Russia, even though it offers a potential windfall for the Kremlin so it can bomb Ukraine harder — and is unlikely to help lower prices or increase supplies much at all. Worse, his aides then asked Ukraine to refrain from attacks on Russia’s oil refineries, without Trump making the same demand of Putin regarding Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. It makes me sick to my stomach to even type this.

Unique among great powers, “the United States has always made the protection and promotion of liberal values part of its foreign policy because it’s part of the country’s political DNA,” Michael Mandelbaum, the author of the new book “The American Way of Foreign Policy: Ideology, Economics, Democracy,” told me. “Different presidents have given these values different emphases, depending on the circumstances and their own personal predilections.”

But none have “ever abandoned them entirely — let alone repudiated them,” Mandelbaum added. “In that sense Trump really is unique. Of course, all presidents, including him, have operated in a domestic political environment in which those values are widely shared, which means that he will pay a political price for violating them. But in the short term that isn’t likely to help Ukraine.”

This is shocking to Ukrainians, who for nearly five years have been resisting Putin’s attempt to wipe their country off the map. My friend Vitaly Sych, the editor in chief of the Ukrainian news outlet NV, texted me from Kyiv the other day:

“When Donald Trump became president, Ukraine lost an ally.” From his first days in office, Trump “started positioning himself as a ‘negotiator,’ as an ‘intermediary’ between Ukraine and the aggressor — Russia,” Sych added. “That was strange enough. And now he is openly siding with Russia, pushing for Ukraine’s capitulation and calling it a peace deal,” Sych said. “If Ukraine hits an oil refinery in Russia, there is always an outraged post from the U. S. president on Truth Social. Is he now the Kremlin’s spokesperson?”

The United States has long stood for freedom and democracy, Sych said. “Now they are just for diesel. What a change.” Russian missiles and drones kill or wound dozens of civilians, including children, every day, he wrote. “Russians are killing us like in a shooting range. No concern comes out about this from the White House. Only about Russian diesel. It is a mix of intellectual and moral bankruptcy to claim we don’t want peace. Of course we want peace,” he said. “But we don’t want capitulation packaged as peace.”

I have to say, it is hard for me to decide who is more despicable: Trump or tough-guy Republican senators like Tom Cotton, who lambasted President Joe Biden for not sending enough military aid to Ukraine and today sits curled up in a corner of the U. S. Capitol, saying nothing while Trump sells Ukraine to Putin outright.

Here’s the beginning of a story in The Hill from Sept. 16, 2023:

A group of Republican senators sent a letter to President Biden Saturday urging him to “immediately” provide the missiles Ukraine needs to win its war against Russia. Senator Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) shared the letter in a post on X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, arguing that not sending the weapons would “only prolong the war and cost lives.” Cotton was joined by Senators Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Lindsey Graham (R-S. C.) in his request. “We … urge you to immediately send MGM-140 Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) to Ukraine,” they wrote. “Additional delay will only further undermine U. S. national security interests and extend this conflict.”

That was then — when Biden was president. This week a bipartisan group of 12 senators (six Republicans and six Democrats) sent a letter to Trump demanding that he rescind the diesel agreement and roll back the Treasury Department’s license allowing it. Cotton, who is the chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, did not sign the letter.

It is hard to tell whether Trump’s democracy-for-diesel idea is his alone or was cooked up with his negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. If those two are part of it, I hope they understand that they will share Trump’s infamy in the history books. The good work they have done to end the Gaza war will all be forgotten. They should speak up now, because history will have its eyes on them, too.
