More students ages 10 to 13 are ending up in the justice system after vaping, making threats and lashing out at school.

A 12-year-old in the Galveston school district was arrested after being disruptive and refusing to head to the school lobby. Credit... Meridith Kohut for The New York Times

Supported by

By Kristian HernándezAsher Lehrer-SmallClare Amari and Rosie Cima

This article was reported in collaboration with The San Antonio Express-News and Big Local News at Stanford University as part of The New York Times’s Local Investigations Fellowship.

Over the past decade, school districts across Texas have sought to make classrooms safer by swelling the number of police officers on campuses and taking a tougher stance on misbehavior. But the crackdown has had an unexpected consequence: sweeping tens of thousands of elementary students and middle schoolers into the justice system.

Children ages 10 to 13 were referred for prosecution after incidents in schools more than 47,000 times since 2014, an analysis by The New York Times and The San Antonio Express-News found. About 4,800 students in that age group were referred during the 2024-25 academic year alone, the most recent school year for which data is available. That is a third more than the number a decade before.

Most of the students were accused of minor offenses, like making threats, using cannabis vapes or lashing out at classmates or teachers, the analysis found. Few caused serious physical harm.

Outside Austin, an 11-year-old bumped into a school counselor. In Victoria, a 10-year-old said he saw someone on campus with a weapon, but later admitted he had made up the story. In El Paso, a 10-year-old kicked an assistant principal after his cellphone was taken away.

All three found themselves in the justice system.

While the case against the boy in El Paso was dropped two months after the incident, court records show, the consequences for his family were immense. His mother, Grace Lee-Vazquez, said she shouldered thousands of dollars in legal bills. The boy, who has attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and still struggles to double-knot his shoelaces, became anxious about school. His grades tumbled.

School district officials would not answer questions about the incident, but wrote in a statement that they were “committed to maintaining safe and inclusive learning environments for all students.”

The ordeal, Ms. Lee-Vazquez said, “broke us.” She moved the family out of state in June for a fresh start.

In rare instances, children 13 and under have been accused of serious offenses. Last year, for example, an 11-year-old boy at Harris Middle School in San Antonio was charged with carrying a weapon in a prohibited place after school officials found a gun in his backpack.

But William Shaw, a juvenile judge in San Antonio, said that many of the cases that came before him could have been handled by a school principal.

“Kids are sometimes not going to get along,” he said in an interview. “They may end up pushing each other, maybe even fighting. That can be considered adolescent behavior. It isn’t necessary to arrest.”

The Times and The Express-News reported this year that Texas’ multi-billion-dollar investment in school policing had transformed discipline, subjecting thousands of students to physical force, at times over seemingly minor misconduct. Some were tackled, blinded with pepper spray or shocked with Tasers.

For the new analysis, our journalists examined data collected by the Texas Juvenile Justice Department, identifying tens of thousands of instances since the 2014-15 academic year in which minors were referred into the justice system after an incident at school. Such referrals, as they are called, typically occur after an officer takes a child into custody. The youngest a child in Texas can be referred is 10; students 17 and older are considered adults.

The number of 10- to 13-year-olds swept into the justice system after incidents at school has increased by more than a third.

Source: Texas Juvenile Justice Department. The New York Times

Some of the children who were referred were required to appear before a judge and assigned community service, counseling or court supervision. In the most serious cases, they were committed to state juvenile justice facilities.

But even when children were released with just a warning, they were often taken from school in handcuffs, separated from their parents for hours and processed into the juvenile system — all of which, research shows, can hurt academic performance and is linked to future contact with law enforcement, feeding the so called school-to-prison pipeline.

Encounters between police officers and schoolchildren have not gone unnoticed. In July, The Texas Observer used law enforcement records to document thousands of arrests and criminal citations involving preteens in about 200 of Texas’ 1,200 school districts over a four-year period.

The analysis by The Times and The Express-News examined referrals statewide. It found that referrals of children 10 to 13 had increased by a greater percentage than referrals of older students. They rose for young children of every race, though Black children were referred at about twice the rate of white and Hispanic children.

After the Covid-19 pandemic, when students returned to in-person instruction, schools reported more fights, state data shows. But referrals of children 10 to 13 grew far faster.

The growth outpaced that of the student population, undoing years of work by advocacy groups and policymakers to end the school-to-prison pipeline.

Some of the state’s largest school districts, including Houston and Dallas, have decreased the number of referrals in recent years, data shows. The statewide increase was driven by roughly 60 districts, which account for about a quarter of Texas’ students. Many added officers to their elementary and middle schools during the period we examined, records show, or had taken a more aggressive approach to policing students.

Certain districts had big increases in the number of 10- to 13-year-olds sent into the justice system.

Note: The increase in IDEA Public Schools may be as high as 52 students; the number was redacted in 2014-15 because it was below five. Source: Texas Juvenile Justice Department. The New York Times

Officials in some of those districts said they believed the referrals represented progress toward safer campuses, a top priority since the 2022 school shooting at Robb Elementary in Uvalde.

Representative Joe Moody, an El Paso Democrat, cosponsored a 2023 state law requiring a police officer at every public school. When shown our analysis, he said that the increase in referrals among young children was alarming, and that he would push for stricter limits on policing in schools when the state legislature convenes in January.

“No one should want that as a result of what we did,” he said.

Laquital Thompson knew that her daughter’s transition to Central Middle School in Galveston might be difficult.

Like many 12-year-olds, the girl enjoyed filming videos for TikTok and trying different hairstyles. She liked school, too, especially math and science. But she had been acting out in class, Ms. Thompson said, and the school district had identified a behavioral disorder that led her to challenge authority. (The Times and The Express-News are not naming the children in this article to protect their privacy.)

Within a week of starting classes in August 2024, records show, the girl was sent to the principal’s office for being “disruptive.” School officials suspended her and told her to wait for her mother in the lobby. But the girl refused to go there.

Eventually, a school police officer, Vincent Ramirez, was summoned. When he arrived, several school employees were hovering nearby.

In an exchange captured by the officer’s body camera footage, one school administrator said that the girl’s mother had consented to the use of handcuffs on her daughter. Another warned that the girl could be arrested if she did not go where she was told.

Officer Ramirez turned to the girl. “You’ve got four seconds to walk over there,” he said. “Otherwise, I’m going to put you in handcuffs, and we’re going to give you a ride.”

She did not budge.

“OK, I’m done,” Officer Ramirez said. He slid off the girl’s pink backpack and handcuffed her wrists behind her back.

His body camera footage shows the sequence.

The girl is in the lower right corner above, facing a glass display case.

The officer confronts her, telling her she has four seconds to comply.

Ninety seconds later, he handcuffs her and leads her down the hall.

In a recent interview, the girl told our reporters that she was confused when the officer detained her. “I didn’t really know why it was happening,” she said. “Why would they put me in handcuffs?”

The officer drove her to the school police headquarters at a nearby campus, where she continued to ignore instructions. When she would not put her hand on a fingerprint machine, officers twisted her opposite arm behind her back until she screamed and complied, according to body camera footage.

Later, as she sobbed and yelled profanities, the school district police chief, Josette Rivas, held up a cellphone and apparently began recording her, body camera footage shows. She told the girl it was for Facebook.

“You all see how she’s acting?” Chief Rivas said as she held the phone.

Chief Rivas and Officer Ramirez declined to comment for this article. The Galveston school district’s superintendent, Matthew Neighbors, wrote in an email that the officers had “remained calm and respectful.” Asked if cellphone video of the girl had been posted online, he said no.

Records show the girl was charged with trespassing. Two former school district police chiefs who reviewed the case at our request said that the arrest and referral were unnecessary.

Threatening to post video of the girl was particularly concerning, added Bryon G. Gustafson, who was previously the police chief for the Stockton, Calif., school district and now teaches at the University of Virginia. “A police chief doing that is just unfathomable to me,” he said.

The girl pleaded guilty and was put on probation for a year, Ms. Thompson said. After that, she had even more trouble paying attention in class.

“She just gave up,” her mother added.

Ms. Thompson said that she had agreed to the handcuffs because in that moment, she did not want to question the administrator’s judgment. But after learning what had happened, she wondered why the school officer had been called to handle the situation at all.

“Why couldn’t they just let her stand in the hallway and be quiet and wait on me?” she said.

In the past, principals and teachers typically handled minor misbehavior themselves. Now, as more schools like Central Middle station officers in their hallways, educators can turn to law enforcement when students are disobedient, even if the children are young or pose minimal threat.

Under state law, school officers are supposed to stay out of “routine student discipline.” But the law does not define the term or detail repercussions for violations.

“The cops are supposed to be there to protect the children from shooters,” said Phillip Lyons, the dean of the College of Criminal Justice at Sam Houston State University in Huntsville and a former police detective who handled juvenile cases. “If there aren’t any shooters, the cops are going to do what cops do, and that is arrest.”

At Walsh Middle in the Round Rock district, near Austin, an assistant principal directed a mother to school police officers when her daughter, a sixth grader, said that three boys had hit her in the head with their fists and a cellphone. The boys, ages 11 and 12, gave different accounts of what happened that afternoon, records show; two said that they had been playing a game and another said he had accidentally hit the girl with a stuffed monkey.

All three were charged with misdemeanor assault, the records show.

“I thought we would sit down and apologize and he would serve lunch detentions,” said Kimmy Lueders, the mother of one of the boys.

The district superintendent, Hafedh Azaiez, said in an interview that the school administrator should have tried to handle the situation before involving law enforcement. “It’s not something we’re proud of,” he said.

In some districts, the expansion of policing has been accompanied by a more hard-line approach to violent behavior. Officers have taken more students into custody for suggesting they might hurt someone. Over the past decade, the count of students 10 to 13 referred for making a “terroristic threat” tripled statewide, to more than 600 annually.

At times, officers’ efforts have thwarted potential school shootings. Last year, officers arrested a 13-year-old who they said was plotting an attack on his San Antonio middle school.

But threats made seemingly in jest or as playground bluster can also attract police attention. In the Wylie school district, near Dallas, district officials told teachers to warn third and fourth graders that once they turned 10, they could be charged with a crime for making a threat they did not mean. In the Hays school district, outside Austin, officials circulated a poster with a row of boys in orange jumpsuits urging students not to have “threat regret.”

The threats did not always involve mass violence. In February 2025, a 12-year-old with an intellectual disability and autism had a meltdown after an aide at his Lubbock middle school unplugged a classroom phone that he wanted to use, records show. “Respect me or you’re dead,” the boy told the aide.

A school police officer came to arrest him. When the boy did not comply with the officer’s orders, a second officer showed up. The two pulled the boy to the ground by his sweatshirt and handcuffed him, police records show. Afterward, the boy was terrified of the police, said his mother, Colette James. He avoided his family’s church because it had hired officers for extra security. For a time, he slept in his parents’ bed.

Lubbock-Cooper school district officials declined to comment, citing student privacy laws. The aide, Jennifer Huckabee, told a reporter she had felt threatened because the boy was bigger than she was.

In another case, in Corpus Christi, a 13-year-old was referred after shouting “I’m going to kill you” at classmates who had beaten him up, his mother said. He was held at a county juvenile detention center for nearly two weeks. The county’s juvenile judge, Timothy J. McCoy, sometimes holds children who make threats for counseling and to ensure they do not follow through, he said.

In an interview in his cell, the boy said he had not meant the threat literally. “I was angry,” he said. “I shouldn’t have said it.”

Of the dozens of children in the facility that day, the youngest was 11. Some of them sat at tables of four in a common area, reading, working on laptops or resting their heads. When a reporter asked how many of them were there because of incidents at school, about half raised their hands.

In some districts where referrals went up, the increases reflect what officials consider a tough love approach.

In an interview last year, Kirby Warnke, the chief of the Corpus Christi school district department and president of the Texas School District Police Chiefs’ Association, said he believed the state’s juvenile justice system gave children a chance to learn from their mistakes.

“It’s a teaching moment for them,” Mr. Warnke said.

Referrals of young children in his district more than doubled over the past decade, state data shows. They reached a record high, of 171, in the 2022-23 school year, more than in the Houston and Dallas districts, each of which have more than four times as many students as Corpus Christi.

The Forney school district, east of Dallas, cracked down on violent behavior and threats when it created its own police department in 2020, said Joseph Sanders, who was then the department’s chief. The following school year, 42 students 10 to 13 were referred by the school police — more than had been referred in the previous six years combined.

“We just set the tone and set the tone early,” said Mr. Sanders, who left the district in 2024 and now trains law enforcement leaders.

But elsewhere, officials who were troubled by the uptick took steps to reverse it.

Donny Lee, the superintendent of the Wichita Falls school district in North Texas, said that before he was hired in 2022, school officers would “arrest kids first and ask questions later.”

“We were having charges put on our elementary kids,” he said.

He hired a new chief who agreed with him that arrests should be a last resort, and they replaced most of the officers. Mr. Lee also convened regular meetings to review law enforcement data.

Referrals dropped for students of all ages, data shows. For children 13 and under, the annual number was cut by more than half, to 44 from about 100.

Mr. Lee said that the district had achieved those results without being “soft” on discipline. Students who broke the rules were assigned in-school suspensions or community service and offered counseling.

“We’re not in the crime and punishment business,” he said. “We’re in the education business.”

Justin Mayo contributed reporting. Kitty Bennett, Alain Delaquérière, Georgia Gee, Sheelagh McNeill and Kirsten Noyes contributed research. This article was reported in partnership with Big Local News at Stanford University, and with support from the Fund for Investigative Journalism.

Produced by Rumsey Taylor.

Juvenile justice researchers helped me wrap my head around an important facet of this story. The number of kids pushed into the justice system has actually gone down across the country in recent years, including in Texas. To me, that made the rising number of kids referred to the justice system after incidents at Texas schools even more striking.

Kristian Hernández is a reporter covering school policing in Texas as part of The Times’s Local Investigations Fellowship.

Asher Lehrer-Small reports on school policing and security in Texas as a part of The Times’s Local Investigations Fellowship.

Clare Amari is a reporter covering law enforcement in Texas schools as part of The Times’s Local Investigations Fellowship.

Para ciertos estudiantes en Texas, una leve falta puede derivar en cargos penales

The New York Times October 15, 2026

The New York Times en Español

Una investigación muestra cómo niños de entre 10 y 13 años son remitidos al sistema legal por exabruptos comunes de su edad, o infracciones como vapear, que no representan una amenaza grave real.

Una investigación muestra cómo niños de entre 10 y 13 años son remitidos al sistema legal por exabruptos comunes de su edad, o infracciones como vapear, que no representan una amenaza grave real.

Una niña de 12 años del distrito escolar de Galveston fue detenida tras comportarse de forma revoltosa y negarse a ir al vestíbulo del colegio. Credit... Meridith Kohut para The New York Times

Supported by

Por Kristian HernándezAsher Lehrer-SmallClare Amari y Rosie Cima

Este artículo se hizo en colaboración con The San Antonio Express-News y Big Local News de la Universidad de Stanford, como parte del programa Local Investigations Fellowship del Times.

Durante la última década, los distritos escolares de todo Texas han tratado que las aulas sean más seguras aumentando el número de agentes de policía en los recintos escolares y adoptando una postura más dura ante las malas conductas. Pero esta campaña de represión ha tenido una consecuencia inesperada: ha llevado a decenas de miles de alumnos de primaria y secundaria a comparecer ante el sistema judicial.

Según un análisis realizado por el Times y The San Antonio Express-News, desde 2014 se ha remitido a procesamiento penal a niños de entre 10 y 13 años tras incidentes en los colegios en más de 47.000 ocasiones. Solo durante el curso académico 2024-25 —el último para el que se dispone de datos— se remitieron a la justicia unos 4800 alumnos de ese grupo de edad. Esta cifra supone un tercio más que la registrada una década antes.

Según el análisis, la mayoría de los alumnos fueron acusados de delitos menores, como proferir amenazas, consumir cannabis mediante vaporizadores o arremeter contra compañeros de clase o profesores. Pocos causaron daños físicos serios.

A las afueras de Austin, un niño de 11 años chocó con un orientador escolar. En Victoria, un niño de 10 años dijo que había visto a alguien en el recinto escolar con un arma, pero más tarde admitió que se había inventado la historia. En El Paso, un niño de 10 años le dio una patada a un subdirector después de que le quitaran el celular.

Los tres acabaron en el sistema judicial.

Aunque el caso contra el niño de El Paso fue desestimado dos meses después del incidente, según muestran los expedientes judiciales, las consecuencias para su familia fueron enormes. Su madre, Grace Lee-Vazquez, afirmó que tuvo que hacer frente a miles de dólares en gastos legales. El niño, que padece un trastorno por déficit de atención con hiperactividad y aún le cuesta hacer el doble nudo en los cordones de los zapatos, empezó a sentir ansiedad por ir al colegio. Sus notas se desplomaron.

Funcionarios del distrito escolar no respondieron a las preguntas sobre el incidente, pero escribieron en un comunicado que estaban “comprometidos con mantener entornos de aprendizaje seguros e inclusivos para todos los alumnos”.

Esta dura experiencia, según Lee-Vazquez, “nos llevó a la quiebra”. En junio, se mudó con su familia a otro estado para empezar de cero.

En contadas ocasiones, se ha acusado a niños de 13 años o menos de delitos graves. El año pasado, por ejemplo, un niño de 11 años de la Harris Middle School de San Antonio fue acusado de portar un arma en un lugar prohibido después de que los responsables del centro encontraran una pistola en su mochila.

Sin embargo, William Shaw, juez de menores en San Antonio, señaló que muchos de los casos que llegaron a su despacho podrían haber sido gestionados por el director del centro educativo.

“A veces los niños no se llevan bien”, declaró en una entrevista. “Pueden acabar empujándose, quizá incluso peleándose. Eso puede considerarse un comportamiento propio de la adolescencia. No es necesario arrestarlos”.

The New York Times y The Express-News informaron este año que la inversión multimillonaria de Texas en la presencia policial en los centros educativos había transformado la disciplina, sometiendo a miles de alumnos a fuerza física, en ocasiones por faltas aparentemente menores. A algunos se les derribó, se les cegó con spray de pimienta o se les aplicó descargas con pistolas Taser.

Para este nuevo análisis, nuestros periodistas examinaron los datos recopilados por el Departamento de Justicia Juvenil de Texas, identificando decenas de miles de casos desde el curso académico 2014-15 en los que menores fueron remitidos al sistema judicial tras un incidente en el colegio. Estas remisiones, como se les denomina, suelen producirse después de que un agente detenga a un menor. La edad mínima a la que un menor puede ser remitido en Texas es de 10 años; los alumnos de 17 años o más se consideran adultos.

El número de menores de entre 10 y 13 años arrastrados al sistema judicial tras incidentes escolares se ha incrementado por más de un tercio.

Fuente: Departamento de Justicia Juvenil de Texas. The New York Times

A algunos de los menores remitidos se les exigió comparecer ante un juez y se les impuso servicios comunitarios, asesoramiento o supervisión judicial. En los casos más graves, fueron internados en centros estatales penitenciarios juveniles.

Pero incluso cuando los menores eran puestos en libertad con una simple advertencia, a menudo eran sacados del colegio esposados, separados de sus padres durante horas y sometidos a los trámites del sistema de menores; todo ello, según muestran las investigaciones, puede perjudicar el rendimiento académico y está relacionado con futuros contactos con las fuerzas del orden, lo que alimenta el llamado “camino de la escuela a la cárcel”.

Los encuentros entre agentes de policía y estudiantes escolares no han pasado desapercibidos. En julio, The Texas Observer utilizó registros policiales para documentar miles de detenciones y citaciones penales que afectaban a preadolescentes en unos 200 de los 1200 distritos escolares de Texas durante un periodo de cuatro años.

El análisis realizado por el Times y The Express-News examinó las remisiones en todo el estado. Reveló que las remisiones de niños de entre 10 y 13 años habían aumentado en un porcentaje mayor que las de los alumnos de más edad. Aumentaron para los niños pequeños de todas las razas, aunque los niños negros fueron remitidos aproximadamente el doble de veces que los niños blancos e hispanos.

Tras la pandemia de la COVID-19, cuando los alumnos volvieron a las clases presenciales, los centros educativos notificaron más peleas, según muestran los datos estatales. Sin embargo, las remisiones de niños de entre 10 y 13 años crecieron mucho más rápido.

Este aumento superó al de la población estudiantil, echando por tierra años de trabajo de los grupos de defensa y los responsables políticos para poner fin al “camino de la escuela a la cárcel”.

Los datos muestran que algunos de los distritos escolares más grandes del estado, entre ellos los de Houston y Dallas, han reducido el número de remisiones en los últimos años. El aumento a nivel estatal se debió a unos 60 distritos, que representan aproximadamente una cuarta parte de los alumnos de Texas. Según los registros, muchos de ellos incorporaron agentes de policía a sus colegios de primaria y secundaria durante el periodo analizado, o adoptaron un enfoque más agresivo en la vigilancia de los alumnos.

En algunos distritos se registraron grandes aumentos en el número de niños de entre 10 y 13 años remitidos al sistema judicial.

Nota: El aumento en el número de alumnos de las escuelas públicas IDEA podría llegar a los 52; esta cifra se ocultó en el curso 2014-15 porque era inferior a cinco. Fuente: Departamento de Justicia Juvenil de Texas. The New York Times

Las autoridades de algunos de esos distritos afirmaron que consideraban que las remisiones representaban un avance hacia unos recintos escolares más seguros, una prioridad máxima desde el tiroteo escolar de 2022 en la escuela primaria Robb de Uvalde.

El representante Joe Moody, demócrata por El Paso, copatrocinó una ley estatal de 2023 que exige la presencia de un agente de policía en cada colegio público. Al mostrarle nuestro análisis, afirmó que el aumento de las denuncias entre los niños pequeños era alarmante y que presionaría para que se impusieran límites más estrictos a la presencia policial en los colegios cuando la legislatura estatal se reúna en enero.

“Nadie debería querer eso como resultado de lo que hicimos”, afirmó.

Laquital Thompson sabía que la transición de su hija a la escuela secundaria central de Galveston podría resultar difícil.

Como a muchas niñas de 12 años, a la niña le gustaba grabar videos para TikTok y probar diferentes peinados. También le gustaba el colegio, sobre todo las matemáticas y las ciencias. Pero se había estado portando mal en clase, según explicó Thompson, y el distrito escolar había identificado un trastorno de conducta que la llevaba a desafiar a la autoridad. (The New York Times y The Express-News no revelan los nombres de los niños en este artículo para proteger su privacidad).

Según los registros, una semana después de comenzar las clases en agosto de 2024, la niña fue enviada al despacho del director por “alterar el orden”. Las autoridades escolares la suspendieron y le dijeron que esperara a su madre en el vestíbulo. Pero la niña se negó a ir allí.

Finalmente, se llamó a un agente de policía escolar, Vincent Ramirez. Cuando llegó, varios empleados del colegio se encontraban merodeando por allí.

En una conversación captada por la cámara corporal del agente, una autoridad del colegio afirmó que la madre de la niña había dado su consentimiento para que se le pusieran esposas a su hija. Otro advirtió de que la niña podría ser detenida si no iba adonde se le indicaba.

El agente Ramirez se dirigió a la niña. “Tienes cuatro segundos para ir hasta allí”, le dijo. “Si no, te voy a esposar y te voy a dar un paseo en el auto”.

Ella no se movió.

“Bien, se acabó”, dijo el agente Ramirez. Le quitó la mochila rosa a la niña y le esposó las muñecas a la espalda.

Las imágenes de su cámara corporal muestran la secuencia.

La niña está en la esquina superior derecha aquí arriba, de cara a un aparador de vidrio.

El oficial la enfrenta y le dice que tiene cuatro segundos para obedecer.

Al cabo de 90 segundos, la esposa y la lleva por el pasillo

En una entrevista reciente, la niña contó a nuestros periodistas que se sintió desconcertada cuando el agente la detuvo. “No sabía muy bien por qué estaba pasando”, explicó. “¿Por qué iban a esposarme?”.

El agente la llevó en coche a la comisaría de la policía escolar, situada en un campus cercano, donde ella siguió ignorando las instrucciones. Cuando se negó a poner la mano en el escáner de huellas dactilares, los agentes le retorcieron el brazo contrario a la espalda hasta que gritó y obedeció, según las imágenes de la cámara corporal.

Más tarde, mientras la joven sollozaba y gritaba improperios, la jefa de policía del distrito escolar, Josette Rivas, levantó un celular y, al parecer, empezó a grabarla, según muestran las imágenes de la cámara corporal. Le dijo a la joven que era para Facebook.

“¿Ven cómo se está comportando?”, dijo Rivas mientras sostenía el teléfono.

La jefa Rivas y el agente Ramirez se negaron a hacer declaraciones para este artículo. El superintendente del distrito escolar de Galveston, Matthew Neighbors, escribió en un correo electrónico que los agentes “se habían mantenido tranquilos y respetuosos”. Cuando se le preguntó si se había publicado en internet el video de la joven grabado con el celular, respondió que no.

Los registros muestran que la niña fue acusada de allanamiento. Dos antiguos jefes de policía del distrito escolar que revisaron el caso a petición nuestra afirmaron que la detención y la remisión del caso habían sido innecesarias.

Amenazar con publicar el video de la niña resultaba especialmente preocupante, añadió Bryon G. Gustafson, que anteriormente fue jefe de policía del distrito escolar de Stockton, California y ahora imparte clases en la Universidad de Virginia. “Que un jefe de policía haga algo así me resulta simplemente inconcebible”, afirmó.

La niña se declaró culpable y se le impuso un año de libertad condicional, explicó Thompson. A partir de entonces, le costó aún más prestar atención en clase.

“Simplemente se rindió”, añadió su madre.

Thompson explicó que había aceptado que le pusieran las esposas porque, en ese momento, no quería cuestionar el criterio del director. Pero, tras enterarse de lo que había sucedido, se preguntó por qué se había llamado al agente policial para que se ocupara de la situación.

“¿Por qué no pudieron simplemente dejarla en el pasillo, callada, esperando a que yo llegara?”, dijo.

En el pasado, los directores y los profesores solían ocuparse ellos mismos de las faltas de conducta leves. Ahora, dado que cada vez más colegios, como el Central Middle, cuentan con policías en sus pasillos, los educadores pueden recurrir a las fuerzas del orden cuando los alumnos desobedecen, incluso si los niños son pequeños o suponen una amenaza mínima.

Según la legislación estatal, los agentes escolares deben mantenerse al margen de la “disciplina rutinaria de los alumnos”. Sin embargo, la ley no define el término ni detalla las consecuencias en caso de incumplimiento.

“Se supone que los policías están ahí para proteger a los niños de los tiradores”, afirmó Phillip Lyons, decano de la Facultad de Justicia Penal de la Universidad Estatal Sam Houston en Huntsville y ex detective de policía que se ocupaba de casos de menores. “Si no hay tiradores, los policías van a hacer lo que hacen los policías, y eso es arrestar”.

En la escuela secundaria Walsh, en el distrito de Round Rock, cerca de Austin, un subdirector remitió a una madre a los agentes de policía del centro cuando su hija, una alumna de sexto grado, contó que tres chicos le habían golpeado en la cabeza con los puños y con un teléfono. Los chicos, de 11 y 12 años, dieron versiones diferentes de lo ocurrido aquella tarde, según muestran los registros; dos afirmaron que habían estado jugando y otro dijo que había golpeado accidentalmente a la niña con un mono de peluche.

Los tres fueron acusados de un delito menor de agresión, según muestran los expedientes.

“Pensé que nos sentaríamos a hablar, se disculparía y que él tendría que cumplir con un castigo a la hora del almuerzo”, dijo Kimmy Lueders, madre de uno de los niños.

El superintendente del distrito, Hafedh Azaiez, afirmó en una entrevista que el director del colegio debería haber intentado gestionar la situación antes de recurrir a las fuerzas del orden. “No es algo de lo que nos sintamos orgullosos”, dijo.

En algunos distritos, la ampliación de la presencia policial ha ido acompañada de un enfoque más duro ante los comportamientos violentos. Los agentes han detenido a más alumnos por insinuar que podrían hacer daño a alguien. Durante la última década, el número de alumnos de entre 10 y 13 años denunciados por realizar una “amenaza terrorista” se triplicó en todo el estado, hasta superar los 600 al año.

En ocasiones, la intervención de los agentes ha frustrado posibles tiroteos en colegios. El año pasado, la policía detuvo a un joven de 13 años que, según afirmaron, estaba planeando un ataque contra su secundaria en San Antonio.

Pero las simples fanfarronadas de patio o amenazas realizadas aparentemente en broma también pueden llamar la atención de la policía. En el distrito escolar de Wylie, cerca de Dallas, las autoridades del distrito indicaron a los profesores que advirtieran a los alumnos de tercero y cuarto de primaria que, una vez cumplidos los 10 años, podrían ser acusados de un delito por proferir una amenaza sin intención. En el distrito escolar de Hays, a las afueras de Austin, las autoridades distribuyeron un cartel en el que aparecía una fila de chicos con monos naranjas instando a los alumnos a no “tener que arrepentirse de sus amenazas”.

Las amenazas no siempre implicaban violencia masiva. En febrero de 2025, un niño de 12 años con discapacidad intelectual y autismo sufrió una crisis emocional después de que una asistente de su escuela secundaria de Lubbock desenchufara un teléfono del aula que él quería utilizar, según muestran los registros. “Respétame o estás muerta”, le dijo el niño a la asistente.

Un agente de policía escolar llegó a detenerlo. Cuando el niño no obedeció las órdenes del agente, apareció un segundo agente. Los dos tiraron del niño al suelo agarrándolo por la sudadera y lo esposaron, según muestran los informes policiales. Después, el niño quedó aterrorizado por la policía, según contó su madre, Colette James. Evitaba ir a la iglesia a la que acudía su familia porque esta había contratado a agentes para reforzar la seguridad. Durante un tiempo, durmió en la cama de sus padres.

Los funcionarios del distrito escolar de Lubbock-Cooper se negaron a hacer comentarios, alegando las leyes de protección de la privacidad de los alumnos. La asistente, Jennifer Huckabee, declaró a un periodista que se había sentido amenazada porque el chico era más grande que ella.

En otro caso, en Corpus Christi, un niño de 13 años fue remitido a un centro de menores tras gritar “los voy a matar” a unos compañeros que le habían dado una paliza, según contó su madre. Permaneció recluido en un centro de detención juvenil del condado durante casi dos semanas. El juez de menores del condado, Timothy J. McCoy, a veces mantiene recluidos a los menores que profieren amenazas para que reciban asesoramiento y para asegurarse de que no lleven a cabo sus amenazas, explicó.

En una entrevista en su celda, el chico dijo que no había querido lanzar la amenaza literalmente. “Estaba enfadado”, dijo. “No debería haberlo dicho”.

De las docenas de menores que había en el centro aquel día, el más joven tenía 11 años. Algunos de ellos estaban sentados en mesas de cuatro en una zona común, leyendo, trabajando con sus computadoras portátiles o descansando con la cabeza sobre los brazos. Cuando un periodista les preguntó cuántos de ellos estaban allí por incidentes en el colegio, aproximadamente la mitad levantó la mano.

En algunos distritos donde aumentaron las remisiones, estos incrementos reflejan lo que las autoridades consideran un enfoque de amor duro.

En una entrevista el año pasado, Kirby Warnke, jefe del departamento del distrito escolar de Corpus Christi y presidente de la Asociación de Jefes de Policía de los Distritos Escolares de Texas, afirmó que creía que el sistema de justicia juvenil del estado ofrecía a los niños la oportunidad de aprender de sus errores.

“Es un momento de aprendizaje para ellos”, dijo Warnke.

Las remisiones de niños pequeños en su distrito se han más que duplicado en la última década, según muestran los datos estatales. Alcanzaron un máximo histórico de 171 en el curso escolar 2022-23, más que en los distritos de Houston y Dallas, cada uno de los cuales tiene más de cuatro veces tantos alumnos como Corpus Christi.

El distrito escolar de Forney, al este de Dallas, tomó medidas drásticas contra el comportamiento violento y las amenazas cuando creó su propio departamento de policía en 2020, según explicó Joseph Sanders, que en ese momento era el jefe del departamento. El año escolar siguiente, la policía escolar remitió a 42 alumnos de entre 10 y 13 años, más de los que se habían remitido en los seis años anteriores juntos.

“Simplemente marcamos la pauta y la marcamos temprano”, afirmó Sanders, que dejó el distrito en 2024 y ahora entrena a responsables de las fuerzas del orden.

Sin embargo, en otros lugares, los responsables, preocupados por este repunte, tomaron medidas para revertirlo.

Donny Lee, superintendente del distrito escolar de Wichita Falls, en el norte de Texas, dijo que, antes de que lo contrataran en 2022, los agentes escolares “primero detenían a los niños y después preguntaban”.

“Se estaban presentando cargos contra nuestros alumnos de primaria”, señaló.

Contrató a un nuevo jefe que coincidía con él en que las detenciones debían ser el último recurso, y sustituyeron a la mayoría de los agentes. Lee también convocó reuniones periódicas para revisar los datos de las fuerzas del orden.

Los datos muestran que las remisiones se redujeron para los alumnos de todas las edades. En el caso de los menores de 13 años, la cifra anual se redujo a más de la mitad, pasando de unos 100 a 44.

Lee afirmó que el distrito había logrado esos resultados sin ser “blandos” en materia de disciplina. A los alumnos que infringían las normas se les imponían suspensiones dentro del centro o servicios comunitarios y se les ofrecía asesoramiento.

“No nos dedicamos a la gestión del delito y el castigo”, dijo. “Nos dedicamos a la educación”.

Justin Mayo colaboró con reportería. Kitty Bennett, Alain Delaquérière, Georgia Gee, Sheelagh McNeill y Kirsten Noyes colaboraron en la investigación. Este artículo se ha elaborado en colaboración con Big Local News de la Universidad de Stanford y con el apoyo del Fondo para el Periodismo de Investigación.

Producido por Rumsey Taylor.

Connections Coach

A winemaker in Northern California is convinced that a dog once bred to herd sheep in the Scottish Highlands is the ideal pet for our uncertain times.

Credit... Kelsey McClellan for The New York Times

Supported by

By Lauren Markham

Reporting from Boonville, Calif.

The sign affixed to a sandwich board outside a wine shop in tiny Boonville, Calif., was straight to the point: “Puppies inside.” Joshua Korbel, a 43-year-old sound engineer liked wine and puppies both. “And so I put the brakes on and pulled over and parked, and then walked into that tasting room,” he said.

The sign hadn’t lied. More than a dozen puppies raced about the wooden floor and sprawled out on the L-shaped leather couch adjacent to the bar. They resembled short-haired Border collies, with pointed noses and floppy ears, but ranged in color from black and white to brown to an almost heather gray. They were some of the cutest dogs Korbel had ever seen.

They were fox collies, explained Andy DuVigneaud, a winemaker and the shop’s owner, as Korbel took a seat at the bar. Not a known breed — not yet, anyway, or not anymore — but DuVigneaud is out to change that. Because in this dog that arrived in California in 1885, he sees the perfect antidote for all that ails us in 2026. “Us” as in humans, that is, lonely and flailing as we are, and also our dogs, bred for work they no longer do.

The fox collie was a descendant of the McNab shepherd, a popular ranch dog with roots in the Scottish Highlands that had all but gone extinct by the middle of the 20th century. This rare pup was, under no uncertain terms, “the best dog in the world,” DuVigneaud told Korbel. The fox collie can work a ranch and run all day but can also play fetch, hang out in the passenger seat of a car for long drives and relax next to you in bed. Unlike Border collies, say, whose breeding seems to prohibit them from sitting still, fox collies are pros at the art of chill.

With his modest operation, DuVigneaud was working on repopulating the Earth with this perfect creature by breeding it back into being, and doing so, some 150 miles north of Silicon Valley, in perhaps the least technological and most old-school way possible: simply finding the dogs he likes most and mating them for more.

DuVigneaud grew up in the Anderson Valley, a gilded, painterly region of Northern California known for its grapes, orchards and livestock ranches.

He still lives on the remote hillside where he was born in the house his father built, with his partner, nearly two dozen dogs and a few cats. DuVigneaud, 49, resembles something between a hippie and a mad scientist.

As a kid, he said, he knew lots of McNab dogs — a shepherd-collie mix popular among the area’s ranchers. This breed was created by a Scottish immigrant, Alexander McNab, who arrived in California in 1866 and found the region’s shepherd dogs so lacking, according to the Continental Kennel Club, that he later imported a pair of so-called Scotch collies from Scotland.

“Briefly worded, he is the ideal shepherd,” Lulu McNab, Alexander’s daughter, wrote of the Scotch collie in The Overland Review in 1898. The dog is prized, she added, “both in the Old World and the New, as one of the best aids money can procure.”

But not all McNabs were the same, DuVigneaud remembers. As a boy, he heard his neighbors talk about a particular strain of the McNab: dogs that tended to be smaller and shorter haired, often reddish in hue. These were not only the hardest workers but also had the most loyal and calm temperament.

DuVigneaud never forgot this lore. He had always wanted to find one of the fabled McNabs, but, having spent his 30s and 40s running a tasting room and starting a cannabis company, he spent too much time out of town. Covid isolation put a stop to that, and he, like approximately 23 million other Americans who got pets during the early pandemic years, bought a McNab named JJ. She had all the qualities of the mythic strain he had been looking for.

Smitten with JJ, DuVigneaud began to do research on the McNab.

He learned that Andrew McNab journeyed back to Scotland several more times over the years to fetch more Scotch collies, which he began breeding with Australian shepherds and Border collies. He called the mixes McNab shepherds and sold them to ranchers throughout California — back when humans and dogs both had clear-cut jobs to do.

Roughly a hundred years after McNab found his way to Northern California, the McNab was a popular breed recognized by the Continental Kennel Club. It assigns the McNab the highest scores possible for its loyalty, temperament and intelligence. (Top kennel clubs do not recognize the McNab as an official breed.) DuVigneaud is now trying to bring back the original Scotch collie, which he has rebranded the fox collie.

JJ was the key. DuVigneaud decided that JJ was the closest living analogue to the original Scotch collie that Alexander McNab first hauled over from Scotland. DuVigneaud found a neighbor with similar McNab strain and bred the two together. The fox collie was born.

Since first mating JJ in spring 2020, he has bred 16 litters of fox collie puppies, which he figured out how to do via a combination of intuition and online research (he works under the guidance and license of a breeder friend), doing extensive DNA testing to avoid debilitating genetic traits that plague many purebred dogs.

He selects which dogs to breed based on “size and temperament,” he said. Over time, word of the fox collie seems to have spread: DuVigneaud said he had received more than 400 serious inquiries about the dogs.

Korbel, who was living in the Bay Area when he first saw DuVigneaud’s sign, remained enchanted with the fox collie puppies, and made a point to visit them each time he passed through town. DuVigneaud added Korbel to his “hope list,” different from a wait list in that it’s not organized in order of appearance, and is not really a list at all. Rather, it is a collection of pastel index cards with contact information and whatever details the applicants feel pertinent about what they are looking for in a dog (Natalia, age 10: “I want a fluffy puppy. I want a dog who wants to sleep in my room”) or about their lives (Sebastian and Rowan: “We have an apartment in SF, 2 blocks from golden gate park. We’re hikers, love the outdoors, and adore our pets”).

Like the Michelin system, DuVigneaud awards particularly compelling cards one or two stars. He then divides the cards into several zip-top bags based on rank.

DuVigneaud liked Korbel: two stars. He offered him a dog just weeks after they met — almost unheard-of. The dog was the only brown one in the litter, so Korbel named her Morena — Spanish for brunette.

Korbel has no regrets. “She has been, like, the best dog ever,” he said. “Like, I cannot believe how good this puppy is.” When we spoke, she was 4 months old and he had had her for only a few weeks, but she was already fully potty-trained and could stroll with him around San Francisco almost entirely off leash. She even taught herself to do tricks on the bike track at a nearby skate park after an afternoon of people-watching.

I visited DuVigneaud’s home in August, greeted by a raucous chorus of barking — and a skitter of freaked-out cats on the roof. DuVigneaud opened the gate, and fox collies began dashing around the yard, rolling over one another and jumping into his lap. I asked him how many dogs he had. He wasn’t sure. His partner, Cory Lester, took out a utility bill and began writing down names clustered by littermates. She got to 20 before she realized that she had forgotten Sweet Potato. A few minutes later, DuVigneaud called from inside the house. “Did you get Winn-Dixie?”

“Winnieeee!” she cried. She had not. Twenty-two in all.

By most estimates, dogs as we know them have been domesticated for over 15,000 years. It used to be that humans bred dogs to do specialized tasks, like corral sheep in the meadow at sundown.

Now, explained David Howe, an anthropologist focusing on how dogs have shaped human society, we train dogs to redirect these behaviors (teaching a golden retriever to fetch a ball instead of a dead duck, say). Until very recently, “most dogs had a utilitarian working role,” Howe said. “In the modern world, we don’t need them for those roles anymore.” As a result, the dog is in most cases “a technological pet for emotional support.” In the United States, where in 2023 the surgeon general declared loneliness to be a public health concern of epidemic proportions, dogs can supplant the connections we lack from fellow humans — and give us a daily purpose.

For now, DuVigneaud is the only one breeding fox collies. With so many stray and abandoned animals in need of homes — last year, 2.8 million dogs entered U. S. shelters and rescues, according to Shelter Animals Count — DuVigneaud has his share of detractors. He rejects the criticism. “We have too many people,” he said. “Is it unethical to have kids?”

Though organizations like the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals emphatically encourage people to pursue adoption, Jennie Lintz, a senior director for the A. S. P. C. A., acknowledged that “there are people who might want a specific kind of dog for a specific reason” and go to a breeder instead. The group’s position is that those people should find what it calls an ethical breeder — someone who tests for genetic traits, has a list of people who want puppies before the puppies are born and vets the people he sells to. DuVigneaud seems to fit the bill.

DuVigneaud is selling the dogs for $1,000 — though he maintains that he isn’t in it for the money. So why is he doing it, then? His answer has all the high-minded egotism of a would-be Silicon Valley titan. He’s doing it, he says, “to change the world.”

DuVigneaud anticipates that the slim share of the world’s herding and working dogs that are still on the job will soon be replaced by drones or other technologies. With its perfect work-play temperament and devotion to humans, the fox collie, he believes, can save purpose-bred dogs from obsolescence.

To be clear, many breeds originally created to serve have found homes by the millions, where little is expected of them beyond companionship. But unlike the fox collie, those dogs often require enormous amounts of exercise and stimulation to compensate for their lack of work.

He sees his mission as helping people, too. Humans are experiencing our own crisis of purpose with the advent of A. I., and a little unconditional love, like the kind Korbel says he has experienced in the three weeks since taking Morena home, might be just what we need.

When I visited DuVigneaud’s home in August, a forest fire was seething not far away, but was being contained; by the time we got to the tasting room, his truck, as usual, packed full of perfect dogs, we could smell the smoke. The future felt particularly bleak, but at least there were puppies.

Connections Coach

The enmity directed toward Mayor Zohran Mamdani from within the pro-Palestinian movement illustrates the challenge the wider left faces in corralling its insurgents.

Credit... Hilary Swift for The New York Times

Supported by

By Matt FlegenheimerSally Goldenberg and Liam Stack

If pro-Palestinian activists had designed a New York City mayor in a political science lab, they would have strained to do much better than Zohran Mamdani.

He is the Muslim son of a prominent anticolonial scholar whose childhood home often teemed with leading Palestinian American thinkers, primed since his youth in Uganda and post-apartheid South Africa to connect the pain of Palestinians to liberation struggles around the world.

Galvanizing at a microphone and disarming in person, he has helped guide and expand the Democratic Socialists of America as the Palestinian cause has become a defining D. S. A. focus locally and nationally.

His unwavering denunciations of Israel amid a rise in antisemitic hate have unsettled many of New York’s roughly one million Jews, most recently last week when he marked the anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, with a statement that dwelled largely on the suffering of Palestinians.

And yet there the mayor stood on this Oct. 7, a veteran protester being protested, stone-faced but visibly emotional as hundreds of people shouted at him from across a police barricade in Union Square.

“Traitor, traitor, come on out!” the chants echoed, interrupting a peace vigil organized by a progressive Israeli group that had hoped to honor those killed both in Israel and in Gaza. “You sold all your people out!”

Every mayor disappoints his friends in due time. The job is too complicated, the compromises too inevitable.

What is remarkable about this fissure is that the blowback has come over an issue for which the mayor has repeatedly and defiantly expended political capital, risking his standing with more moderate voters to remain in league with activists who are now demanding more from him anyway.

The anger at Mr. Mamdani over a matter so central to his political rise as the plight of Palestinians has doubled as an early test of the wider left’s capacity to corral its agitators, even with an avowed former agitator in charge.

It arrives at a moment when the left generally, and the D. S. A. in particular, is grappling more broadly with how to reconcile its rapid ascent into expanded power with a boisterous, largely hierarchy-averse coalition in which dissent is often encouraged and valorized.

Segments of the movement are debating in real time how much latitude Mr. Mamdani and other elected leaders deserve in areas as varied as policing, housing and comportment toward the Trump administration. And the answers can diverge sharply, sometimes dividing 30-something organizers — relative pragmatists who helped put socialists into office — and college-aged activists who remain skeptical about involving the D. S. A. in electoral politics at all.

Mr. Mamdani’s allies have sought to play down the tensions, especially around Gaza, as the attention-seeking spasms of a fringe faction. Many pro-Palestinian activists have come to the mayor’s defense.

The accusations against him include things that are plainly untrue — like being a Zionist, a term that has become a slur across much of the left as public opinion turns strongly against Israel.

And he is being asked to fulfill an activist wish list unlike any delivered to mayors in the recent past. It includes abolishing the City University of New York Board of Trustees (over investments tied to Israel); intervening in the programming decisions of local synagogues; and halting any military shipments to Israel through the city’s major airports, which the mayor does not control.

Practically, the movement from which Mr. Mamdani emerged is really several, with political goals and strategic instincts that only sometimes overlap.

It is young and socialist and left-of-socialist, and consumed with rent and grocery prices and public transit, but also with anti-Zionism and divestment and the Middle East views of Mr. Mamdani’s police commissioner, Jessica Tisch, who is Jewish and comes from a billionaire family that supports Israel.

The rancor has also coincided with escalating left-wing criticism over Mr. Mamdani’s handling of police affairs after an Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agent shot and wounded a man on Oct. 8 while the man was in a car with his 5-year-old son in Marble Hill, a neighborhood straddling Manhattan and the Bronx.

Taken together, the tumult has reinforced and deepened some knotty conflicts that have, until now, mostly burbled quietly.

Mr. Mamdani is caught between advisers who have privately urged him to promote the pro-Palestinian movement even more forcefully, according to people close to him, and those who think the city is hearing quite enough from its mayor on this subject.

Organizers are balancing a longstanding instinct to hold power to account, even and especially in their own ranks, against a growing recognition that Mr. Mamdani will not (or in some cases cannot) use his power in all the ways they might prefer.

The base is decentralized and strong-willed, a source of its potency and its volatility.

The D. S. A. itself is working to negotiate these disparate impulses internally.

The New York City chapter, with which Mr. Mamdani is closely affiliated, has afforded him some space. “Every force opposed to the democratic socialist project would like to divide the mayor from his organizational base,” Gustavo Gordillo, the chapter’s co-chair, said in a text message.

The national organization, which is generally considered more incendiary, has called for Ms. Tisch’s removal. The New York City chapter has also found itself in the precarious position of talking down the Young Democratic Socialists of America. The Y. D. S. A. initially endorsed the demonstration that disrupted the Oct. 7 vigil at Union Square, which began with a rally at City Hall.

Members from several college chapters participated in the protest, where some attendees chanted in support of Hamas and called for the deaths of Israeli soldiers. But the Y. D. S. A. withdrew its support for the gathering amid pressure from N. Y. C.-D. S. A., according to people familiar with the conversations. N. Y. C.-D. S. A. also issued a statement distancing itself from the protest.

“I think it pained him tremendously to hear the word ‘traitor’ being shouted at him,” Asad Dandia, an activist and historian who is friendly with Mr. Mamdani, said in an interview. “Oct. 7, 2026, and Oct. 8, 2026, were probably the two hardest days of his mayoralty. It’s the first time he’s been confronted with a real crisis that brings him in some tension with the movement. At the same time, he’s very good at responding to crises.”

In a brief interview last week, Mr. Mamdani suggested he understood why emotions were so raw, alluding to violence from Hamas, Israel and ICE.

“I think that people are restive, and so am I,” he said. “I am, frankly, furious.”

In some ways, activists said, Mr. Mamdani has been a victim of his own rhetorical success.

Only a few years ago, it would have been close to unthinkable that someone with Mr. Mamdani’s posture toward Israel could win citywide election in the nation’s ostensible Jewish capital — let alone that his rise might help to affirm an increasingly mainstream disapproval of Israel’s conduct in Gaza.

But the realities of local government, even in a global city, can be bracing.

“Zohran proved you can be elected mayor of New York City with a principled position on Palestine and the genocide, paving the way for this year’s congressional primary winners, who will be closer to the levers of foreign policy,” said Andrew Bard Epstein, a mayoral campaign aide last year and a D. S. A. member, nodding at the success of left-wing candidates endorsed by Mr. Mamdani in House primaries. “But public opinion barely steers domestic policy, let alone empire.”

Nerdeen Kiswani, a founder of Within Our Lifetime, a pro-Palestinian group that endorsed the protest that marched to Union Square, suggested that anyone asking the movement to give the mayor grace was misunderstanding the purpose of advocacy.

“People want to remind him of why we voted for him and why we made him mayor to begin with,” Ms. Kiswani said. “It feels like a lot of people are like, ‘Oh, well, you know, we got someone in power. We don’t need to keep looking at what’s happening.’”

She lamented that Mr. Mamdani “issues so much condemnation when it comes to any slight, any perceived slight even, against folks in Jewish and Zionist communities” while he “barely says a whisper when it comes to things like this on Palestine anymore.”

Jewish leaders reject this assessment, to put it mildly, and they say the mayor’s statement on Oct. 7 was an example of why.

“I think the job of all leaders is to try and bring people together and try and bring down the temperature,” said Mark Levine, the city comptroller. “And on that front, I’m not sure that statement met that standard.”

At minimum, Mr. Mamdani’s loyalists and his Israel-defending detractors seem to agree on one thing.

“We are indeed living in a time of artificial intelligence,” said Amit Singh Bagga, a Democratic strategist who served in the administrations of Mayor Bill de Blasio and Gov. Kathy Hochul, “for that’s what’s required to think that Mayor Mamdani has somehow abandoned the Palestinian cause.”

Matt Flegenheimer is a correspondent for The Times focusing on in-depth profiles of powerful figures.

Sally Goldenberg is a Times reporter covering New York City politics and government.

Liam Stack is a Times reporter who covers the culture and politics of the New York City region.

Trump Aides Admit the House Is a Lost Cause

Wired October 14, 2026

Trump White House aides see almost no paths to Republicans keeping control of the House in the midterm elections and are more focused on redoubling their efforts to save the Senate majority.

That has been the takeaway for officials in GOP groups who have been discussing the state of play with White House aides in recent weeks, according to three sources familiar with the situation.

It all comes as the White House moves into damage-control mode after contemplating for the first time earlier this month, as Inner Loop previously reported, that Republicans could possibly lose both chambers of Congress.

The general expectation is that the House has become a lost cause. Races that Republican congressional leadership once thought they could flip in order to offset Democratic gains are no longer considered attainable.

The Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Speaker Mike Johnson, has now pulled ad buys in Democratic districts in Michigan and Ohio they were hoping to flip, as well as in the Republican seat being vacated in Nebraska by the retiring Don Bacon. The fund also started canceling remaining ad reservations in two House races where Republicans are seeking reelection in New Jersey and Iowa.

White House aides have shifted their focus to pushing an all-out defense of the Senate majority, which is also looking problematic but to a lesser degree than the House, the sources say. (Polling models and prediction markets agree.)

The aides see the Senate as still in play in large part because early returns for mail ballots have been relatively strong and comparable to 2024 presidential election levels in key Senate battleground states, sources say.

Trump officials at MAGA Inc. have also privately discussed how if Republicans can win some combination of senate seats in Alaska, Iowa, and Ohio, that would form a firewall that complicates Democrats' path to snatching control of the Senate.

Still, Trump officials appear to have conceded they are unlikely to win in North Carolina. Senate Republicans’ campaign arm has paused ad spending in North Carolina since the start of October, mirroring pullbacks by other outside groups.

“President Trump is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in both the House and Senate,” says White House spokesperson Liz Huston in a statement.

The state of play—retreating from a state like North Carolina, where Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair is on the ballot—would have been unthinkable just a few months ago.

But it speaks to the torrid political climate for Republicans heading into the last stretch of the midterm cycle, which appears to worsen by the week as high gas and living prices caused by the Iran war remain sticky in voters' minds.

With 20 days until the election, sources say, Trump officials are looking to get maximum turnout from the MAGA base in November, rather than trying to capture swing voters who polls show are not breaking for Republicans.

"Republicans remain laser focused on winning and protecting and expanding President Trump's majorities,” says Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassare in a statement. “We're thinking outside the box to fight the typical midterm precedent.”

The effort has manifested in a direct voter outreach play with the president crisscrossing the country to reach out directly to his supporters, showing up at rallies in states that should have been reliably Republican.

Trump started the week by hitting the trail in Ohio, where Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown has been polling consistently ahead of Republican Jon Husted, who has weathered negative ads branding him as "the face of data centers."

On Tuesday, the president flew to Wasilla, Alaska—once the home of former governor and vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin—to help the Republican Senate incumbent Dan Sullivan, who has been trailing Democrat Mary Peltola.

And after stumping in Arizona and Kentucky later this week, Trump is set to host a $1 million-per-plate fundraiser dinner for MAGA Inc. at his Mar-a-Lago club, replenishing a war chest that is being emptied at an increasing rate.

Trump has remained steadfast in his belief that he can drive his supporters to vote in November if he hits the trail, as he did in the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections, a person familiar with his thinking tells Inner Loop.

But Trump, whose polling continues to be among the worst on record for any president, is not always wanted at rallies. To date, the president has not done a rally in Iowa with Republican candidate Ashley Hinson, who recently began to buck the president and called for measures that would help end the Iran war altogether.

AI Came for Math. Now It’s Chasing the Rest of Science

Wired October 14, 2026

Last week, I attended a talk at MIT by Neil Thompson, who studies progress in computing and artificial intelligence. Over the course of just half an hour, Thompson made a convincing case that several scientific fields are about to be upended by AI.

As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down.

“Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson.

Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun, a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them.

Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online.

The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry.

In September, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes, which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU—who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress.

OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI, warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer.

As with math, Thompson says, we should expect advances in other areas to have both positive and negative effects. He notes that theoretical advances sometimes drive practical advances in science and suggests that greater use of AI may mean that more progress happens this way.

Some prominent AI researchers have already founded new labs focused on AI for science, and the big AI labs are all ramping up scientific research. These efforts explore how AI could be empowered to conduct real experiments alongside theoretical analysis. AI may mean that theorists are no longer required to solve key problems, but the researchers say that doesn’t mean that experts won’t be needed to make sense of solutions and to make sure they’re sound.

“We are still going to need people to generate good ideas to connect the dots,” says Manso. He adds that for very complex problems, it’s possible that AI might make mistakes. (OpenAI, in fact, withdrew several solutions in its latest dataset post-publication.) “We also need ways to verify what was done, because it's very easy for a model to tell you ‘this is the right answer,’ and when you look at the entire solution, you start to see maybe it is not.”

Dune: Part Three’s Cowriter Has a New Comic on the Way

Wired October 14, 2026

Brian K. Vaughan would like to apologize. He knows everyone is dying for details about Dune: Part Three, which he cowrote with director Denis Villeneuve, but his lips are pretty sealed until December 18 when the film finally hits theaters.

“Sorry to be coy,” he says as we’re about to leave the New York coffee shop where we’ve been chatting. “I hope the day will come where I’m able to say much, much more. It was truly so awesome. I can’t believe it happened.”

Vaughan is in the city for New York Comic Con, but not to talk about Dune. Ostensibly, he came to the convention to talk about Paper Girls, the comic he created with Cliff Chiang that was turned into a 2022 Amazon Prime Video series. During the Paper Girls panel, however, the pair announced that they’re working on a new comic, Roam, a superhero sci-fi series set to come out in February of next year.

Roam, Vaughan tells me, came from a deep desire to work with Chiang again. They’d considered doing a short eight-page story or maybe a one-shot, but eventually they said “Fuck it. Let’s do an ongoing series.”

Vaughan has the kind of career writers of a certain ilk would kill for. He started working on comics in the 1990s and has been the pen behind favorites like Saga, Y: The Last Man, and Marvel’s Runaways. (Those last two got turned into TV series; the outlier, Saga, is a story people have wanted to see adapted for years.) He also served as a writer on Lost and created CBS’s adaptation of Stephen King’s Under the Dome.

Still, his heart remains in comics. “I think sometimes people are like, ‘Oh, are you just going to sell out, Vaughan? Are you just going to go to Hollywood full-time?’” he says. “But I’m only able to do work in Hollywood because I have comics.”

Here, he speaks about Roam, his worries about AI, and maybe a little bit about Dune: Part Three as well.

On Roam, his forthcoming comic with Cliff Chiang:

It's completely unlike Paper Girls, completely unlike anything I've ever done. It’s set in the distant, distant future. The logline, as it were, is that in the future, everyone will get to be a superhero, but only while they're young. We're trying not to reveal too much more than that.

I remember seeing The Matrix, and having no idea what the fuck it was gonna be about. That was such a delight. So we're trying to do that here. I've been doing this for 31 years. I started when I was a teenager. I have a Spider-Man story here and there. I did a little Batman, and Ex Machina was my sci-fi political comic that sort of deconstructed the superhero. But this is certainly my first true superhero book.

On his fears about AI impacting comics, film, and TV:

It's terrifying. My friends who work in previsualization and as storyboard artists, these jobs are going away. I've heard about editors going away as well. Show business is a business, first and foremost. I’m lucky to sort of have been grandfathered in. I think there will always be people who are interested in bespoke human-made stories. But the future is terrifying and unknowable, and coming at us very, very quickly.

I’m heartened by the fact I've got two teenagers who are so disgusted by AI and grossed out if they ever hear I used it—and I’ve certainly never used it for anything creative. But I do think we're getting pretty close to the day that someone could be like, “I'm tired of waiting for the next issue. Give me the next issue of Saga.” That's when you get to the point of, do you just want content, something that's a distraction?

In Roam there's an element of this as well; AI is a component in the story. So, it's something I guess I need to write about with my human meat machine to process, but I'm in the middle of thinking about it, as you are, every day.

OK, a little bit about Dune: Part Three, which he has seen:

I can't say very much other than it’s a tremendous, insane, ridiculous honor to be involved with it, and my contributions are modest. Denis’ true cowriter on this is Frank Herbert. The novel is the star. And it's obviously the greatest cast and crew ever assembled. It's a fucking beautiful movie. It's my favorite of the three. which I can say with genuine humility. I can't say anything other than it's just as wonderful as you can imagine.

I got special thanks in the first movie. I was doing a tiny amount of consulting. I was working at Legendary [the media company that owns the rights to Dune] at the time, and they just invited me in to see an early cut, which was as fantastic as the finished product. But I just ended up talking to Denis, honestly. Never before has a director been that talented, also that decent and warm as a human being. I wasn't anticipating getting this call at the beginning of three, but it's obviously a call I could not refuse.

I should probably just be discreet at this point. The movie doesn't need me to promote it. I'm reluctant to do anything that makes me sound more important to this process.

On the future of Hollywood:

I am a small worker in the world of Hollywood. It is changing so rapidly that who knows what it's gonna be like tomorrow, six months from now.

But again, I've got teenagers and I see how delighted they were by Backrooms, by Obsession. It feels like Gen X has been force-feeding them a lot of my childhood stories that we have gussied up, and they are clearly hungry for something new.

On why he doesn’t write adaptations of his own comics:

I've taken stabs at it in the past. Richard Price, the novelist, I once heard him say in response to “Why don't you adapt your own stuff more?” that adapting your own work is like being a dentist and giving yourself a root canal. Just because you can do it, doesn't mean you should. Let some other motherfucker handle that. I believe those were Mr. Price's words.

It's been constructive and a thrill to adapt other people, and I like getting to watch other people adapt me, but I've also been doing a lot of it for the last decade, where it feels like I've either been adapting or being adapted. I think that was part of the siren song of Roam. It’s time to break some new ground.

Denis says that to adapt something you love is to do violence to it. When I've been adapted, that has always been what I've told people. It is much more important for this to be good than to be faithful. He's a master of cinema, and cinema is rarely about people sitting in a room having dialog. How do you transliterate this to cinema? That's an alchemy that I don't understand. He's just unparalleled at that.

On Lost and why writing for commercial breaks was a challenge:

I love my prestige drama without commercials, but there was a degree of difficulty working on Lost and having a cliff-hanger five times an episode. To have that was such a challenge and so rewarding when you were able to pull it off. Can you write something where people are like, “OK, I'll just wet my pants. I cannot risk not coming back [before the break is over].”
